Major themes include source localization from incomplete cascades; recovery of hidden network structures and infection probabilities; epidemic cost, stability, containment, and resilience; and influence maximization for marketing, recruitment, conservation, and social advertising.

Typical methods combine probabilistic diffusion models—including independent cascade, SIS/SI, linear threshold, continuous-time Markov chains, and complex contagion—with graph-theoretic analysis. Optimization is central: submodular and adaptive-greedy algorithms, community-based heuristics, mixed-integer programming, particle-swarm optimization, and resource-allocation formulations select seeds, interventions, prices, or network modifications. Jordan centers, covering algorithms, message passing, random-matrix theory, random walks, sampling, and diffusion-based signal metrics provide analytical and computational tools.

Recent directions emphasize realism and limited information. Studies address temporal, adaptive, and growing networks; myopic or online feedback; partial observations and aggregate cascades; non-submodular influence; and continuous-time dynamics. Applications increasingly distinguish influence from adoption, incorporate online activities and incentives, and use diffusion to recruit workers or predict content popularity. Emerging learning approaches include optimization-based inference and contrastive training of cascade models using temporal and textual features.

c70a89353954549a2ac1ee32ef17942d13697da2.text:
## Community Detection in Complex, Dynamic, and Multilayer Networks

This community centers on identifying, evaluating, and interpreting cohesive groups in complex networks. Major themes include defining community quality—especially for overlapping, fuzzy, and multilayer partitions—understanding detectability and resolution limits, and distinguishing core, peripheral, bridge, and low-degree nodes. Applications span social, wireless, web-service, bibliometric, biological, dating, and image networks, including peer influence, risky behavior, adoption, and churn.

Typical methods include modularity and multislice modularity optimization, label propagation, density-based clustering with manifold learning, clique percolation, local spectral and personalized-PageRank methods, and locally biased dynamics. Probabilistic approaches use generative multilayer models, variational Bayes, latent trees, and survival or regression models for behavioral analysis. Evaluation increasingly uses multiple criteria, Pareto frontiers, conductance, spectral analysis, and algorithm-selection frameworks rather than a single modularity score.

Recent trends emphasize scalable and localized detection for very large graphs; overlapping, attributed, weighted, multiplex, and heterogeneous communities; dynamic visualization and time-varying prediction; debiasing against the exclusion of weakly connected nodes; and principled treatment of uncertainty, stability, and shared versus layer-specific structure.

00c9f14eaff62e6274da6b994c2d59baa9a9682c.text:
**Topic Modeling and Social Media Intelligence**

This community centers on extracting latent structure, events, interests, and actionable knowledge from large, dynamic digital collections. A major theme is topic modeling: extensions of LDA and related probabilistic models address hypertext links, temporal birth/death and evolution of topics, clustered and scalable learning, multi-grain review aspects, scientific-article bundling, and creative cross-domain discovery. Topic representations also support visualization, summarization, biomedical hypothesis generation, and semantic retrieval.

A second strong theme is social-media analytics. Studies detect and summarize real-world events from Twitter and geo-tagged streams, identify bursty spatial regions and collective action, model popularity and revisits, infer user interests, analyze retweets and misinformation, and support tourism, libraries, disaster response, and environmental warning. Spatial, temporal, and network structure are repeatedly combined with text.

Typical methods include probabilistic topic models, neural networks and character embeddings, machine learning ranking and clustering, ontology similarity with fuzzy logic, statistical burst and power-law analysis, information extraction, visualization, and mathematical propagation models. Evaluation uses large-scale datasets, multilingual comparisons, surveys, expert or historical validation, and operational case studies.

Recent work trends toward real-time processing, scalable/parallel modeling, multimodal and geo-temporal analysis, automated validation, and decision-support applications.

0d6822ac3acdd6c81a88a23f2abb051a518c2a62.text:
### Scalable Semantic Retrieval and Data Processing

This community spans three connected themes. First, it develops text clustering and classification, including probabilistic mixture models, k-nearest-neighbor and k-medoids methods, association-rule pruning, hyperonymization, genetic feature selection, ontology-aware search, opinion-spam detection, and topic-diversity estimation. User-guided clustering and quality-aware subject indexing emphasize controllability and reliable annotations.

Second, substantial work targets mathematical information services. Systems combine textual and formula queries, compare presentation- and content-based retrieval, extract identifier definitions and namespaces, and provide repositories, faceted interfaces, and accessible MathML rendering. NLP techniques such as part-of-speech tagging, pattern matching, canonicalization, and semantic enrichment are adapted to mathematical notation.

Third, the community studies scalable data infrastructure and formal data models. Accumulo, D4M, Graphulo, BigSparse, associative arrays, and the BigDAWG polystore support high-throughput ingest and graph analytics across heterogeneous stores. Relational lattices, relational semantics, and Lara provide algebraic foundations for query transformation and cross-system computation. Query optimization and cloud resource pricing address cost and uncertain performance.

Recent directions emphasize distributed and external-memory processing, GraphBLAS-style kernels, dynamic scaling with feedback control or learning, probabilistic performance guarantees, deep quality estimation, and semantic rather than purely lexical retrieval.

cf97df3b4cda6025e112eb3d936483ed565b0083.text:
## Multilayer Social Networks and Dynamic Community Intelligence

This community centers on modeling and analyzing social systems as multilayer or multiplex networks, where online, offline, semantic, professional, and interaction ties coexist. Core themes include multilayer centrality, degree and reciprocity measures, homophily, layer entanglement, missing-data effects, identity integration across platforms, and unified combinatorial models.

A major strand studies community structure and evolution. Methods include GED and SGCI for detecting group changes, dynamic Louvain and Infomap variants, modularity maximization, stochastic block models, and prediction from historical evolution chains. Related work examines influential bloggers, information-cascade seed selection, epidemic thresholds, viral campaigns, and diffusion using branching, independent-cascade, spectral, and multiplex dynamical models.

Typical empirical resources include Facebook, Twitter, blogs, email, Wikipedia, browse logs, mobile-phone proximity and mobility data, student networks, and cross-platform identity datasets. Computational approaches also include PageRank with evolving teleportation, heterogeneous network sampling, synthetic graph generation, topic modeling, sentiment classification, association-rule mining, and machine-learning-based user matching.

Recent directions emphasize dynamic and scalable analysis, cross-device and cross-platform identity, privacy-aware or synthetic data, and applications to misinformation, recommendations, disease containment, HR, and personalized information campaigns.

36b541291293cf09bbce40ad6f38b36a56e47307.text:
## Online Social Networks: Structure, Diffusion, and Societal Impact

This community studies online social networks as dynamic systems for interaction, information diffusion, influence, and risk. Major themes include community structure and network assembly; strong and weak ties, homophily, diversity, and gender; anomaly, malicious-URL, privacy, and systemic-risk detection; and the spread and popularity of memes, videos, reviews, rumors, and scholarly ideas. Applications include political discussion, disaster response, emergency-aid retrieval, sports-event sensing, suicide ideation, financial guarantee networks, and criminal-network investigation.

Typical methods combine graph analytics—centrality, pair-dependency, modularity-based community detection, structural-balance modeling, vulnerability indices, and cascade analysis—with large-scale platform data. Researchers use statistical and dynamical models, including rumor-propagation models, popularity-growth models, Hawkes processes, randomized baselines, and early trend prediction. Machine learning, NLP, topic modeling, visual-meme detection, multimodal analysis, and visual analytics support classification, ranking, and prediction.

Recent directions emphasize temporal and heterogeneous networks, external drivers such as mass media and incentives, indirect interactions through shared locations, and richer outcome measures such as engagement rather than views. The community also increasingly integrates multimodal disaster data, content-agnostic explanations of popularity, interpretable privacy controls, and interventions for steering diffusion or managing network risk.

413d58bd1d28260dda2e474f75b803d7c1fe34d6.text:
### Scholarly Impact, Discovery, and Digital Communication

This community studies how scholarly work is disseminated, discovered, evaluated, and used across journals, books, repositories, libraries, and social platforms. Major themes include validating altmetrics against peer assessments and citations; measuring readership, downloads, loans, tweets, Mendeley saves, hyperlinks, and online reviews; and assessing open-access, self-archiving, and arXiv effects on visibility and citation impact. Other work addresses book and publisher evaluation, venue and article recommendation, conference classification, and reviewer–paper matching.

Typical methods combine large bibliographic and usage datasets from Web of Science, Scopus, Book Citation Index, F1000Prime, Altmetric, Mendeley, Twitter, arXiv, ADS, and library systems. Analyses use correlation, regression, principal-component and factor analysis, citation and download distributions, expert interviews, visualization, machine learning, and integer programming. Systems also employ text search, OCR correction, reference matching, and hyperlink classification.

Recent trends emphasize heterogeneous and potentially dependent altmetric data, rapid indicators based on online activity, and richer content-level evaluation of books and papers. Repositories and open-access platforms increasingly function as central communication and discovery infrastructures, while recommender systems and automated tools address information overload and peer-review management.

3d99abdf9a985bbf02ddd656b00d29345c6fdf82.text:
### Bibliometrics, Research Evaluation, and Academic Inequality

This community centers on measuring scientific performance and understanding the institutional and social factors shaping it. A major theme is the evaluation of researchers, universities, and national systems through productivity, citations, field-standardized impact, FSS, MNCS, journal impact factor, and alternative impact measures. Many studies critically examine Italian assessment exercises, especially VQR, highlighting ranking distortions, publication-selection effects, counting methods, author-order contributions, and the appropriate evaluation period.

A second theme concerns inequality and stratification. Research addresses gender differences in productivity, recruitment, collaboration, and university rankings; age, seniority, nepotism, and the North–South divide; and the persistence of “top scientist” status. Collaboration is examined through co-authorship, internationalization, interdisciplinarity, academic rank, and editorial-board networks.

Typical methods include large-scale bibliometric datasets from Web of Science and Google Scholar, citation and co-authorship analysis, field normalization, regression and quantile regression, Granger causality, stochastic models, network analysis, distributional statistics, clustering, and uncertainty visualization with funnel plots.

Recent directions emphasize probabilistic rather than deterministic evaluation, fairness across fields and demographic groups, robust institutional comparisons, and more nuanced accounting for authorship and collaboration. Newer work also considers publication recommendation data limitations and systematic arguments for alternative counting methods.

d8c1e49de7a87f168b356372a039e175c16341ab.text:
**Data Integration, Quality, and Scalable Entity Resolution**

This community focuses on making heterogeneous, noisy, and conflicting data usable. Major themes include entity resolution and record linkage, entity consolidation into “golden records,” multi-source data fusion and truth discovery, and cleaning scholarly, Web, governmental, and open-platform data. Integrity constraints—including functional, order, and ontology dependencies—support error detection, data exchange, and semantic validation.

Typical methods combine blocking and similarity search (locality-sensitive hashing, partitioning, string-edit joins, and source-code indexing), probabilistic and graph-based matching, distributed representations such as DeepER and Column2Vec, and combinatorial optimization for one-to-one or collective matching. Truth-discovery models estimate source reliability, account for copying and dependence, and can represent multiple truths. Crowds are used for labeling, route evaluation, worker assessment, and human–machine quality control, with explicit cost, latency, precision, recall, and confidence guarantees.

Other work addresses wrapper robustness, Web-scale extraction, pattern and dependency discovery, uncertainty in aggregates and fact-checking, and scalable aggregation.

Recent directions emphasize deep and representation-learning approaches, collective and distributed matching at massive scale, source-dependence-aware fusion, prediction-based spatial task assignment, and tighter integration of automation with targeted human judgment.

c508ac8648fb93010a69dd4b1554b7b682f41a57.text:
## Social Media Communities, Polarization, and Information Integrity

This community focuses on how online social networks shape political behavior, collective narratives, misinformation, and security. Major themes include polarized communities and echo chambers; political preference, voting, and demographic inference; fake news, rumors, conspiracy theories, and disinformation campaigns; and malicious activity such as bots, spam, extremist content, Sybil devices, and unsafe applications. Several studies also address search bias, information verification, and the societal effects of social platforms.

Typical methods combine large-scale Twitter, Facebook, YouTube, and Gab datasets with network analysis, community detection, structural-balance and signed-graph models, propagation analysis, and temporal modeling. Machine-learning approaches include nonnegative matrix factorization, sparse learning, latent Dirichlet allocation, regression, semi-supervised and real-time classification, embeddings, image-based demographic inference, and metadata/network/temporal feature models. Surveys, user studies, and simulations complement computational analysis.

Recent work increasingly examines cross-platform and coordinated influence operations, including Russia-sponsored content, Italian election disinformation, extremist adoption, autogenerated tweets, and misinformation verification. Other emerging directions include intervention-oriented systems—crowd-signal fact checking, targeted health bots, rumor spreading—and privacy, resilience, and decentralized search.

c9431770fc0167c08dee44e2f0c88ce598e7abfa.text:
## Computational Social Sensing for Social and Urban Issues

This community applies large-scale social-media analysis to public health, food culture, politics, mobility, and urban resilience. A central theme is using user-generated content to characterize collective behavior and information ecosystems: Instagram food imagery reveals globally shared preferences, while Twitter discourse exposes information sources and needs surrounding obesity and diabetes. Political hashtags are examined as indicators of campaigning, news circulation, and online communities during India’s 2019 Lok Sabha elections.

Typical methods include collecting millions of posts, analyzing hashtags and textual content, identifying frequently cited information sources, and comparing patterns across countries or topics. Geospatial inference from tweet text supports fine-grained road-traffic monitoring, addressing the scarcity of explicitly geolocated tweets. For cities, the work also evaluates how urban resilience can be conceptualized and quantified through indices, linking institutional initiatives with academic measurement.

Recent trends emphasize computational social science at substantial scale, near-real-time monitoring, geographic grounding, and application to societal challenges. At the same time, the studies critically assess the quality, limitations, and possible consequences of online representations—from unhealthy food ideals and unreliable health information to the ambiguity of resilience metrics and the interpretation of political hashtags.

61178456727c05ae844d62ebcec6cd280c7e79e5.text:
## Recommender Systems: Personalization, Robustness, and Diversity

This community centers on improving recommender systems beyond basic collaborative filtering. Major themes include combining long-term preferences with short-term sequential behavior; session- and inter-session recommendation; playlist, news, music-event, educational, and advertising applications; and addressing cold start, sparse feedback, and long-tail items.

Typical methods include matrix factorization, slope-one predictors, neighborhood models, Markov chains, context trees, co-clustering, metric learning, ontologies, and hybrid content–collaborative approaches. Neural methods are prominent, including variational autoencoders, nonlinear user–item models, recurrent networks, factorization-machine architectures such as DeepFM, and joint deep feature/interaction models. Content signals increasingly include text, tags, images, audio, video, and multimodal representations.

A second research strand addresses system quality and societal effects: popularity bias, recommendation diversity, filter bubbles, fraudulent reviews, noisy ratings, reputation, and social influence. Personalized re-ranking, determinantal point processes, signed-network ranking, and iterative reputation estimation are used to improve fairness, robustness, interpretability, or coverage.

Recent directions emphasize neural and reinforcement-learning approaches, modeling mixtures of user interests, learning with missing modalities, fast large-scale inference, and optimizing multiple objectives such as advertising revenue alongside user experience.

7a473552706a3e9f2f4046112c950d125fc048c4.text:
## Social Media, Spatial Intelligence, and Human Behavior

This community studies how user-generated and social-network data can reveal, predict, and shape human behavior across physical and digital spaces. Major themes include inferring locations and mobility from Twitter, Reddit, Weibo, Flickr, and mobile records; reconstructing urban regions, boundaries, neighborhoods, and visited-place networks; and understanding group colocation, event scheduling, and travel patterns. Other work applies social data to political behavior, sports outcomes, business-site selection, ratings, promotions, and emotional experiences of urban parks, routes, smells, and sounds.

Typical methods combine natural-language processing, sentiment and semantic analysis, machine-learning classifiers, convolutional neural networks, Gaussian mixture models, low-rank approximation, density-based spatial clustering, and graph representations. Researchers also aggregate social signals for forecasting, extract latent features and influence patterns, and use probabilistic approaches to represent qualitative geospatial information. Large-scale mobility studies quantify destinations, commuting, spatial interaction, and temporal activity, often with population-synthesis bias correction and independent survey validation.

Recent trends emphasize geolocation without explicit geotags, confidence calibration and standardized evaluation, scalable distributed analysis, multimodal urban sensing, and richer behavioral prediction. The work increasingly addresses limitations of social-media data through bias modification, out-of-sample validation, selective digital traces, and network-aware modeling.

f1d10232405d2ba9d4b58a2ac114fe4f554f73da.text:
## RDF and Graph Querying: Optimization, Semantics, and Usability

This community focuses on managing, querying, and validating RDF and broader graph data. A major theme is SPARQL foundations and performance: algebraic and multiset semantics, complexity analysis, query rewriting, OPTIONAL/left-outer-join optimization, runtime and partition-based planning, entailment under OWL, provenance, preferences, and hybrid SPARQL–keyword search.

Federated Linked Data is another central area. Studies address source selection, heuristic query reordering, replicated fragments, heterogeneous Web resources, and large-scale deployments such as Bio2RDF. Graph querying extends beyond RDF through Gremlin traversal, SPARQL-to-Gremlin translation, regular and context-free path queries, property-graph type systems, and graph traversal frameworks over relational databases.

Typical methods include formal semantics and complexity proofs, algebraic rewrites, cost and cardinality-aware optimization, indexes and summary graphs, incremental evaluation, graph partitioning, and empirical benchmarking. Schema and quality concerns are addressed through relational-to-RDF mappings, RDF descriptions, incomplete-information semantics, ShEx validation, XML schema learning, and unordered regular expressions.

Recent directions emphasize interoperability between RDF and property graphs, usability for non-expert users through example-based and similarity search, response-time-bounded top-*k* querying, provenance and annotations, analytical RDF data cubes, and systematic workload and geospatial benchmarks.

018efa81eaf5260e852f6c17b54a80e8e7654ddb.text:
## Learning to Rank and Enrich Search

This community centers on information retrieval, ranking, and search applications across web, email, e-commerce, mobile apps, datasets, bibliographic networks, and personal memories. Major themes include improving relevance through query expansion, intent and entity understanding, document and passage retrieval, expert and aspect recommendation, and content-quality or spam detection. Non-factoid question answering and answer presentation form a substantial application area.

Typical methods combine supervised learning-to-rank with neural representation learning. DeepRank models relevance through local evidence detection, local scoring, and aggregation; BERT-based monoBERT and duoBERT support multi-stage pointwise and pairwise reranking. Other work uses word2vec/query2vec, locally trained embeddings, knowledge-enriched entity representations, kernels, convolutional networks, multitask learning, and bipartite ranking. Classical and scalable approaches remain important, including probabilistic ranking, hashing, signatures, clustering, graph models, and active learning.

Recent directions emphasize pretrained language models for ranking and question answering, particularly under passage-length and data constraints; dynamic, temporal, and event-aware retrieval; heterogeneous-network and web-knowledge integration; and unified search across apps and data sources. The community also increasingly addresses practical deployment concerns—latency, massive-scale similarity search, continuous review, online evaluation, and reliability—alongside interpretability, post-hoc explanations, and user interaction with answers.

63e2218d6e232d2184676ffe5efd8438eb74fa87.text:
## Graph Learning for Dynamic and Heterogeneous Networks

This community studies methods for representing, modeling, searching, and mining complex networks, especially social, information, knowledge, and temporal graphs. Major themes include network representation learning and embedding evaluation; community detection and clustering; link prediction and relationship formation; graph similarity search; and structural analysis of motifs, triangles, convexity, centrality, and clustering.

Dynamic-network research models evolving edges and communities using temporal event graphs, dynamic stochastic blockmodels, latent-space generative models, continuous-time prediction, and temporally robust representations. Heterogeneous and multi-relational settings are addressed through metapaths, cross-modal embeddings, predicate-path mining, and structural representations that preserve triangular and parallelogram patterns.

Typical methods combine probabilistic graphical models, random walks and Markov chains, local structural indices, random forests, neural networks, deep embeddings, and MapReduce or distributed external-memory algorithms. Applications include fact checking, entity normalization, urban dynamics, fraud and insider-trading detection, privacy prediction, criminal and covert networks, and team recommendation.

Recent trends emphasize neural and deep representation learning, dynamic and continuous-time modeling, uncertainty-aware inference, scalable graph generation and sampling, and stronger benchmarking. Research also increasingly combines graph structure with text, knowledge bases, behavioral signals, and multimodal information.

aa21ef319f8644b3fb3610f6304c1eee04d86086.text:
## Dynamic Networks, Scalable Queries, and Temporal Influence

This community centers on modeling and analyzing large, evolving networks. A major theme is temporal and multilayer structure: stream graphs, link streams, time-varying graphs, and temporal quantities represent interactions whose nodes, edges, layers, and attributes change over time. Studies develop temporal distances, foremost and fastest journeys, temporal betweenness, time centrality, density, clustering, and layer centralities, with applications to hospitals, mailing lists, knowledge mobilization, scientific communities, narratives, and recommender systems.

A second strong theme is efficient graph querying. Numerous works build indexes, labels, sketches, and oracles for reachability, bounded or regular reachability, shortest distances, shortest paths, and temporal paths. Techniques include landmark and pruned landmark labeling, hop doubling, interval labeling, independent-set labeling, hub acceleration, hierarchical/distribution labeling, pruning, and distributed or vertex-centric computation. Dynamic indexes and graph window analytics address evolving graphs and localized structural neighborhoods.

Other work studies information diffusion, dynamic monopolies, opinion spreading, contagion, trust-aware recommendation, and media influence.

Typical methods combine graph algorithms, preprocessing with theoretical size/time guarantees, semiring and algebraic formulations, scalable parallel or distributed execution, and empirical evaluation on social, information, transportation, communication, and interaction data. Overall, the research trends from static graphs toward temporal, multilayer, dynamic, and application-aware analysis while emphasizing real-time scalability.

3828b59d51a47c0814f64f5e893e350e127db854.text:
### Durable, Semantic Archives for Evolving Web and Scholarly Data

This community studies how to preserve, represent, discover, and analyze digital objects whose meaning and value depend on context, relationships, and time. Major themes include digital-object repositories and life-cycle modeling; preservation of web pages, linked datasets, scholarly artifacts, and social-media content; and interoperability through RDF, Linked Data, OAIS, MPEG-21, provenance vocabularies, and annotation models.

Typical methods combine modular repository architectures, persistent identifiers, aggregation and versioning models, semantic layers, SPARQL and temporal query languages, and machine-readable metadata. Researchers also use large longitudinal collections—including the Internet Archive, Archive-It, Twitter, Wikipedia, and Delicious—together with crawling, link analysis, entity linking, supervised classification, and retrieval experiments. Studies evaluate archive completeness, resource disappearance, annotation orphaning, timestamps, titles, popularity, and collection topicality.

Recent work increasingly addresses evolving and “born-digital” materials: fresh web collection driven by social signals, temporal knowledge graphs, historical linked data, nanopublications, formal scientific claims, and scholarly objects neglected by conventional archiving. Other trends emphasize user-facing exploration, such as ranking archived documents for structured queries, detecting breaking news, recovering missing pages, and exposing large annotated corpora. Persistent challenges remain interoperability, data quality, provenance, trustworthy time representation, and scalable access to heterogeneous archives.

ee473fc44fab409a5fa90cd670781a327d169a57.text:
### Principles and Systems for Intelligent Data Management

This community centers on making relational and distributed data processing faster, more scalable, and easier to use. Core themes include query optimization—especially join ordering, cardinality and cost estimation, index design, and transaction execution—and efficient parallel evaluation of conjunctive queries under communication, skew, and correctness constraints. Graph analytics is repeatedly recast as relational joins or SQL, supported by systems such as Vertica, EmptyHeaded, and TrieJax.

Typical methods combine formal complexity and communication analyses with practical engines and cost models. MILP formulations, sampling algebras, sketches, sparse representations, functional dependencies, and probabilistic summaries support optimization and approximate query processing. Deep neural and generative models increasingly estimate cardinalities, choose plans, and answer aggregates. Systems research emphasizes high-level languages, compilation, columnar and specialized hardware, distributed execution, and collaborative dataset versioning.

The community also addresses integrated machine learning over normalized data, fast-stream analytics, what-if provisioning, and revenue-aware recommendation. Complementary work studies replication consistency, outsourced-data security, blockchain/database design, and cloud MapReduce privacy. Recent directions favor learned and declarative automation, approximate interactive analytics, hardware-conscious graph processing, and unified platforms that bridge databases, machine learning, and large-scale distributed applications.

4d80143b1f023b7728a3f9adcc58561d86bcb447.text:
### Social Networks, Opinion Dynamics, and Scalable Network Analysis

This community studies how information, products, and opinions propagate through social and communication networks, and how network structure shapes influence, disagreement, polarization, discoverability, and robustness. A major theme is opinion dynamics: DeGroot, Friedkin–Johnsen, bounded-confidence, Bayesian, signed-network, biased, and multi-topic models analyze consensus, quasi-consensus, instability, antagonism, and polarization. Related work examines evolving social power and strategic modification of interpersonal weights.

Another theme is diffusion and influence: competing-product adoption, influence maximization, PageRank manipulation, communicability, delay reduction, and node discovery address how to optimize exposure and information flow, including fairness across social groups. Social-media studies model topic-specific behavior, controversy, political affinity, and temporally coherent events.

Typical methods combine graph Laplacians, spectral embeddings, centrality and resistance-based measures, dynamical-systems and asymptotic analysis, randomized interactions, optimization, and complexity/algorithmic analysis. Data-driven approaches include motif mining, feature selection, representation learning, and large-scale empirical evaluation.

Recent trends emphasize dynamic and signed networks, feedback between recommendations and opinions, heterogeneous individual thresholds and biases, scalable algorithms for very large graphs, and integrating structural, temporal, topical, and behavioral data.

963c99aa75a7880a067f64e21065c47eea95616b.text:
## Probabilistic, Causal, and Explainable Database Querying

This community focuses on extending database systems beyond clean, certain relational data. A major theme is probabilistic and uncertain databases: representing correlations and attribute-level uncertainty, evaluating joins, aggregates, similarity and top‑k queries, and making massive probabilistic workloads practical. Because exact evaluation is often #P-hard, typical methods include safe query plans, lifted inference, relational representations such as U-relations and Markov views, structural decompositions, knowledge compilation, probabilistic pruning, and approximation algorithms.

A second theme is explanation and causality. Provenance, lineage, why/why-not explanations, responsibility, causal effects, abductive diagnosis, and database repairs are used to explain query answers, non-answers, inconsistencies, and workflow results. Answer-set programming, repair semantics, and data differencing are recurring techniques.

Theoretical work characterizes tractability and decidability through chase procedures, dependency classes, attack graphs, finite controllability, treewidth, and circuit-width parameters. Related research addresses query answering under conceptual dependencies, schema mappings, XML policies, and peer-to-peer constraints.

Additional themes include mining tree-shaped patterns, summarizing pattern collections, SQL test-data generation, interactive relational browsing, and web-wrapper languages.

Recent directions emphasize scalable approximate inference, richer correlation models, principled probabilistic ranking, integrated inconsistency management, and tighter connections between provenance, causality, repairs, and knowledge compilation.

c96dca4b8aa23a36377812940f5439ad19c6c74e.text:
## Scholarly Graphs, Ranking, and Knowledge Infrastructures

This community studies how network structure and bibliographic data can improve scholarly discovery, evaluation, and understanding. Major themes include author-name disambiguation; coauthorship, citation, and scientific-community analysis; ranking scholars, publications, universities, and patents; and information retrieval over scientific and social-science resources. Related work addresses knowledge maps, semantic-web knowledge organization systems, metadata enrichment, and the stewardship, durability, privacy, and reproducibility of research data.

Typical methods combine social-network analysis and bibliometrics with PageRank, CheiRank, reduced Google matrices, weighted and bipartite graph models, centrality measures, spectral analysis, and community detection. Studies evaluate disambiguation through labeled datasets, simulations, triangulation, and semi-automatic “seed+expand” procedures. Retrieval research uses discipline-specific query expansion, user interaction signals, visual mapping, and relevance-agreement statistics. Large-scale mining commonly draws on DBLP, Web of Science, ACM data, patent citations, and multilingual Wikipedia.

Recent directions emphasize dynamic and predictive analysis: stochastic block models and LSTMs forecast patent-community growth, while citation dynamics trace emerging technologies. Multilingual Wikipedia enables cross-cultural and geopolitical analysis, and reduced Google matrices expose indirect interactions. Graphons offer scalable models for massive networks, while Linked Data, integrated digital libraries, Jupyter notebooks, and open-data stewardship support richer, more reproducible scholarly infrastructures.

c66d43c23ef98f6fdd8b7efba36496ebce8be2f4.text:
**From XML Warehousing to Adaptive Data Analytics**

This community centers on scalable data management and analysis for complex, heterogeneous data. A dominant theme is XML data warehousing and XOLAP: reference architectures, tree-pattern querying, complex hierarchies, summarizability, fragmentation, rollup operators, and query-performance optimization. Related work addresses business intelligence for small enterprises, personalized medicine, archaeology, and web data integration.

A second major theme is warehouse and database self-optimization. Studies select indexes and materialized views—often jointly—using query-workload mining, frequent itemsets, clustering, affinity analysis, and incremental adaptation. Object-oriented database research similarly examines clustering policies, access-pattern changes, simulation, and dynamic evaluation frameworks.

Benchmarking and evaluation are recurring methodological contributions, including XWeB, DWEB, LSHTC, T2K2/T2K2D2, and benchmarks for summarizability and top-*k* processing. Typical methods combine formal models, workload analysis, data mining, clustering, simulation, and prototype experimentation.

More recent directions broaden the scope toward high-volume, real-time and learning-based analytics: scalable document architectures, Twitter event detection through mention anomalies or entity clustering, temporal community modeling, hierarchical text classification with deep reinforcement learning, and exact top-*k* inference for multi-target prediction. Overall, the trajectory moves from static optimization of structured warehouses toward adaptive, distributed, and intelligent processing of complex data streams.

6dda5cad89d1e77c850436d4358c050d5fb54315.text:
## Scholarly Knowledge Extraction and Recommendation

This community focuses on making scientific literature machine-readable, discoverable, and more useful. Major themes include metadata and structure extraction from articles, bibliographic reference and citation matching, Linked Open Data, and scholarly knowledge graphs such as GrapAL and CL Scholar. These systems support semantic search, visualization, expert discovery, quality assessment, and exploration of research trends.

A second strong theme is recommendation for digital libraries, repositories, and reference managers. Work covers recommendation-as-a-service (Mr. DLib), algorithm selection, user modeling, related-article recommendation, and large-scale datasets such as RARD II. Evaluation considers online interactions, choice overload, position bias, temporal variation, and metrics beyond aggregate accuracy.

Typical methods combine NLP, hybrid rule-based and statistical extraction, text reuse and similarity detection, graph databases, citation networks, MapReduce/Hadoop, and machine learning. Recommender studies compare terms, keyphrases, embeddings, collaborative filtering, and meta-learning models, often using real-world deployments and click data.

Recent directions emphasize scalable, automated knowledge-graph construction; richer semantic interlinking; per-user or per-instance algorithm selection; and more realistic evaluation accounting for ranking position, time, and user behavior. Parallel work examines scholarly integrity through plagiarism, citation-sentence reuse, duplicate content, and contradictory information.

c81d537a2179b330a40b47c0d5c6877cf0386299.text:
### Schema.org Semantics, Validation, and Scalable Knowledge Graphs

This community centers on making Schema.org annotations useful, reliable, and scalable for machine-readable web content. Core themes include domain-specific semantic modeling, annotation creation and publication, and automated consumption by search engines, chatbots, intelligent personal assistants, and Web APIs. Tourism is a prominent application, particularly through efforts in Tyrol/Tirol to define tourism domains, annotate service providers, and construct a public tourism knowledge graph.

Typical methods include defining domain specifications as constrained subsets of Schema.org, using SHACL operators to generate formal patterns, and applying verification and validation to test syntactic correctness, completeness, consistency, and agreement with web-page content. Other work develops platforms and mappings for producing, distributing, and storing annotations, as well as action annotations for automated service processing. Context-dependent heuristics address scalable publication of dynamic data while limiting overload, latency, and disclosure.

Graph databases support Schema.org-based knowledge-graph ecosystems, while related papers survey NoSQL/NewSQL systems and simulate graph-database models for large-scale sensor surveillance. Recent trends move beyond static markup toward validated, domain-customized, dynamically published data and machine-readable APIs that enable automated actions and richer domain applications.

48949ee9a676ee9ad605ffc2739de5f46f8c8b86.text:
## Privacy-Preserving Data Analysis and Publishing

This community centers on enabling useful analysis of sensitive, high-dimensional, and distributed data while limiting disclosure. Differential privacy is the dominant framework, applied to histograms, range and predicate-counting queries, marginal statistics, frequent itemsets, clustering, decision trees, search logs, data exploration, cleaning, and hierarchical population estimates. A parallel line studies the limitations and risks of k-anonymity, l-diversity, t-closeness, generalization, bucketization, slicing, and anonymization under strong adversarial background knowledge.

Typical methods include calibrated noise, wavelet and hierarchical decompositions, sparse-vector variants, matrix mechanisms, linear query strategies, convex optimization, adaptive workload selection, and data/workload-aware partitioning. Researchers also develop approximation algorithms for set-valued anonymization and provenance views, surrogate graph structures, and LinkMirage for social links.

The community increasingly emphasizes utility–privacy tradeoffs in realistic applications: local differential privacy for recommendation and marginals, fairness impacts of private decisions, privacy-aware mobility and search-log release, and private data cleaning. Systems research is expanding toward federated querying, secure multiparty computation, trusted hardware, encrypted databases, and analyst-facing exploration platforms. Recent work also stresses efficiency, optimal or near-optimal query error, reconstruction and inference risks, and robustness when adversaries know the anonymization algorithm.

d7cb07f4da99c42c8c80aa58dbdcad0150b6a2a2.text:
## Scholarly Search, Metrics, and Networked Communities

This community centers on measuring, retrieving, ranking, and visualizing scholarly information. A dominant theme is the evaluation of Google Scholar alongside Web of Science, Scopus, and Microsoft Academic Search, including coverage, citation counts, highly cited documents, journal h-indices, database size, and citation aging. Studies also examine the reliability and limitations of metrics for assessing researchers, journals, institutions, and doctoral programs.

A second theme concerns information retrieval and library discovery. Research proposes learning-to-rank methods for selecting evaluation topics, intelligent trade-offs between deep and shallow judging, query expansion, credibility signals, and search-engine technologies for improving library catalogs.

Open access is another major focus, including large-scale identification of freely available articles, indicators combining multiple data sources, repository mandates, and self-archiving costs. Several papers address vulnerabilities in scholarly profiles, such as publication-merging errors and h-index manipulation.

Typical methods include large-scale citation and web-data collection, cross-database comparisons, longitudinal analysis, correlation and benchmarking, automated querying, network analysis, motif and clustering measures, and computational modeling. Online communities such as Wikipedia and science parks are studied through temporal, social, and normative networks.

Recent work trends toward broader bibliographic coverage, open-science monitoring, automated evaluation, and critical scrutiny of platform reliability, ranking practices, and metric manipulation.

934c6386f6664d86dad58a4a5bf486fdb1689a4a.text:
### Ontology-Enriched Semantic Text Retrieval

This community investigates semantic extensions of keyword-based information retrieval, emphasizing the complementary roles of keywords and named entities. A central theme is the use of latent ontological features of entities—aliases, classes, and identifiers—as well as, in some work, WordNet properties such as synonyms, hypernyms, hyponyms, and senses. These representations aim to capture meaning hidden from the surface text, including information implied by interrogative words in Wh-queries and related entities absent from the original query.

Typical methods extend the traditional Vector Space Model into generalized ontology-based models that combine keywords with selected entity features. Query expansion is another major approach, using query-oriented spreading activation to introduce semantically related concepts or named entities. Later algorithms seek to improve precision by restricting activation to entities connected through explicit relations and to the query’s original entities, avoiding irrelevant expansion.

Across the papers, experiments report improved retrieval and document/query representation compared with keyword-only baselines such as Lucene. The research trend moves from combining explicit ontological features with keywords toward richer semantic search using latent relations, controlled spreading activation, and ontology-guided query expansion.

a789220170ecf85b353a49f7739c3f02178f31be.text:
## Scalable, Data-Intensive Database Systems

This community investigates how database systems can scale with growing data volumes, parallel hardware, and demanding scientific and online workloads. Major themes include multicore and in-memory OLTP, distributed and multi-datacenter data management, crash recovery, concurrency control, and analytical processing under mixed workloads. A second strong focus is scientific and spatial data, especially astronomy: large catalogs, streaming observations, multidimensional arrays, metadata, geospatial indexing, and public data services. Applications also include social-network analysis, finite-element simulations, and graph storage.

Typical methods exploit application semantics and hardware parallelism. Systems use command or adaptive logging, parallel replay, log-structured storage, snapshot and MVCC variants, conflict repair, relaxed coordination, and actor-based execution. Query performance is improved through data-aware batching, workload-driven scheduling, automatic application partitioning, imperative-code optimization, relational spatial indexes, hierarchical triangular meshes, zones, and specialized graph layouts. Evaluation commonly uses large real-world datasets, prototype database systems, and performance, scalability, recovery, or energy measurements.

Recent trends emphasize full-life-cycle scientific data services combining streaming ingestion with real-time and historical analysis; predictable actor databases; transactional graph systems that retain analytical scan efficiency; exascale metadata and provenance; and energy-aware cluster design. The work also increasingly addresses usability through business-user SQL generation and post-mortem transaction debugging.

dbef65af5b87e596233b5d7a543cdb14b9d5e96d.text:
**Utility-Aware Sequential and Episode Mining**

This community studies how to discover useful, nonredundant patterns in ordered event and transaction data. A central theme is utility-oriented mining: identifying high-utility sequential patterns, episodes, and multidimensional sequences using profit, weight, quantity, importance, cost, or risk rather than frequency alone. Extensions address individualized or item-specific thresholds, recent/trending utility, uncertainty, and privacy preservation.

Episode mining is another major focus, including serial, parallel, strict, general, and simultaneous-event episodes. Researchers seek compact and meaningful outputs through closed episodes, non-derivable itemsets, generic bases, minimum-description-length compression, and statistical or partition-based screening of redundant and “free-rider” patterns. Constraint-based sequence mining unifies length, gap, span, regular-expression, hierarchy, and other subsequence constraints.

Typical methods exploit utility upper bounds, projected databases, sequence/episode-growth procedures, closure and equivalence-class structures, concise representations, encoding schemes, and statistical significance tests. Scalability is pursued through parallel sequential mining and MapReduce algorithms for n-gram statistics.

Recent trends move beyond uniform frequency and static utility toward richer real-world settings: complex sequences, multi-sequence data, recency, heterogeneous thresholds, uncertain IoT data, privacy requirements, and distributed processing, while emphasizing output reduction and actionable pattern quality.

fb9dc5072b7f8aa6c1611f725ef96942df822a47.text:
**Rich Semantic Models for Historical and Scientific Knowledge**

This community explores structured, semantic representations that move beyond document-centric information systems. A central theme is extending ontologies to capture objects, activities, infrastructures, mechanisms, state changes, instances, and scenarios. Work on foundries uses object-oriented modeling to describe artifacts, production processes, and aesthetic differences, while the mechanisms study proposes Transitionals and hierarchies of Aggregates and Mechanisms, potentially implemented in XFO.

A second theme is applying these representations to historical research. A machine-learning framework automatically constructs people gazetteers for quantitative prosopography from heterogeneous biographical and documentary sources. Related projects seek richer access to digitized newspapers through text-mining coordination, exploratory search, and formative user-interface design. The proposed Norfolk directory combines structured entity descriptions with links to newspaper mentions, supporting browsing and contextual interpretation.

Typical methods include ontology and semantic-model design, object-oriented and frame-based representations, machine learning for entity and people identification, text mining, linked references, and user-centered interface development.

Recent trends favor repositories and directories with direct, richly structured representations rather than collections of documents, integrating entities, relationships, mechanisms, and historical evidence to support discovery, exploration, and meaningful contextual analysis.

8493f88b657f3b7d0d8f84d0ac4f632fd9c9cfa6.text:
### Acknowledgements as Data for Mapping Research Collaboration

This community examines acknowledgements as an underused source for understanding research funding, credit, collaboration, and leadership. A major theme is the systematic analysis of funding acknowledgements in Web of Science, whose coverage began in 2008. Studies characterize their distribution and emphasize limitations related to database coverage, language, acknowledgement type, and potential analytical bias.

Another theme is making otherwise invisible contributions visible, particularly in the humanities, where acknowledgements complement traditional authorship and citation-based measures. Combining authors and acknowledged individuals reveals disciplinary differences in credit attribution and can substantially narrow apparent differences in collaboration and team size.

Typical methods are bibliometric and quantitative: large-scale analyses of Web of Science records, classification of acknowledgement types, comparisons across citation indexes, languages, and disciplines, and network analysis of co-authorship, acknowledgees, and institutional relationships. Research leadership is operationalized through the corresponding author’s affiliation and examined using geographical, cognitive, institutional, social, and economic proximity.

Recent trends move toward broader definitions of scholarly contribution and collaboration, integrating funding, acknowledgements, authorship, and proximity-based network indicators. The literature consistently recommends cautious interpretation because acknowledgement data are valuable but incomplete and unevenly indexed.

3de461f3e6367cbd755c9b89219792c5e71243f2.text:
### Socioeconomic Stratification in Communication and Consumption Networks

This community studies how social ties, communication behavior, demographics, and economic status are reflected in large-scale digital networks. A central theme is socioeconomic stratification: coupled mobile-phone and bank-transaction datasets show that consumption patterns correlate strongly with socioeconomic classes and shape social structure. Merchant-category correlations are further represented as meaningful correlation networks.

Several papers address demographic and socioeconomic inference from online activity. Twitter age is inferred from social-graph structure, while socioeconomic status is estimated from combinations of location, occupation, communication semantics, census data, and professional profiles.

Typical methods include constructing communication and transaction networks, extracting demographic and purchasing indicators, measuring correlations between user attributes and network structure, and building validated or correlation-based networks. Statistical testing is used to identify preferential communication and significant edges in mobile-phone calling networks, including comparisons of directed, reciprocal, and Bonferroni networks.

Recent work trends toward multimodal, population-scale analysis: integrating behavioral, financial, semantic, geographic, and social-network data to infer latent socioeconomic characteristics and explain how these characteristics organize communication and consumption patterns.

fe4f2d0764eaf3e0f9855be0291fba458b868c72.text:
## Scalable Event and Stream Processing

This community centers on extracting meaningful events from massive, heterogeneous, and continuously changing data streams. Complex Event Processing (CEP) is the dominant theme, spanning formal foundations, pattern languages, automata-based detection, adaptive evaluation structures, join optimization, and load shedding under resource constraints. Applications include RFID tracking, IoT sensing, monitoring, and enterprise event processing.

Typical methods include non-deterministic and lazy-chain automata for incremental pattern matching; query-plan and join-order optimization; adaptive reconfiguration based on stream characteristics; distributed inference combined with stream queries; and time-coherent, decentralized sensor joins. The work also addresses unifying event processing, data streams, and asynchronous messaging under shared consistency and query models.

A second major theme is evaluation infrastructure for big-data and stream-processing systems. Benchmarking studies compare Storm, Spark, and Flink using throughput, latency, and windowed workloads. Complementary work develops scalable generators and feature-tweaking tools to produce varied, controllable, application-specific datasets while preserving important data characteristics. Benchmark suites draw on Internet services and search-engine workloads.

Overall, the research trends toward distributed scalability, adaptive processing, realistic and diverse workloads, stronger theoretical foundations, and integration of event processing with IoT data acquisition and general-purpose streaming platforms.

42a1fdb33a3bfd9e52449c4dffb7ac20a4ea442b.text:
## Network Diffusion, Influence, and Epidemic Control

This community studies how information, influence, infections, and failures propagate through social, technological, ecological, and interdependent cyber-physical networks. Major themes include influence maximization and marketing, epidemic cost and containment, diffusion-source localization, hidden-network and transmission-parameter inference, and diffusion-aware network design.

Typical methods combine probabilistic cascade models—including independent-cascade, SIS/SI, complex-contagion, continuous-time, temporal, and adaptive-network models—with optimization and theoretical analysis. Submodularity, adaptive submodularity, approximation guarantees, mixed-integer programming, random-walk and Markov-chain analysis, random matrix theory, message passing, particle-swarm heuristics, and Jordan-center/cover algorithms are prominent. Limited observations and resource constraints motivate sampling, probing, aggregate-data learning, and partial-feedback approaches.

Recent work increasingly addresses dynamics beyond static networks: adaptive and temporal interventions, online and sequential seed selection, myopic or full-adoption feedback, adaptivity gaps, and continuous-time diffusion. Applications broaden from advertising and worker recruitment to conservation, student networks, mobile sensing, malware, and epidemic response. There is also growing emphasis on non-submodular and complex contagion, multiple-source detection, resilient self-healing infrastructures, activity-aware influence, and learned cascade representations using contrastive training and message/text features.

b6370356fb77018855f18f6924f9ff71e431d86b.text:
### Scientometrics, Research Mapping, and Fair Impact Evaluation

This community focuses on measuring, mapping, and evaluating scientific research through bibliometric data. Major themes include citation-based assessment of authors, journals, institutions, countries, and fields; field delineation and cognitive distance; technology and journal-network mapping; and reconstruction of research fronts and historical roots.

Typical methods are citation, co-citation, bibliographic-coupling, author–paper, and journal–journal network analysis; centrality measures such as PageRank and the K-index; clustering, similarity measures, overlays, and visualization. Studies also use field normalization, percentiles, percentile classes, fractional counting, Gini and diversity indices, and statistical or benchmark comparisons. Large-scale analyses draw on Web of Science, Scopus, Microsoft Academic, Dimensions, PubMed/MeSH, and patent databases.

Recent trends emphasize more responsible and context-sensitive evaluation. Researchers question journal impact factors, h-index limitations, statistical inference, and national assessment exercises, proposing integrated, normalized, contribution-aware, or “universal” indicators. Digital dissemination is weakening the link between journal impact factor and paper citations, while database coverage and linked-reference quality remain concerns. Newer work examines diversity in collaboration, fairness for large-team research, conference-publication incentives, interactive tools such as RPYS i/o and CRExplorer, and algorithmic tracing of emerging fields, seminal works, and research histories.

ecf14194b118fcf2d2a73d864b11e97d6b909e59.text:
### Community Detection Across Complex, Dynamic, and Multilayer Networks

This community centers on defining, detecting, evaluating, and exploiting community structure in complex networks. Major themes include disjoint, overlapping, fuzzy, attributed, multiplex, multilayer, bipartite, and heterogeneous communities, as well as core–periphery organization and dense subgraphs. Several works address practical biases, including the treatment of low-degree nodes, resolution limits, and the absence of a universally accepted community definition.

Typical methods range from modularity and multislice modularity optimization to label propagation, clique percolation, local spectral diffusion, density-based clustering with manifold learning, stochastic and geometric block models, and variational Bayesian inference. Multi-criteria and Pareto-optimal formulations evaluate or extract families of solutions rather than a single partition. Theoretical analyses use random matrix theory, metastable dynamics, axiomatic models, and algorithm-selection frameworks.

Recent directions emphasize scalable and localized analysis for very large graphs, temporal evolution and mental-map preservation in visualization, shared and layer-specific structure in multilayer networks, and active or adaptive detection. Personalized and evolving PageRank methods support local community discovery and dynamic node importance. Applications span social influence, churn and smartphone adoption, recommendations, web services, bibliometrics, dating markets, geo-social grouping, and public-private networks.

4271313c28f3c138cde9210df5480bd3ec4ec63a.text:
**Multiplex Social Networks: Structure, Dynamics, and Applications**

This community centers on analyzing social systems as multilayer or multiplex networks, where actors are connected through heterogeneous online, offline, semantic, professional, and interaction ties. Major themes include layer-aware centrality and similarity, inter-layer entanglement, missing-data effects, sampling, and unified models of distributed online identities.

A second focus is network dynamics: community extraction and evolution (GED, SGCI), dynamic clustering, influence identification, information cascades, viral campaigns, and interacting epidemic processes. Studies combine theoretical threshold and branching-process analyses with empirical evaluation on Facebook, Twitter, blogs, email, mobile-phone, and student-network data. Typical methods include graph metrics, community detection (Louvain and Infomap), diffusion and independent-cascade models, topic modeling, sentiment analysis, association-rule mining, language models, feature engineering, and supervised or unsupervised embedding for identity linkage. Synthetic-network generation and statistical sampling address scale, reproducibility, and privacy constraints.

Applications span recommendations, human-resource talent discovery, cross-device and cross-platform user matching, misinformation fact checking, marketing, and disease surveillance. Recent directions emphasize integrating heterogeneous layers and partial observations, modeling temporal evolution rather than static structure, exploiting large-scale digital traces and mobile sensing, and developing scalable or unsupervised techniques for identity, content, and diffusion analysis.

856107dce8edfd8ead85d221d7e18b23d6684081.text:
### Recommender Systems: From Collaborative Filtering to Context-Aware Optimization

This community centers on personalized recommendation across products, media, news, travel, education, and advertising. Core themes include collaborative filtering and matrix factorization, top-\(N\) ranking, sequential and session-based prediction, playlist continuation, and modeling diverse or long-tail preferences. Researchers also address cold-start and sparse data, missing modalities, popularity bias, recommendation diversity, interpretability, fraudulent reviews, reputation, and the effects of social ties.

Typical methods combine user–item and item–item similarities, Markov chains, slope-one predictors, neighborhood models, signed bipartite graphs, metric learning, ontologies, and content representations such as LSA, topic models, and multimodal audio-visual-text features. Neural approaches increasingly use VAEs, nonlinear latent-factor models, recurrent networks, context trees, factorization machines, attention, and graph neural networks. Re-ranking with diversification and determinantal point processes targets variety and long-tail exposure.

Recent work emphasizes deep sequence and session modeling, including inter-session history, latent user states, complex item transitions, and mixture-of-tastes representations. Multimodal learning tackles incomplete information and cold-start settings, while reinforcement learning considers advertising revenue alongside user experience. Cross-domain and shared-account recommendation, real-world online evaluation, and explicit analysis of robustness, manipulation, popularity, and business objectives signal a broader move beyond accuracy alone.

e3e71bf81a51879b649796de0badabac4e65c884.text:
## Networked Social Systems: Structure, Diffusion, and Risk

This community studies online and complex social networks as dynamic systems. Major themes include information diffusion, rumor and meme propagation, cascade structure, virality, attention, and popularity; network organization through communities, strong/weak ties, homophily, bridges, and centrality; and the detection of anomalies, malicious URLs, criminal intermediaries, suicide-related behavior, and systemic financial risk. Other applications address disasters, political discussion, sports events, scholarly trends, and video remixing.

Typical methods combine graph analysis with large-scale platform data from Twitter, Facebook, YouTube, Yelp, and scholarly databases. Researchers use betweenness, pair-dependency, modularity-based and generalized Louvain community detection, clustering, centrality, structural paradox analysis, and visual analytics. Diffusion is modeled with rumor and cascade models, SIR-family delay differential equations, probabilistic contagion and immunity, indirect co-location links, and multivariate Hawkes processes. Statistical learning predicts content popularity, engagement, topic trends, gender, and emergency-aid relevance, while multimodal and visual-meme extraction incorporates text and imagery.

Recent directions emphasize dynamic and heterogeneous network assembly, adaptive ties and collective intelligence, exogenous influence beyond the observed graph, content-agnostic drivers of popularity, multimodal disaster intelligence, and more targeted measures of bridges, vulnerability, attention, and influence.

92a01c4aa5bc4638e7e2426a747c48936c0bbce6.text:
## Social Media as a Lens on Place, Mobility, and Behavior

This community studies how user-generated and location-based social media can reveal human behavior, urban structure, and geographically grounded preferences. Major themes include inferring locations from non-geotagged text; mapping mobility, visited places, commuting, urban boundaries, and functional regions; and measuring perceptions of cities through emotional, visual, sound, and smell-related content. Other work predicts voting intentions, sports outcomes, business ratings and locations, special-offer responses, social influence, and sexual-violence reports.

Typical methods combine text, user profiles, timestamps, check-ins, images, and network ties. Researchers use convolutional neural networks, supervised classifiers, probabilistic and Gaussian-mixture models, heuristic labeling, sentiment and semantic analysis, graph-based feature extraction, low-rank approximation, density-based spatial clustering, trajectory clustering, and network reconstruction. Crowdsourced judgments and external surveys provide labels or validation.

Recent trends emphasize scalable inference under missing geotags, quantified confidence and standardized evaluation, multimodal and cross-platform data, and correction of social-media sampling bias through population synthesis and out-of-sample validation. Applications increasingly support urban planning and navigation, including emotionally pleasant routes, neighborhood signatures, park-related wellbeing, business-site selection, and fine-grained mobility analysis.

27867b7063735e9bc02ea43febadb9d9047d0dcf.text:
### Network Science: Dynamic Structure, Embeddings, and Graph Mining

This community studies the modeling, analysis, and practical use of complex, social, and information networks. Major themes include dynamic and temporal networks, heterogeneous relationship forecasting, community detection, link prediction, graph similarity, and network representation learning. Several works address knowledge-graph tasks such as entity normalization, triple scoring, and path-based fact checking.

Typical methods combine probabilistic models (stochastic blockmodels, latent-space models, graph grammars, and Markov chains), machine learning (random forests, deep neural networks, neural embeddings, and ensemble scoring), and structural heuristics based on triangles, clustering coefficients, paths, and degree correlations. Sampling, graph generation, MapReduce counting, and external-memory algorithms target large-scale network analysis.

Applications span social-network fusion, urban dynamics, privacy protection, fraud and insider-trading detection, criminal and covert networks, team formation, and search-ranking abuse. Work also examines adversarial community deception and uncertain network structure.

Recent trends emphasize time-aware representation learning, including continuous-time prediction, dynamic embeddings, temporal event graphs, and evolving stochastic blockmodels. Other directions seek robustness to temporal offsets, uncertainty, and attacks; improved evaluation through graph-embedding benchmarks; and methods that connect structural signals with text, attributes, and knowledge bases.

75d1700e245a8ad6963a2544a4ef795dbed91519.text:
## Neural, Semantic, and Structured Information Retrieval

This community centers on improving search and ranking across web, enterprise, bibliographic, e-commerce, mobile, and personal collections. Core themes include learning-to-rank, query understanding and expansion, passage and document retrieval, entity and expert search, semantic similarity, and web-quality or spam detection. It also addresses dataset search, heterogeneous bibliographic networks, temporal entity aspects, and dynamic or multi-stage retrieval.

Typical methods combine traditional IR principles with machine learning: pointwise, pairwise, listwise, bipartite, and groupwise ranking; query and document embeddings; neural architectures, BERT, multi-task learning, kernel models, and semantic hashing. Researchers exploit graph structures such as heterogeneous networks, dependency graphs, k-nearest-neighbor graphs, and knowledge bases. Other recurring strategies include pseudo-relevance feedback, concept hierarchies, fielded retrieval, ensemble models, axiomatic regularization, and post-hoc interpretability. Benchmark collections and evaluation resources, including LETOR and WikiPassageQA, support comparative experimentation.

Recent trends emphasize pretrained language models for multi-stage ranking, non-factoid question answering, passage reranking, and cross-lingual transfer. Models increasingly capture interactions among documents, entities, fields, and neighboring items rather than scoring documents independently. There is also growing interest in efficient large-scale retrieval through hashing and graph indexing, dynamic and temporal relevance, privacy-constrained search, and interpretable or principled neural ranking.

9c69b0f13a905c8e10307e134be321b31de4c20c.text:
## Social Media Networks, Polarization, and Misinformation

This community studies online social networks as environments for political behavior, information diffusion, public-health intervention, and security risk. Major themes include partisan community formation and polarization; misinformation, disinformation, fake news, and extremist propaganda; bot, spam, Sybil, and malicious-node detection; and inference of users’ preferences, demographics, and behavior.

Typical methods combine network analysis with machine learning. Researchers construct retweet, followership, endorsement, and interaction graphs; apply community detection, assortativity, PCA, matrix factorization, and diffusion models; and use supervised, semi-supervised, sparse, embedding-based, and topic-modeling approaches. Temporal and continuous-time models capture tie decay and propagation. Studies also use regression on likes, stance classification, crowd signals, sampling analysis, surveys, and cross-platform datasets.

Recent work increasingly examines election-related influence campaigns, polarized or fringe communities, and disinformation ecosystems across Twitter, Reddit, Facebook, YouTube, search engines, and news websites. It emphasizes distinguishing data and ranking bias, evaluating sampling and benchmark limitations, modeling segregation and fact-checking backfire, and developing real-time detection or intervention systems. Alongside analysis, the community addresses practical defenses, including social bots for health messaging, expert review of flagged content, and protections for crowdsourced and decentralized systems.

f9ad03ea3145c08487b3b3ff3c15b0ee7f475fac.text:
## Graph Querying, Semantics, and Interoperability

This community centers on managing, querying, and reasoning over RDF, SPARQL, property graphs, and related semi-structured data. A major theme is SPARQL optimization: algebraic rewriting, constraint- and chase-based optimization, runtime/incremental evaluation, summary- and partition-driven processing, and specialized handling of OPTIONAL/left-outer joins. Federated querying addresses source selection, heuristic reordering, large-scale endpoint deployments, heterogeneous relational–RDF sources, and replicated fragments.

Research also develops formal foundations and expressive extensions, including multiset semantics, OWL entailment, incomplete information, preferences, provenance, keyword–SPARQL hybrids, and static-analysis complexity. Graph querying is broadened through Gremlin translation, regular and context-free path queries, simple-path complexity, and query-by-example interfaces.

A parallel focus is graph data modeling and interoperability: direct mappings among relational, RDF, and property-graph databases; property-graph type systems and DDLs; RDF shapes and XML schemas; and programmable view updates and maintenance. Methods are predominantly formal—complexity and undecidability proofs, semantics, Datalog, automata, and relational algebra—combined with indexing, heuristics, systems implementation, and extensive experiments.

Recent directions emphasize practical scalability and reliability: federations with replication, runtime adaptation, provenance and data-science graph summarization, usability for non-experts, controllable graph benchmarks, and convergence between RDF and property-graph ecosystems.

e6e1c12cf7a312db43a82b9b34a8136ba18f4d99.text:
## Scalable Search, Querying, and Fair Data Systems

This community focuses on making large, heterogeneous data searchable, queryable, and efficiently executable. Major themes include flexible querying over fuzzy, incomplete, hierarchical, spatial, graph, and hidden-web data; keyword and experiential search; skyline, preference, influence, and aggregate queries; and crawling databases exposed through search interfaces.

Typical methods combine specialized indexing and data structures—bitmap and Roaring indexes, inverted-list compression, variable-byte and Huffman coding, locality-sensitive hashing, set-intersection algorithms, and semantic hidden-web crawlers—with query rewriting, reranking, pruning, and top-*k* retrieval. Systems research emphasizes parallel and hardware-aware execution, including SIMD compression, GPU and CPU–GPU spatial processing, GPU transaction engines, distributed graph mining, and learned graph query planning. Workflow grammars, association rules, fuzzy linguistic summaries, and machine-learning representations support richer retrieval and recommendation.

Recent trends increasingly address societal and user-centered concerns. Fairness-aware ranking and diversity reranking explicitly manage demographic bias, while antidote data seeks to reduce polarization without changing recommender internals. Bias studies examine semantic representation and proxy effects in high-stakes classification. Alongside these concerns, work continues to reduce storage and latency overhead through compact indexes, faster hashing, improved bitmap ordering, and scalable dataflow systems.

46ab7f4042fabce3f85580ad783ef4a784f585d5.text:
## Graph Algorithms, Temporal Networks, and Narrative Social Analysis

This community studies graph structure, dynamics, and scalable analysis across social, temporal, and fictional networks. A major theme is efficient querying: shortest paths, distances, reachability, and temporal paths are supported through landmark labeling, hop-doubling, pruning, sketches, hub acceleration, interval labeling, and distributed or vertex-centric computation. Several works address dynamic graphs and large-scale analytics, including window queries and fully dynamic reachability indexes.

A second theme is temporal-network modeling. Stream graphs, link streams, time-varying graphs, and temporal quantities provide formalisms for time-aware connectivity, journeys, latency, density, centrality, and community structure. Algebraic semirings and temporal betweenness offer systematic computational tools, while empirical studies examine hospitals, mailing lists, knowledge mobilization, and financial transactions.

Narrative analysis forms another strong application area. Character-interaction networks, multilayer movie-script models, conversational dynamics, genre classification, plot smoothing, and extraction-method comparisons support summarization, role detection, prediction, and recommendation. Studies also analyze Game of Thrones, Friends, and other fictional worlds.

Typical methods combine theoretical bounds, indexing and preprocessing, network statistics, machine learning, link prediction, and empirical case studies. Emerging directions emphasize temporal rather than static representations, scalable dynamic indexing, richer multilayer models, and prediction or recommendation using network dynamics.

e7264c069ef9912fdd8b00eac7801ffd0ced0a2c.text:
## Principles and Systems for Intelligent Data Management

This community studies scalable, adaptive data management across query processing, analytics, machine learning, graphs, and distributed systems. A central theme is query optimization: MILP formulations, memory-aware cost models, learned cardinality estimators, neural optimizers, index tuning, and predictive models for distributed OLTP seek better plans under complex workloads and hardware constraints.

Parallel and distributed query evaluation emphasizes communication efficiency, worst-case-optimal multiway joins, single-round processing, parallel correctness, dynamic query maintenance, and coordination-free computation. Relational joins also serve as a foundation for graph analytics, including Vertica-based SQL processing, EmptyHeaded, and TrieJax’s hardware-accelerated pattern matching.
