This community studies how online social networks shape political discourse, information diffusion, and collective behavior. Major themes include community formation and polarization, echo chambers, conspiracy narratives, political disinformation, extremism, controversy, and demographic inequalities. Several papers examine coordinated or automated activity, including bots, autogenerated tweets, crowdturfing, Sybil devices, spear-phishing, and state-sponsored influence campaigns. Other work addresses privacy, malicious applications, spam, and decentralized search, alongside applications in public health and disaster management.

Typical methods combine large-scale collection of Twitter, Facebook, YouTube, Gab, crowdsourcing, and browser data with network analysis, temporal analysis, surveys, and simulation. Machine-learning approaches include nonnegative matrix factorization for community detection, semi-supervised and real-time spam classification, stance and extremism prediction, spectral embeddings for link prediction, image-based demographic inference, and content, metadata, network, and linguistic features. Mathematical models include contagion, misinformation, fact-checking, conflict, and rumor-spreading models.

Recent work increasingly focuses on measuring rather than merely detecting bias and misinformation, separating data from ranking effects, modeling emotional and intra-community dynamics, comparing platforms, and evaluating practical interventions such as fact checking, social bots for health messaging, curated user lists, and defenses against malicious actors.

5a75b11874e1505a49d62d61169590b593db54a6.text:
## Social Media Geolocation, Political Information, and Movement Reconstruction

This community studies how incomplete or noisy digital traces can support geographic, behavioral, and political analysis. One theme is geolocation on Twitter: researchers combine tweet text with user-profile metadata in convolutional neural networks to predict a user’s location from a single tweet. Complementing prediction, a large-scale empirical study examines geotagging behavior using more than 40 billion tweets from 20 million users, questioning assumptions behind analyses based on geotagged data.

A second major theme is political communication and misinformation. Studies use dictionaries of news-source types, self-reported locations, and social-media sharing patterns to measure junk-news consumption, polarization, and geographic concentration during US elections. Related work examines misinformation and conspiracy networks targeting military personnel and veterans, while the *Junk News Aggregator* addresses transparency and systematic examination of Facebook content around the 2018 midterms.

A further methodological contribution concerns movement data: location-order recovery reconstructs the sequence of events when trails have insufficient temporal resolution and apparently place an object in multiple locations simultaneously.

Recent trends emphasize neural multimodal geolocation, very large-scale behavioral measurement, cross-platform misinformation monitoring, and methods for correcting missing or ambiguous temporal-spatial data.

9d9d8ee764441d2d0616fae2b7ae407d0ee6e0d2.text:
## Temporal Graph Analytics and Scalable Network Querying

This community centers on modeling, analyzing, and querying networks whose structure and interactions evolve over time. Core themes include temporal reachability, shortest and fastest paths, latency, temporal centrality, diffusion, influence, and the evolution of network structure. Several works develop formalisms such as time-varying graphs, link streams, stream graphs, temporal quantities, and semirings, enabling temporal generalizations of density, connectivity, betweenness, and other static measures.

A strong methodological focus is scalable indexing and query processing. Landmark and independent-set labeling, interval-based reachability indexes, hub acceleration, topological and dense-block indexes, and distributed algorithms support reachability, bounded or regular reachability, distance, shortest-path, and window queries on massive graphs. Parallel vertex-centric implementations and optimized database window functions address construction and execution costs.

Applications include information diffusion and dynamic monopolies, opinion spreading, recommendation, movie narratives, mailing lists, hospitals, knowledge mobilization, scientific communities, and biological network comparison. Recent directions emphasize fully dynamic and temporal-aware indexes, algebraic and journey-based analysis, dynamic graph alignment and graphlets, time centrality, and extracting temporal features for prediction and recommendation rather than collapsing data into static snapshots.

59d5b71ed6297319e6bfae7ceb3dcf760ee90142.text:
## Learning to Rank and Semantic Search

This community centers on information retrieval as a pipeline for understanding queries, ranking content, and delivering answers. Major themes include neural document and passage ranking; query expansion, clustering, and intent refinement; entity salience, linking, and temporal/event-aware retrieval; and specialized search for experts, datasets, mobile apps, email, and personal memories. Non-factoid question answering and answer interaction extend retrieval beyond documents, while web spam, content quality, and recommendation attacks address reliability.

Typical methods combine supervised learning-to-rank, pointwise/pairwise objectives, multi-stage retrieval, and feature-based ranking with representation learning. Word2vec/query2vec, locally trained embeddings, semantic hashing, convolutional networks, kernels, and BERT-based mono- and duo-rankers are prominent. Systems also use heterogeneous graphs, knowledge bases, dependency graphs, geo-temporal signals, pseudo-relevance feedback, and entity-aware features. Evaluation relies on benchmark collections such as LETOR and WikiPassageQA, user studies, clicks, and multileaved online comparisons.

Recent work shifts toward pretrained language models for ranking and question answering, end-to-end and multi-task learning, dynamic and interactive retrieval, and scalable similarity search. At the same time, interpretability, explainable search, adversarial robustness, latency-quality tradeoffs, and retrieval over continuously changing news and temporal information are increasingly emphasized.

4ec911ba55c8f9d24743eff30142e080ca80a419.text:
## Scalable, Declarative, and Learning-Aware Data Management

This community explores how database systems can process increasingly large, diverse, and dynamic data efficiently while remaining programmable and usable. Core themes include query optimization and evaluation—MILP-based join ordering, worst-case-optimal and parallel joins, conjunctive queries with inequalities, dynamic query answering, XQuery complexity, and coordination-free distributed computation. Graph analytics is another major focus, with relational translations of graph algorithms, Datalog engines, and specialized hardware for graph joins.

Typical methods combine theoretical complexity and communication analyses with system building and benchmarking. Techniques include column stores, relational algebra, MapReduce optimization, adaptive and divergent indexing, sampling and probabilistic summaries, sketches, approximate and speculative execution, and high-level compilation. Several works integrate machine learning directly with relational data, using sparse tensors, functional dependencies, aggregate computation, and declarative resource management.

The community also addresses practical data infrastructure: dataset version control, metadata cleaning and record linkage, stale materialized views, cloud privacy, replication consistency, and data-structure design. Recent directions emphasize unified platforms for analytics and learning, lifecycle management for deep-learning artifacts, automated visual insight discovery, revenue-aware recommendation, multi-tenant resource sharing, and hardware-conscious acceleration.

3aa934d4c8870819a50b32f24af493e749024adc.text:
### Network Science: Dynamic, Heterogeneous, and Learning-Based Graph Analysis

This community studies computational methods for understanding complex, social, semantic, and temporal networks. Major themes include network representation learning and embedding; community detection, clustering, core–periphery structure, and centrality; link, relationship, and category prediction; and analysis of temporal and uncertain graphs. Applications span urban dynamics, privacy, fraud and insider-trading detection, criminal networks, fact checking, entity normalization, team formation, and information diffusion.

Typical methods combine structural properties with node content, text, knowledge bases, and relation types. Frequently used approaches include random walks, Markov chains, local algorithms, stochastic blockmodels, maximum-likelihood inference, machine learning classifiers, discriminative path mining, and ensemble scoring. Neural networks and deep embeddings are increasingly used for clustering, heterogeneous-network prediction, multimodal urban modeling, and continuous-time relationship forecasting.

A parallel focus is scalable graph computation: MapReduce triangle counting, hop-doubling distance indexes, graph sampling with quality guarantees, and external-memory distributed generation. Temporal modeling is a strong recent direction, including temporal event graphs, dynamic stochastic blockmodels, latent-space generative models, and temporally robust representations. Research also increasingly emphasizes realistic graph generation, multi-relational structural motifs, indirect temporal co-location links, and systematic benchmarks for evaluating graph embeddings.

0fb47680dbcac8375cf6f8869a0907339b02b8b0.text:
**Network Dynamics, Influence, and Structural Analysis**

This community studies how information, opinions, influence, and traffic evolve over networks, with particular emphasis on social and online systems. Major themes include consensus and polarization in DeGroot, Friedkin–Johnsen, bounded-confidence, biased-assimilation, and signed-network models; evolving social power and interpersonal weights; and feedback between opinions and personalized recommendations. Other work examines centrality, discoverability, navigability, robustness, network backbones, PageRank, tagging, and the design of links or nodes to optimize exposure, coverage, delay, or influence. Web crawling provides a complementary systems perspective on discovering and indexing complex applications.

Typical methods combine graph theory, dynamical-systems and control analysis, stochastic processes, Markov chains, random walks, optimization, and information-theoretic objectives. Researchers derive convergence, stability, consensus, polarization, and sensitivity conditions; formulate centrality and network-design axioms; and develop scalable algorithms for backbone extraction, dynamic Random Walk with Restart, node discovery, and delay minimization. Empirical studies use voting records, traffic activity, and large-scale social-media networks, alongside simulations and robustness tests.

Recent trends emphasize temporal and multilayer interactions, signed and antagonistic relationships, heterogeneous susceptibilities and thresholds, topic-specific user behavior, and closed-loop recommendation effects. There is also growing interest in data-driven network sensing, estimation from partial observations, theoretical guarantees on dynamic graphs, and strategic manipulation or concealment of influence.

7a69d457bf4fcaf6b6ed3f8ffb3bc1d2f0b8a641.text:
## Data Management Under Uncertainty, Inconsistency, and Causality

This community studies reliable query answering and analysis when databases are uncertain, inconsistent, incomplete, distributed, or difficult to interpret. A dominant theme is probabilistic data management: uncertain relations, probabilistic databases, correlations, aggregates, top-*k* ranking, similarity search, and scalable processing of massive possible-world spaces. Work develops U-relations, Markov views, lifted inference, knowledge compilation, structural decompositions, pruning, and approximate query evaluation.

A second major theme is explanation and causality. Papers characterize causes, responsibility, and causal effects for query answers and non-answers, connect causality with provenance, abductive diagnosis, database repairs, and answer-set programs, and develop provenance graphs and workflow-differencing techniques for auditing, debugging, and reproducibility.

Other recurring topics include integrity constraints and repairs, peer-to-peer consistent answers, schema mappings, XML access-control consistency, conceptual dependencies and the chase, finite determinacy, and tractability frontiers for conjunctive and regular-path queries. Data mining work addresses graph/tree-query associations and concise representations of frequent patterns.

Typical methods combine formal semantics, reductions and complexity analysis, Datalog and answer-set programming, relational query rewriting, probabilistic bounds, and experimental algorithm comparisons. Recent directions emphasize practical scalable inference, interactive exploration, contextual data quality, belief annotations, and causal reasoning for algorithmic fairness.

36fb71879175b52bb59c633c46659f69b6c1b1b9.text:
## Social Commerce, Trust, and Influence

This community studies how social relationships shape online marketplaces, recommender systems, consumer choice, and information diffusion. A central theme is combining marketplace behavior with social-network, trust, and location-based data to recommend products, categories, and items, while addressing sparsity and cold-start problems. Several works examine social commerce as the integration of friendship and economic exchange, including strong-tie platforms where friends become sellers and marketplace messaging supports product advice.

Typical methods include collaborative filtering augmented with explicit or implicit trust, regular equivalence to exploit weak ties, multi-source data integration, and empirical analysis of transactions, social graphs, triads, and directed closure. User studies compare the effects of friend recommendations and aggregate ratings on decisions. Other work develops scalable, service-based recommendation architectures and implements social classified platforms emphasizing privacy, security, usability, ranking, and communication.

A parallel theme models rumor dissemination computationally, relating convergence to social homogeneity, desires, and trust. Recent trends move toward richer, multi-modal social-commerce data, scalable deployable recommender services, and finer-grained measurement of social influence—distinguishing friends, crowds, weak ties, and negative versus positive opinions.

769bc3643b42ae3a54b03834729f9fcbf6a04b24.text:
### Scalable High-Dimensional Similarity Search

This community focuses on approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) and similarity search over massive, high-dimensional vector databases, motivated by the curse of dimensionality and applications including image retrieval, document retrieval, image search, and mass spectrometry. A central goal is balancing query speed, scalability, storage efficiency, and search accuracy.

The papers investigate several indexing paradigms. Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) is examined for real-time processing, including its limitations and possible improvements. Cosine threshold search is addressed through inverted indexes and adaptations of Fagin’s Threshold Algorithm, with emphasis on optimality guarantees and empirical performance. HD-Index introduces hierarchical RDB-trees organized using Hilbert keys for approximate \(k\)-nearest-neighbor search. Graph-based methods build on NSG and Monotonic Search Networks, while the Satellite System graph seeks more efficient navigation through improved graph structure. Multi-index hashing maps vectors to binary codes to reduce storage and accelerate cosine similarity search.

Recent trends emphasize pushing scalability and accuracy boundaries, achieving stronger theoretical guarantees, improving real-time behavior, and exploring complementary hash-, tree-, and graph-based indexes for increasingly large datasets.

c278924a1f2b3c691dc6cc69f8af51fd8b355277.text:
### Utility-Oriented Sequential Pattern Mining

This community focuses on discovering informative patterns in complex, time-ordered, and multi-dimensional sequences beyond traditional frequency-based mining. Central tasks include high-utility sequential pattern and episode mining, motivated by applications such as marketing, e-commerce, click-stream analysis, recommendation, route planning, IoT, medical analysis, and bioinformatics.

Typical methods develop utility-aware mining frameworks and efficient search algorithms, including UMEpi for high-utility episodes, projection-based mining (ProUM), and fast utility mining for complex sequences. Because sequence mining is computationally and memory intensive, parallel processing and scalability are recurring concerns. The literature also investigates privacy-preserving utility mining to balance useful discovery with protection of sensitive information.

Recent trends extend the basic uniform-threshold setting. Researchers propose item-specific or individualized minimum-utility thresholds, enabling patterns involving lower-utility but important items to be retained. Temporal extensions incorporate recency and trend information to identify recently emerging high-utility patterns. Other directions address multi-dimensional and multiple-sequence data, as well as uncertainty and heterogeneous item importance in IoT analytics. Survey papers consolidate advances in utility-oriented mining, privacy preservation, and parallel sequential pattern mining, indicating a shift toward more realistic, scalable, timely, and application-aware analytics.

0ba95505f94e805f65f7ef09967facc8554a9a58.text:
## Structured Discovery and Querying of Web and Data-Lake Information

This community studies how to make heterogeneous web, open-data, enterprise, and knowledge-base content comparable, searchable, and navigable. A foundational theme is defining shared, ordered, multidimensional domains so information can be represented precisely and compared across sources.

Several works focus on structured search: keyword queries are mapped to relevant table schemas, column combinations, entity joins, or knowledge-graph patterns to produce multi-column table answers. Methods include pattern discovery over directed knowledge graphs and ranking or matching collections of noisy, redundant web tables.

Another major theme is data-lake organization. Organizations are modeled as graphs whose nodes represent attribute sets and whose subset edges support navigation. Probabilistic user models and optimization objectives are used to maximize the likelihood of discovering relevant tables, complementing conventional search.

For large-scale domain search, Jaccard set containment and LSH ensembles enable efficient matching of query domains to web and open-data domains, particularly when dataset sizes differ substantially. Schemaless querying extends accessibility to document-embedded tables by combining table transformations, RDF/SPARQL, and database dependencies, reducing manual schema mapping.

Overall, the work trends toward integrated discovery: combining search, navigation, semantic representations, and scalable approximate retrieval for heterogeneous structured data.

9ec9fc426e7d05d7d1502813899f6ff352825e25.text:
## Width, Structure, and Probabilistic Query Inference

This community studies knowledge compilation for Boolean circuits and database query evaluation, with emphasis on how structural properties determine computational tractability. A central theme is connecting circuit width parameters—especially treewidth and pathwidth—with structured representations such as deterministic structured NNFs, OBDDs, decision-DNNFs, and FBDDs.

Typical methods include compiling query lineages into Boolean circuits, transforming bounded-width circuits into structured classes, and proving matching or contrasting upper and lower bounds on representation size. The work also analyzes exact model counting and weighted model counting, including their use for probability computation in tuple-independent probabilistic databases.

Several papers examine the relationship between grounded inference—constructing a lineage and then counting models—and lifted or extensional inference, which exploits query structure directly. Lower bounds for decision-DNNFs and FBDDs clarify limitations of propositional approaches. In parallel, new PTIME techniques construct deterministic decomposable circuits for classes of safe unions of conjunctive queries.

Recent trends therefore move toward a systematic taxonomy linking width, circuit structure, and compilation complexity, while developing deterministic decomposable representations that narrow the gap between intensional and extensional probabilistic query evaluation.

054f3e20a7aea3243e48961131d5b61adfc3afd7.text:
### Learning, Scaling, and Stewarding Data Systems

This community spans database performance, distributed transaction processing, scientific data management, and emerging data-centric infrastructures. A central theme is scaling OLTP on multicore and distributed hardware, especially under contention, cross-partition execution, and multi-datacenter replication. Work addresses recovery through parallel and adaptive logging, conflict repair for MVCC, specialized partitioning, and analyses of consistency, latency variance, and availability.

A second major theme is applying machine learning to database internals. Deep generative and likelihood models support approximate query processing, cardinality/selectivity estimation, and interactive analytics; neural and reinforcement-learning models optimize query plans and join orders. Learned indexes extend this idea to mutable relational data and DNA sequence search. Other systems improve throughput through query batching, spatial indexing, flat combining, and portable relational algorithms.

The community also emphasizes scientific and heterogeneous data: petabyte-scale astronomy, multidimensional search, finite-element data, video analytics, and integration across organizational silos. SkyServer, Jupyter notebooks, and library maps illustrate efforts toward accessible, navigable, and reproducible knowledge infrastructures, balanced against privacy and stewardship concerns.

Recent trends move toward learned and adaptive components, approximate results, fast-network distributed execution, energy- and predictability-aware optimization, and treating infrastructure maintenance, openness, and usability as integral to data management.

1f3603a13af051e669eb432d54b060dd872d1093.text:
### Unbiased Ranking, Evaluation, and Preference Learning

This community focuses on learning and evaluating search and recommender rankings under biased, sparse, or costly feedback. A central theme is presentation and examination bias in implicit signals such as clicks and dwell times, especially position bias in search and advertising. Work develops counterfactual and unbiased learning-to-rank methods using inverse propensity weighting, including unbiased LambdaMART and extensions to additive metrics such as DCG and Precision@k, nonlinear models, and deep rankers.

Several papers address estimating observation propensities. They propose non-intrusive methods that avoid manual judgments and disruptive interventions, as well as intervention harvesting for context-dependent examination bias through contextual position-based models. Reinforcement learning is applied to optimize sponsored-search ranking strategies, balancing advertiser and user objectives.

A second theme is reliable evaluation with limited resources. Active sampling and probabilistic Monte Carlo estimators reduce the cost of collecting relevance judgments while supporting unbiased comparative evaluation across ranking metrics. The community also compares offline and online recommender evaluation in small e-commerce settings, where interaction volumes and user loyalty are limited.

Finally, preference-elicitation interfaces seek dense datasets containing rich user information, connecting recommender research with behavioral science. Overall, recent trends move toward principled counterfactual estimation, contextual and deep ranking models, resource-efficient evaluation, and richer human-centered data collection.

6398ac20043aefe02bf9586ca9b64335a296fecc.text:
## Complex Networks for Science, Software, and Social Systems

This community applies complex-network analysis to understand structure, evolution, and quality across diverse systems. Major themes include scientific collaboration and citation networks, interdisciplinarity and knowledge structures, online social status and communication, healthcare collaboration, web-site topology, and software dependency networks.

Typical methods involve constructing graphs from web crawls, bibliographic databases, coauthorship, citations, keywords, entities, or software dependencies. Researchers use degree and centrality measures, community and group detection, mixing patterns, small-world and scale-free analyses, longitudinal and multilevel comparisons, and evolving-network models. Sampling and simplification techniques are systematically evaluated for their effects on graph properties. Network-based indicators are also proposed for software quality, entity impact, and research influence. Data matching, merging, and database-consistency analysis address reliability problems in heterogeneous scientific sources.

Recent work increasingly emphasizes dynamics rather than static structure: preferential attachment shifts toward betweenness in collaboration growth; social networks are studied through changing status and links; knowledge graphs and keyword networks support prediction of emerging literature-based discoveries; and interdisciplinary trajectories are quantified across fields and decades. Overall, the trend is toward scalable, context-aware, and predictive network frameworks that integrate heterogeneous data while validating the distortions introduced by sampling and incomplete databases.

be1dc573f37fdf1d7fd542ede5a7259b91870924.text:
### Personalized POI and Venue Recommendation

This community focuses primarily on personalized point-of-interest (POI) and venue recommendation in location-based social networks (LBSNs), alongside a broader effort to improve recommender representations beyond conventional matrix factorization. Core challenges include sparse check-in histories, contextual relevance, geographical influence, temporal variation, and effective user modeling.

Typical methods include collaborative ranking models enhanced with multiple location-based similarities, geographical signals, and temporal regularization based on changing popularity and user activity. Other work uses probabilistic mappings between user-generated tags and location taste keywords to address sparsity, and scoring-function approaches that combine venue content, reviews, social information, and user context. Context-aware models explicitly predict the appropriateness of locations under different circumstances.

A complementary line replaces dot-product factorization with metric factorization, representing users and items in a Euclidean space where closeness satisfies the metric inequality. More recent work shifts toward neural representation learning, generating POI embeddings from sequential behavior while incorporating categorical information. Overall, the research trends from basic collaborative filtering toward hybrid, context-aware, spatially and temporally sensitive models, with increasing use of richer side information and learned embeddings.

cb4f466125c060562fdb105d6303b13983df322e.text:
### Complex Event Processing for IoT and Streaming Systems

This community centers on processing, correlating, and interpreting continuous event streams from distributed sources, especially RFID and IoT sensors. Core themes include unifying event processing, data streams, and asynchronous messaging; detecting complex patterns; and transforming raw observations into actionable events. Several papers address the theoretical foundations of CEP, seeking principled models beyond ad-hoc APIs and enabling clearer extension and generalization.

Typical methods include specialized complex-event query languages (notably SASE), pattern matching over real-time streams, stream-query processing combined with location and containment inference, and distributed architectures for scalable RFID monitoring. The work also examines operational challenges: load shedding under resource constraints, consistency across time and heterogeneous synchronization regimes, and scalable event joins that reduce centralization bottlenecks in throughput, latency, and network use.

Recent trends move from standalone CEP toward integrated, distributed, and data-centric stream infrastructures. The emphasis is increasingly on IoT-scale acquisition, guaranteed time coherence, distributed inference, and graceful degradation, while preserving the immediacy and reliability needed for enterprise and physical-world applications.

410f35c0f866075a59ae8c63c321fa91a011e6f6.text:
## Adversarial Privacy Protection in Social Networks

This community studies how network-analysis algorithms can expose sensitive relationships, communities, and individual information, and how targeted perturbations can reduce their effectiveness. A central theme is adversarial manipulation of structural signals used by community detection, node similarity, and link prediction.

Typical methods modify the observed network by rewiring or removing a small number of edges. These changes aim to disrupt local similarity measures—especially neighborhood overlap and common-neighbor signals—or to conceal sensitive links that link-prediction algorithms might recover. Community deception is addressed through efficient attack strategies, including genetic-algorithm-based rewiring. Other work evaluates attack tolerance and systematically investigates how privacy-preserving individuals can hide relationships from link predictors.

Recent work increasingly focuses on targeted defense rather than only generic attacks. In particular, Resource Allocation-based attacks are countered using heuristic and evolutionary perturbation methods designed to protect selected links. Overall, the papers show a progression from exposing vulnerabilities in similarity-driven network analysis to developing adaptive, evolutionary defenses for privacy protection, while emphasizing the trade-off between limited network modifications and effective concealment.

55fe4777487030b9736ccd131138f122aa2e7f88.text:
### Big Data Benchmarking and Synthetic Workload Generation

This community focuses on building representative, scalable benchmarks and evaluating distributed data-processing systems. A central theme is the challenge of capturing big data’s 4V requirements—volume, variety, velocity, and veracity—while supporting diverse applications, workloads, and rapidly evolving architectures.

Typical methods include benchmark-suite construction, application-specific synthetic data generation, and feature-based dataset scaling. BDGS targets configurable generation across multiple data types and rates, whereas the feature-tweaking framework seeks more flexible control over synthetic datasets than fixed feature sets allow. BigDataBench addresses benchmark diversity through workloads derived from Internet services and, initially, web search engines, where proprietary data and access logs motivate alternative construction strategies and incremental development.

A second major methodological thread is empirical comparison of distributed stream-processing engines. Frameworks evaluate Apache Storm, Spark, and Flink using controlled workloads, particularly windowed operations, and measure key metrics such as throughput and latency. These studies emphasize detailed performance characterization rather than simple comparisons.

Recent trends include moving from narrow, system-specific generators and simple workloads toward general, scalable, application-oriented benchmark ecosystems. The papers also reflect increasing attention to workload diversity, controllability, benchmark fairness, and the practical difficulty of reproducing confidential or changing industrial data.

74f6f04f766b7cd1d581ab1036519b47820f0901.text:
## Recommender Systems: Personalization, Robustness, and Diversity

This community centers on improving personalized recommendation across products, news, music, movies, education, and advertising. Major themes include collaborative filtering and matrix factorization; sequential and session-based recommendation; multimodal and content-enhanced modeling; cold-start prediction; and long-tail exposure, diversity, and popularity-bias mitigation.

Typical methods range from slope-one predictors, neighborhood and signed-bipartite ranking, co-clustering, ontologies, and hybrid content/CF models to latent factor, metric-learning, collective-factorization, and mixture-of-tastes approaches. Neural methods are prominent, including variational and semi-autoencoders, nonlinear collaborative filtering, recurrent session models, DeepFM, and joint feature–interaction networks. Context trees, LSA, topic models, audiovisual features, and missing-modality dropout incorporate behavioral and item-side information. Re-ranking with personalized diversification and determinantal point processes targets diversity and tail discovery.

The papers also address reliability and societal concerns: shilling attacks, reputation and rating reliability, filter bubbles, and advertising’s effect on user experience. Recent work trends toward deep, nonlinear, multimodal, and sequential models; modeling users’ multiple interests and cross-session behavior; exploiting heterogeneous relationships and context; and producing scalable, interpretable, robust recommendations under sparsity, missing data, and cold-start conditions.

8b4f63acc51f40dde78918effaa3b243565e994e.text:
## User-Centered Learning and Evaluation for Complex Search

This community studies how search systems can learn from user behavior and optimize ranking, presentation, and evaluation across web, image, and aggregated search. A major theme is online learning to rank under imperfect feedback: list-level feedback, pairwise preferences, and implicit interactions. Methods include policy-gradient learning (PGLearn), dueling-bandit evaluation with merged double Thompson sampling, and Null Space Gradient Descent, which narrows exploration using poorly performing gradient directions.

Several papers develop richer behavioral models. They investigate image-search intent and two-dimensional browsing, construct interaction models for sparse and presentation-specific feedback, and predict sequences of clicks using neural encoder–decoder architectures. These models support more realistic interpretation of user satisfaction than isolated click prediction.

The community also addresses ranking beyond a simple linear list. Work on complex layouts jointly considers item relevance and display preferences, while context-aware module embedding selects heterogeneous aggregated-search modules using information from top blue-link results. SERP evaluation incorporates clicks and satisfaction, recognizing that no click can reflect successful immediate answers rather than dissatisfaction.

Recent trends move toward scalable online experimentation, structured and sequential interaction modeling, context-aware heterogeneous results, and evaluation frameworks that account for rich layouts and non-click user satisfaction.

0d3a79df98eb93213d2469135041dc42903b4181.text:
### Explainable and Empirical Machine Learning for Legal Review

This community focuses primarily on predictive coding and text classification for legal document review, where machine learning reduces the cost and effort of identifying responsive or privileged electronically stored information. A central theme is explainability: the work addresses lawyers’ concerns about “black box” systems and develops explainable classification and predictive-coding approaches, including a case study.

Methods are largely empirical. Studies compare Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines, Random Forest, Convolutional Neural Networks, and other deep-learning approaches across legal review datasets. One contribution evaluates CNNs on four real-world reviews containing documents of varied lengths, addressing limitations of experiments on short texts. Another examines how preprocessing parameters affect predictive-coding effectiveness, challenging reliance on fixed preprocessing settings and a single algorithm.

Recent trends include movement beyond traditional LR and SVM models toward deep learning, while retaining comparative evaluation against established methods. The community also increasingly emphasizes transparency, practical deployment, and systematic tuning of preprocessing choices. A related cybersecurity study extends analytics beyond legal review by using Google Analytics web-traffic data—such as visitor locations, timestamps, webpages, and search keywords—to support monitoring and evaluation of malicious cyber activity.

8f9aa1c8bd386efd3b572786c4a99c91bea7c567.text:
## Network Diffusion, Influence, and Epidemic Control

This community studies how information, influence, disease, and failures propagate through complex, social, temporal, and interdependent networks. Major themes include influence maximization and marketing, epidemic containment and cost, source localization, hidden-network recovery, cascade prediction, and diffusion-based signal comparison. Applications span social advertising, worker recruitment, wildlife dispersal, cyber-physical resilience, online popularity, and public-health interventions.

Typical methods combine probabilistic diffusion models—including independent cascade, linear threshold, SIS/SI, continuous-time Markov chains, and complex contagion—with optimization and learning. Common techniques include greedy and adaptive submodular policies, approximation guarantees, mixed-integer programming, random-walk and random-matrix analyses, message passing, particle-swarm heuristics, soft-thresholding, Jordan-center/cover algorithms, and contrastive learning over cascade trees. Sampling and unbiased estimation address resource-limited network observation.

Recent directions move beyond static, fully observed settings toward temporal, adaptive, and partially observed networks; online and feedback-driven seed selection; collective diffusion and aggregate observations; and explicit modeling of adoption, revenue, and social cost. The community also increasingly considers robustness and resilience, fairness across social groups, non-submodular cascades, external spreaders, and scalable inference under changing network structure.

a697d623fb50f9bbcdf9ecb826c2a5b4578a0f38.text:
### Online Social Networks: Structure, Diffusion, and Prediction

This community studies online social networks as dynamic systems for interaction, information diffusion, influence, and risk. Major themes include community structure and polarization; tie strength, homophily, heterogeneity, and network assembly or decay; information cascades, meme and video popularity, attention, engagement, and virality; and the detection of anomalies, misinformation, malicious URLs, criminal intermediaries, and systemic financial risk. Other work uses social data for demographic inference, event response, scholarly trend discovery, sports prediction, and suicide-ideation analysis.

Typical methods combine graph construction and network measures—centrality, pair-dependency, modularity, assortativity, fractal dimension, community detection, and strong/weak-tie analysis—with statistical modeling, game theory, diffusion and continuous-time network models, machine learning, embeddings, topic models, and multimodal content analysis. Large-scale datasets from Twitter, YouTube, Facebook, Yelp, scholarly graphs, transaction records, and disaster reporting are common; visualization and crowdsourced signals support risk monitoring and fact-checking.

Recent directions emphasize temporal and heterogeneous dynamics, content beyond simple social links (mass media, absent nodes, visual remixes, and transaction relations), early prediction of popularity and engagement, multimodal disaster intelligence, polarized political discourse, and interventions designed to limit misinformation or malicious influence.

b001d33cbc3504f8e57cf3e69900252854c733b1.text:
### Community Detection Across Complex Networks

This community centers on defining, detecting, evaluating, and exploiting community structure in complex networks. Major themes include ambiguity in what constitutes a “good” community, comparison of partitions using multi-criteria and Pareto-based evaluation, and quality measures for overlapping or fuzzy communities. Research addresses increasingly realistic settings: multilayer and multiplex networks, weighted and attributed graphs, dynamic networks, two-mode and public-private graphs, and networks with heterogeneous shared and unshared groups.

Typical methods include modularity optimization (including multislice and adaptive signed-weight variants), stochastic block and geometric block models, variational Bayes inference, label propagation, clique percolation, density-based clustering with manifold learning, local spectral diffusion, k-truss and core decomposition, and motif or dynamical-process analyses. PageRank variants support node importance, localization, link prediction, and community exploration.

Theoretical work studies spectral detectability limits, metastability, surface-tension interpretations of block models, neighborhood quality, and global bridge identification. Practical studies examine peer influence, risky behavior, churn, and information extraction in social networks.

Recent directions emphasize scalable local methods for massive graphs, stability and inclusiveness for low-degree nodes, algorithm selection, dynamic visualization and evolving influence, adversarial community deception, active learning, and richer models combining topology with attributes and multiple interaction types.

815b3a353199233faa10368fa9106c2e77bb857d.text:
### Scientometric Mapping, Metrics, and Responsible Evaluation

This community focuses on measuring and mapping scientific and technological activity. Major themes include citation and publication indicators for authors, journals, institutions, countries, and research programs; field delineation and cross-disciplinary comparison; and the construction of technology, journal, citation, and collaboration networks.

Typical methods combine Web of Science, Scopus, Microsoft Academic, Dimensions, and patent data with co-citation, bibliographic coupling, keyword/MeSH mapping, network centrality, similarity measures, clustering, overlays, and visualization. Researchers develop or assess indicators such as the h-index, K-index, I3, SNIP, percentile-based measures, internationality scores, and contribution-adjusted indices. Fractional counting, field normalization, benchmarking, and analyses of statistical significance address disciplinary differences, collaboration size, and skewed citation distributions.

A second methodological strand reconstructs intellectual history through citation networks and Reference Publication Year Spectroscopy (RPYS), including interactive tools such as RPYS i/o and CRExplorer. Studies also examine database coverage and concordance, especially for linked references and conference proceedings.

Recent trends include evaluating newer platforms such as Dimensions, exploiting digitally accessible article-level data, and questioning the declining connection between journal impact factors and individual paper influence. The literature increasingly emphasizes scale invariance, fair credit allocation, responsible assessment, and the unintended effects of national evaluation systems.

c6ec0ecaba755de9caaa7f9ea1c430649ceada65.text:
## Recommender Systems: Sequential, Neural, and Responsible Personalization

This community covers collaborative, content-based, hybrid, and graph-based recommender systems, with particular emphasis on modeling user preferences, sequential behavior, and item relationships. Core themes include combining long-term preferences with short-term dynamics, session-based and cross-domain recommendation, cold-start and missing-modality handling, and representing diverse user interests through mixture-of-tastes models.

Typical methods range from slope-one predictors, matrix factorization, nearest-neighbor and co-clustering techniques to latent-variable models, metric learning, Bayesian approaches, and ontologies. Neural methods increasingly model nonlinear interactions using autoencoders, recurrent networks, convolutional models, DeepFM, and joint feature-learning architectures. Graph formulations capture signed user–item relations, complex session transitions, trust, temporal information, and local network structure. Content signals include text, tags, subtitles, audio, visual features, and multimodal representations.

A strong secondary focus is recommendation quality beyond accuracy: popularity and long-tail exposure, diversity via personalized reranking and determinantal point processes, interpretability, reputation, and robustness to fraudulent reviews and noisy ratings. Recent work emphasizes anonymous session recommendation with graph neural networks, inter-session context, reinforcement learning for advertising, multimodal learning under missing data, and challenging settings such as shared accounts and cross-domain sequential behavior.

fba344e55e792fe76ac17dd06c8616dc78541fca.text:
## Social Media Networks, Misinformation, and Online Influence

This community focuses on analyzing social-media ecosystems as networks of political discourse, misinformation, polarization, and security risk. Major themes include community detection and echo chambers; political disinformation, conspiracy narratives, extremist and ISIS content; search and platform bias; bot-, spam-, and autogenerated-content detection; and demographic inequalities in Twitter participation. Several studies examine interventions, including fact-checking, targeted public-health social bots, curated user lists, and strategies for accelerating or limiting information diffusion. Related work addresses Sybil attacks, malicious-node removal, Facebook application privacy, and decentralized search.

Typical methods combine network construction and graph analytics—centrality, clustering, spectral embedding, link prediction, structural balance, and community segregation—with machine learning using textual, temporal, metadata, and interaction features. Nonnegative matrix factorization, semi-supervised and real-time classifiers, stance detection, image-based demographic inference, surveys, and computational diffusion or epidemic models are also prominent. Large-scale platform datasets, including Twitter, Facebook, YouTube, Reddit, Gab, and search logs, support comparative and temporal analyses.

Recent work increasingly studies election-related disinformation, computational propaganda, extremist-content adoption, cross-platform influence, emotional and narrative dynamics, and the limitations of evaluation and sampling practices.

3719a4721df9108102bbdef7de89b46201bba299.text:
**Scholarly Impact, Discovery, and Digital Communication**

This community studies how scholarly communication is changing through repositories, social media, digital libraries, and online academic platforms. Major themes include validating altmetrics as indicators of societal or scientific impact; relationships among citations, downloads, readership, tweets, and Mendeley activity; open-access and preprint effects; and the evaluation of books, publishers, journals, and conferences. Another substantial strand develops tools for discovering and recommending articles and venues, categorizing conferences, and matching manuscripts with suitable reviewers. Peer-review processes, hyperlink behavior, and bibliographic data quality are also examined.

Typical methods combine large-scale bibliometric and webometric datasets with citation, download, readership, loan, review, and social-media logs. Studies use correlations, regression, principal-component and factor analysis, distributional modeling, comparative case studies, expert interviews, and visualization. Technical contributions apply machine learning to hyperlink classification, reference disambiguation, recommendation, and reviewer assignment, including integer programming and learned suitability scores.

Recent work emphasizes heterogeneous and noisy online traces, their dependencies and validity, and the need to distinguish audiences and meanings across platforms. Preprints, open repositories, and early usage signals are increasingly treated as mechanisms for rapid dissemination and possible citation advantage, while altmetrics are framed more broadly as traces of the computerization of research and as complements—not replacements—for traditional evaluation.

fb4e550cfbc9792b5f07c6a26f8222a1b3eea7e7.text:
### Social Media Analytics for Human Behavior and Urban Intelligence

This community studies how user-generated and location-based social media can reveal preferences, influence, mobility, place perception, and collective behavior. Major themes include computational political analysis (voter preferences, ideological orientation, polarized voting, and candidate engagement), geolocation and mobility inference, urban sensing, and commercial recommendation. Researchers also examine group scheduling, co-location, event diffusion, online reputation, business-site selection, and influential users.

Typical methods combine large-scale Twitter, Facebook, Instagram, Flickr, Reddit, Yelp, Weibo, cellphone, and check-in data with machine learning and network analysis. Techniques include sparse learning, supervised classifiers, convolutional neural networks, latent Dirichlet allocation, regression on likes, graph and signed-network models, low-rank approximation, trajectory clustering, sentiment analysis, and graph-based feature extraction. Geospatial studies infer locations, home places, urban boundaries, functional regions, and emotionally or sensorially pleasant routes; several construct dictionaries from text, images, or tags to map smell and sound.

Recent work emphasizes scalable distributed processing, multimodal and semantic representations, uncertainty calibration, bias correction, and out-of-sample validation against surveys or independent mobility data. It also moves toward fine-grained behavioral prediction, automated tracking of sensitive reports, and parsimonious digital traces that achieve strong prediction with limited data.

9c993c58637bed53516400728f7d801f8604e6f6.text:
## Social Media Geolocation, Information Quality, and Political Polarization

This community studies how social-media data can reveal users’ locations, mobility, news consumption, and political information environments. Geolocation research develops neural models for predicting Twitter users’ locations from tweet text, profile metadata, and noisy language. Convolutional networks, character-aware embeddings, feature fusion, and hierarchical country-to-city prediction are recurring methods. Large-scale empirical analysis—covering billions of tweets and millions of users—also examines who geotags content and whether geotagged users can represent broader populations.

A second major theme is junk news, misinformation, and polarization around US elections and military affairs. Studies use curated source dictionaries, user self-reported locations, platform-specific datasets, and network or ideological analyses to measure the spread and concentration of extremist, conspiratorial, Russian-linked, and other low-quality content. Controlled social bots on Weibo provide an experimental method for testing how content preferences affect news diversity.

Recent work increasingly emphasizes political events, subgroup targeting, cross-platform analysis, and transparency through junk-news aggregation, while continuing to improve automated location inference. The community also addresses imperfect observational data more broadly, including methods for recovering movement order when location trails have low temporal resolution.

05f6e854d92ea2876e940bb008feab50ed1402bc.text:
## Dynamic and Applied Graph Mining

This community studies complex, social, heterogeneous, and temporal networks, emphasizing how structure, content, and evolution support prediction and decision-making. Major themes include dynamic network representation, community detection, link and relationship prediction, graph classification, centrality, clustering, and structural analysis. Knowledge-graph applications address entity normalization, triple scoring, predicate-path mining, and fact checking, often combining textual evidence with graph connectivity and type information.

Typical methods range from stochastic blockmodels, latent-space and probabilistic graph grammars to random walks, Markov chains, min-cut optimization, and axiomatic models. Neural and embedding-based approaches are increasingly prominent, including deep clustering, metapath-guided cross-modal embeddings, dynamic walks, continuous-time heterogeneous prediction, and neural inference for generative models. Ensemble learning, random forests, and machine learning are applied to fraud, criminal, insider-trading, and team-composition problems.

A parallel systems-oriented strand develops graph sampling, triangle counting, distance indexes, external-memory generation, and MapReduce algorithms for massive networks. Theoretical work examines locality, convexity, core-periphery structure, clustering thresholds, and complexity. Recent directions emphasize temporal robustness, continuous-time dynamics, uncertainty-aware inference, cross-network fusion, privacy prediction, fraud de-anonymization, and more realistic evaluation benchmarks tied to downstream or business objectives rather than reconstruction alone.

6348b6d808a57b58d1164d521eb63ff55e6b1518.text:
## Network-Based Science Mapping and Information Retrieval

This community studies how graph structure can represent, rank, and explain scholarly, web, patent, and geopolitical information. Major themes include bibliometric evaluation of authors, papers, universities, conferences, and communities; Wikipedia link-network analysis across languages and cultures; knowledge organization and visualization for digital libraries; and scalable data mining.

PageRank, CheiRank, weighted and reduced Google matrices are recurring methods for measuring prestige, popularity, influence, and cross-entity interactions. Studies also use centrality measures, coauthorship and citation networks, community detection, stochastic block models, graphons, spectral analysis, and PageRank-ordered matrix patterns. Bibliographic work addresses author disambiguation through “seed+expand,” citation-label bias, prestige versus popularity, career development, and community stability. Information-retrieval research explores knowledge maps, discipline-specific query expansion, user mouse-fixation signals, relevance-assessment reliability, linked-data metadata enrichment, and integrated digital libraries. MapReduce Apriori addresses scalable itemset mining.

Recent trends emphasize longitudinal and multilingual Wikipedia datasets, multicultural and geopolitical inference, dynamic prediction of patent-cluster growth and emerging technologies, and visual or interactive science mapping. Neural title simplification and richer digital-library interfaces indicate growing attention to discoverability and user-facing scholarly services.

c5852a70a24b9973e19bcfc23c264b09480faeb2.text:
### Information Retrieval: Neural Ranking, Semantic Search, and Conversational Systems

This community centers on improving information retrieval and ranking across web, enterprise, e-commerce, bibliographic, entity, dataset, and personal collections. Major themes include learning-to-rank, relevance modeling, query expansion and clustering, passage and document retrieval, and quality or spam detection. Specialized applications address expert finding, mobile app selection, email search, event-image retrieval, and temporal entity-aspect recommendation.

Typical methods combine traditional retrieval principles with learned representations. Deep architectures model local relevance, cross-document interactions, groupwise scoring, or field-level semantics. BERT and multilingual BERT support multi-stage pointwise/pairwise reranking, non-factoid question answering, and cross-lingual relevance transfer. Other approaches use word/query embeddings, knowledge-enriched entity representations, kernels, semantic hashing, graph models, bipartite ranking, and axiomatic regularization. Benchmark collections such as LETOR and WikiPassageQA support evaluation.

Recent work increasingly emphasizes conversational and interactive retrieval: personal-memory question answering, history-aware conversational QA, conversational recommendations, and dynamic multi-stage search. It also explores unified search across mobile apps, agents for retrieval, and temporal or event-driven relevance. Interpretability, adversarial recommendation attacks, web-based data imputation, and permutation-invariant or latency-aware ranking reflect growing concern for robustness, transparency, scalability, and deployment constraints.

de449020a4bc84c0a1fd957c417c945fc5b126fd.text:
## Graph Querying, Semantics, and Interoperable Data Management

This community centers on graph data systems, especially RDF/SPARQL and property graphs. Major themes include efficient SPARQL evaluation and optimization—covering joins, OPTIONAL/left-outer joins, federations, replicated fragments, runtime planning, provenance, entailment, preferences, keyword integration, and OLAP data cubes. A parallel focus is the formal study of query semantics, complexity, containment, subsumption, path queries, multiset behavior, and incomplete information.

Typical methods combine algebraic rewriting, cost- and summary-based optimization, incremental evaluation, structural indexing, source selection, Datalog and chase-based reasoning, and formal complexity analysis. Systems-oriented work introduces graph traversal languages, property-graph type systems, RDF–relational and RDF–property-graph mappings, and benchmarking generators such as gMark. Graph analytics also addresses uncertain-network reliability and provenance-graph summarization.

Additional strands concern XML schema and wrapper inference, regular and context-free path querying, view updates, and query answering under tuple-generating dependencies. Recent trends emphasize interoperability across RDF, relational, and property-graph platforms; scalable federated and replicated querying; usability through keyword, example-based, and preference-driven interfaces; and richer semantics for trust, uncertainty, provenance, and OWL entailment.

444f4d4e29299e78fbb334aae097693ec7888a07.text:
## Efficient, Flexible, and Responsible Data Retrieval

This community advances data management and search across structured, uncertain, graph, spatial, and web data. Major themes include fuzzy databases and linguistic summaries for imprecise information; skyline, ranking, reranking, and recommendation methods supporting diverse preferences; and crawling or querying hidden databases through public interfaces. Fairness is an emerging concern, addressed through bias measurement, demographic-aware reranking, image representations, and “antidote” data to reduce polarization.

Efficiency is a central methodological focus. Work develops compact indexes and summaries, including bitmap and Roaring indexes, wavelet histograms, compressed inverted lists, variable-byte and Huffman coding, and specialized set-intersection and hashing algorithms. Other studies accelerate workloads with SIMD, GPUs, hybrid CPU/GPU systems, and in-memory execution. Query processing contributions cover top-k and any-k graph pattern retrieval, learned graph query planning, workflow search, incomplete-data skylines, aggregate skyline joins, and geometric pruning for ride sharing.

Recent directions emphasize scalable distributed processing, notably Spark/Flink frequent-subgraph mining and MapReduce summarization; practical third-party query reranking; machine learning for query planning; and socially aware retrieval and recommendation. Across the papers, the recurring goal is to balance expressive, user-centered search with low latency, compact representation, and scalable computation.

176f316568aa0a33f8b1198049d964b0b9d7e8e2.text:
### Learning, Scale, and Resilience in Data Management

This community centers on building faster, more adaptive, and more scalable data systems. A major theme is **learned data management**: deep neural, autoregressive, embedding, and reinforcement-learning models estimate cardinalities, optimize query and join plans, integrate heterogeneous relational data, select materialized views, and replace or augment indexes. Learned indexes such as ALEX and LISA extend these ideas to dynamic and domain-specific workloads.

A second theme is **high-performance transaction processing**. Work addresses multicore OLTP under contention, distributed transactions over fast networks, adaptive execution, MVCC conflict repair, synchronization tradeoffs, predictable latency, recovery, and consistency checking. Blockchain research compares decentralized systems with distributed databases and explores lightweight emulation and blockchain layers for existing DBMSs.

The community also studies **large-scale scientific and heterogeneous data**: multidimensional indexing, batch query processing, petabyte-scale astronomy, relational backends for finite-element analysis, and systems that traverse siloed data. Related work emphasizes open science, Jupyter-based reproducibility, and the stewardship and long-term durability of research infrastructures.

Recent trends move from hand-tuned heuristics toward data-driven adaptation, deep learning, and reinforcement learning, while exploiting multicore hardware, RDMA networks, and integrated blockchain/database architectures.

111a57ecbc5a35d8c926894778294901854c7c71.text:
### Network Centrality, Dynamics, and Influence

This community studies how network structure shapes visibility, influence, information flow, and collective behavior. A major theme is defining and evaluating node importance through PageRank, Bonacich, degree variants, harmonic and distinctiveness centrality, navigability, discoverability, robustness, and influence-based measures. Several works address strategic network design: rewiring links to maximize centrality or PageRank, improve coverage and delay, alter social dominance, expose target nodes, or conceal influential actors in covert networks.

Opinion dynamics form another core theme. DeGroot, Friedkin–Johnsen, bounded-confidence, Bayesian, and multi-topic models examine consensus, polarization, stability, biases, antagonistic signed ties, heterogeneous thresholds, and logical dependence between issues. These models increasingly account for time-varying interactions, randomized gossip, recommendations, and feedback between opinions and content exposure.

Typical methods combine graph theory, spectral and asymptotic analysis, game theory, optimization, mean-field approximations, dynamical systems, and simulation. Empirical studies mine voting, traffic, and social-media data, while algorithms target scalable backbone discovery and dynamic random-walk computation.

Recent directions emphasize dynamic and signed networks, robustness under noise or disconnection, topic-specific user behavior, adaptive personalization, and theoretically guaranteed algorithms for large, evolving graphs.

37f6d75de33bf3a46ffd4d88eec8611c648c7ec5.text:
## Data Integration, Entity Resolution, and Crowdsourced Quality

This community centers on making heterogeneous, noisy, and conflicting data reliable. Major themes include entity resolution and consolidation, truth discovery and data fusion, schema and constraint discovery, Web information extraction, and quality-aware crowdsourcing. Applications span open and linked data, social networks, government addresses, scientific and urban spatio-temporal data, and fact checking.

Typical methods combine probabilistic models, source-reliability and dependence modeling, graph matching, collective inference, and hybrid human–machine workflows. Entity-resolution systems use blocking, locality-sensitive hashing, edit-distance and similarity joins, distributed representations, progressive comparison ordering, and neighborhood message passing to improve scalability. Data quality is addressed through functional and order dependencies, ontology constraints, pattern and schema mining, and golden-record construction. Crowdsourcing techniques estimate worker reliability, control precision and recall, reduce labeling latency, and optimize spatial task assignment and human verification costs.

Recent trends emphasize democratizing and automating traditionally expert-driven integration: deep learning and embeddings reduce feature engineering; schema-agnostic and large-scale methods support Web-scale data; models increasingly account for copying, source dependence, multiple truths, uncertainty, and unknown data. Human input remains important, but is increasingly targeted through active cleaning, confidence guarantees, adaptive task selection, and cooperative systems that balance accuracy, coverage, latency, and cost.

f845db77dac51a70af9056a641bcc5ec54ffd8e3.text:
### Privacy-Preserving Data Analysis and Publishing

This community focuses on releasing and analyzing sensitive data while balancing formal privacy, accuracy, and practical utility. Differential privacy is the dominant framework, applied to histograms, sparse and high-dimensional data, marginal and range queries, frequent itemsets, clustering, community detection, decision trees, search logs, and hierarchical population statistics. Complementary work studies k-anonymity and its variants, slicing, perturbation, provenance views, surrogates, and anonymization of set-valued, graph, mobility, and social-network data.

Typical methods add calibrated noise, privately construct hierarchical decompositions or data-dependent partitions, and use wavelet transforms, matrix mechanisms, strategy-query selection, convex optimization, and adaptive workload-aware query answering. Other approaches use approximation algorithms, synthetic data generation, randomized response, local differential privacy, and reconstruction-resistant randomization. Several papers explicitly model adversarial background knowledge, algorithm-aware attacks, membership disclosure, and privacy leakage from supposedly useful outputs.

Applications increasingly extend beyond static tabular release to recommendation from private mobility data, data cleaning through noisy interfaces, graph path queries, dynamic social links, and fair allocation decisions. Recent directions emphasize local privacy, high-dimensional and sparse workloads, near-optimal accuracy, scalable and efficient implementations, data- and workload-adaptive mechanisms, and guarantees that incorporate fairness or analyst-specified accuracy rather than privacy alone.

69ac4d445a4e94f30a3bdb66fb7a573a2087cc84.text:
## Approximate Nearest-Neighbor Search and Graph-Based Retrieval

This community focuses on efficient similarity search and retrieval across high-dimensional, binary, non-metric, and database-integrated settings. A central theme is approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) indexing: methods include locality-sensitive hashing (LSH), hybrid LSH schemes for radius-neighbor reporting, angular multi-index hashing for cosine search over binary codes, and approximate neighborhood graphs for complex or asymmetric distances.

Several works address the practical construction and evaluation of ANN systems. One studies merging independently built \(k\)-NN graphs, while ANN-Benchmarks provides standardized interfaces, datasets, parameter sweeps, quality measures, and visualizations for comparing in-memory ANN algorithms. Graph-based retrieval is also extended beyond conventional metric assumptions, with index construction potentially using modified or symmetrized distances to improve performance.

The papers additionally explore system integration, exemplified by IDEL, which embeds neural entity linking into the MonetDB relational database through Python user-defined functions and machine-learning libraries.

Recent trends emphasize robust performance across diverse data distributions, sublinear querying, scalable index construction and merging, support for non-metric data, and reproducible benchmarking rather than reliance on a single indexing paradigm.

f9f1e1303604fcdc7735cb4c5a8af38498899a27.text:
## Computational Analysis of Fictional Character Networks

This community studies fictional narratives as social graphs, representing characters as nodes and interactions—such as conversation, friendship, or killing—as edges. The main goals include plot summarization, subplot and role detection, narrative classification, recommendation, and understanding the social dynamics of films and television series.

Typical methods include manual, co-occurrence-based, and machine-learning extraction of character networks, with comparisons of their precision and analytical effects. Network analysis is applied to static structure, causality, centrality, temporal evolution, and changing relationships across episodes or seasons. Case studies focus particularly on *Friends* and *Game of Thrones*, examining balanced prominence, shifting friendship patterns, dramatic deaths, and the relation between narrative structure and popularity. Link-prediction techniques are used to forecast killer–victim pairs from prior interactions and metadata.

Recent directions emphasize dynamic and temporally smoothed conversational networks for reconstructing plots, automated extraction at scale, and predictive modeling. Beyond interaction graphs, ecological-diversity measures based on Shannon entropy and Jensen–Shannon divergence estimate effective cast sizes and compare character composition across movies, supporting classification and recommendation.

e706578d985b755b46530ef9d0c6d3202b4d7553.text:
## Distributed Representations for Sparse Text and Music

This community focuses on learning semantic representations when surface-level overlap is insufficient, spanning very short social-media texts, folksong motifs, playlists, and music-consumption histories. A central theme is replacing traditional tf-idf or co-occurrence methods with distributed embeddings that capture latent semantic, melodic, or sequential relationships.

Typical methods include word2vec-style skip-gram models with negative sampling, cosine similarity, and aggregation of word embeddings for short-text comparison. Weighted aggregation using inverse document frequency (idf) improves representations, while a median-based loss reduces the influence of outliers in noisy text. For music, embeddings represent folksong motifs and support melodic-similarity evaluation and analysis of variation. Sequence-to-sequence models are explored for playlist representation and recommendation, while recurrent neural networks model users’ music preferences across multiple time scales, addressing temporal consumption and the limitations of explicit-rating collaborative filtering.

Recent trends emphasize robust, reusable representations that work across contexts without retraining, richer evaluation tasks beyond simple word overlap, and neural models that incorporate sequence and temporal structure. The applications increasingly extend from semantic similarity toward large-scale personalization and recommendation.

3bbd4cb7f44888ca3e0b8ee4500ccbad0fad022a.text:
### Provenance and Scalable Interactive Analytics

This community explores systems that make data analysis and visualization interactive despite expensive queries, large datasets, and complex workflows. A central theme is avoiding repeated computation: compact provisioning constructs a polynomial-size sketch supporting queries across exponentially many hypothetical scenarios. Provenance and lineage provide a complementary foundation, representing interactions and tracing relationships between individual input and output items for visualization, debugging, auditing, explanation, cleaning, and iterative analytics.

Typical methods include provenance-based modeling of visualization interactions, fine-grained lineage capture and query processing, and transparent delegation from browser applications to backend services when local resources are insufficient. The work also investigates execution directly in the browser: Afterburner implements an analytical relational DBMS in JavaScript, using compiled query plans, typed arrays, and asm.js to approach native MonetDB performance on simple queries.

Recent trends emphasize shifting analytics toward interactive, user-facing environments while hiding system complexity. Rather than requiring extensive application rewrites or repeated computation, these systems seek transparent scaling, reusable computational summaries, and responsive fine-grained data explanations.

56f5755a79caa1b3a10f93ea6c2c946c09cf74a9.text:
## Recommender Systems Under Sparse and Changing Feedback

This community focuses on practical recommendation and ranking in e-commerce and travel marketplaces. Central themes include matching users with items or providers, optimizing destination recommendations for user preferences, candidate generation, and especially cold-start settings.

Typical methods combine latent-factor recommendation with content-based modeling: convolutional neural networks are used to predict item representations from descriptions when interaction-derived factors are unavailable. Deep learning is also examined broadly for candidate generation and cold-start recommendation. Marketplace research frames recommendation as a two-sided matching problem, balancing guests’ needs with accommodation providers’ reach and revenue. Evaluation includes large-scale online experiments against production systems and standard offline baselines.

A major recent trend is moving beyond the traditional “new user or new item” cold-start definition. The work on continuous cold start emphasizes that even known users may provide sparse, noisy, outdated, or contradictory history because they visit infrequently, change interests, or adopt different personas. This motivates methods that do not depend solely on personal interaction histories and instead exploit item content and broader interaction data. Overall, the papers reflect a shift from static collaborative filtering toward deep, content-aware, production-tested personalization.

188ab2a8137b2a9eb2b77dadf76fa475c41697d3.text:
## Structured Discovery and Querying Across Web Data Lakes

This community focuses on making heterogeneous web and enterprise data searchable, navigable, and usable as structured information. A central theme is table-centric retrieval: systems answer keyword or column-keyword queries with relevant multi-column tables, discover knowledge-graph patterns for composing table answers, and automatically complete tables from natural-language descriptions, desired columns, and example rows.

A second theme is data-lake organization and discovery. Proposed navigation structures represent attribute sets as graph nodes and subset relationships as edges, with probabilistic models estimating users’ likelihood of finding relevant datasets. Complementary domain-search work treats datasets as value sets and ranks them using Jaccard set containment, enabling scalable search across open-data and web repositories.

Typical methods include knowledge graphs, RDF/SPARQL, database dependencies, semantic table transformations, graph-based organizations, probabilistic user models, and locality-sensitive hashing for internet-scale retrieval. Foundational work also advocates globally defined, ordered, multidimensional domains to make information comparable and searchable.

Recent trends move away from expensive schema engineering and isolated keyword search toward automated, semantic, and interactive discovery. The papers increasingly integrate navigation with search, exploit weakly structured tables directly, and use knowledge bases and learned or probabilistic structures to support scalable table construction and data exploration.

fbf968444e25f96e8f6ab7f971b89b0b26ea8aa0.text:
### Knowledge Compilation for Probabilistic Query Inference

This community studies exact inference for unions of conjunctive queries (UCQs) over tuple-independent probabilistic databases, focusing on the relationship between extensional and intensional approaches. Extensional methods exploit query structure directly, often using inclusion–exclusion, while intensional methods compile query lineages into tractable Boolean representations and then compute probabilities.

Typical methods include weighted model counting, decision-DNNFs, deterministic decomposable negation normal forms (d-DNNFs), structured circuits, OBDDs, and free binary decision diagrams. The work systematically relates these knowledge-compilation classes to circuit width parameters such as treewidth and pathwidth, providing both transformations and upper/lower bounds on representation size.

A recurring concern is the limitation of propositional or grounded inference for query expressions, motivating lifted and extensional alternatives. Other results establish lower bounds for exact model counting by relating decision-DNNFs to FBDDs with quasipolynomial overhead. Recent trends emphasize constructing deterministic decomposable circuits in polynomial time for safe query classes, resolving parts of the intensional–extensional conjecture, and clarifying when bounded-width lineage circuits can yield compact structured representations.

fab9dd21604a22fbe408955fd5c99ba12dea0645.text:
## Acknowledgements, Funding, and Evidence-Based Research Evaluation

This community examines scholarly acknowledgements as an underused source of information for understanding research funding, collaboration, credit, and evaluation. Several studies characterize Web of Science funding-acknowledgement data, documenting its growth since systematic indexing began in 2008 and assessing distributions across databases, languages, and acknowledgement types. They emphasize substantial coverage limitations and interpretive biases, recommending caution in bibliometric use.

A related humanities-focused study argues that acknowledgements expose otherwise invisible contributions and interactions, complementing conventional authorship and citation indicators. Combining authorship with acknowledged individuals further reveals disciplinary differences in credit attribution: accounting for acknowledgees substantially narrows apparent contrasts in collaborative team size.

Typical methods include large-scale bibliometric and database analyses, comparative examination of disciplinary and language patterns, and the integration of authorship and acknowledgement networks.
