The community also includes a data-driven evidential-reasoning approach to multi-criteria R&D project selection, which weights expert-derived evidence by reliability and produces belief-based rankings, demonstrated through a National Natural Science Foundation of China case study.

Recent trends therefore move toward broadening research assessment beyond authors and citations, while improving methodological transparency, bias awareness, and evidence integration for funding and project-selection decisions.

0352cbfd7616226f484b69bc1d56adf84e89c2bf.text:
## Personalized POI and Venue Recommendation

This community focuses on personalized point-of-interest (POI) and venue recommendation in location-based social networks, addressing sparse check-in data while modeling users’ preferences, context, geography, time, and venue characteristics. A broader theme is improving collaborative filtering beyond conventional matrix factorization: metric factorization replaces dot-product similarity with Euclidean closeness, while logistic matrix factorization incorporates local geographical effects.

Typical methods include collaborative ranking, learning-to-rank models, probabilistic mappings between user tags and location taste keywords, and user-modeling through relevance or social-centric scoring functions. Several approaches exploit auxiliary signals—geographical similarity, venue content and reviews, contextual appropriateness, popularity, user activity, and categorical information—to reduce sparsity and improve personalization. Time-sensitive regularization and a two-phase ranking procedure explicitly model changing popularity and activity patterns.

Recent trends move toward richer, multimodal representations and neural methods. Category-aware location embeddings combine sequential and categorical POI information, while context-aware systems increasingly integrate users’ situations with venue features. Overall, the research trajectory progresses from classical factorization and handcrafted similarity scores toward joint models that combine spatial, temporal, social, semantic, and contextual signals.

cd736e039a525e1b13bf61c0237a48c4f634a35a.text:
### Supporting Completeness and Participation in Collaborative Knowledge Bases

This community focuses on improving the coverage, organization, and usability of collaboratively built knowledge resources, especially Wikipedia and Wikidata. A central theme is identifying missing or underrepresented knowledge: recommending Wikipedia articles that exist in one language but not another, completing movie entities across multiple online knowledge libraries, and estimating the completeness of ontology-defined classes in Wikidata.

Typical methods combine recommendation and statistical inference. Systems identify candidate gaps, rank them by importance, and suggest articles or sections for creation and expansion. Cross-library completion exploits complementary information among multiple sources. For Wikidata, nonparametric class-cardinality estimation provides a way to assess how fully classes are represented without relying solely on explicit counts. Other work personalizes participation by automatically mining questionnaires to elicit new users’ interests and recommend articles or potential collaborators.

Recent trends move beyond simple content recommendation toward holistic ecosystem support: multilingual and multi-library knowledge integration, structural recommendations for article organization, quantitative monitoring of class coverage, and personalized onboarding designed to convert newcomers into sustained contributors.

0ce83899e153895a817ed26fc6a19c60f4c54163.text:
### Quality Control and Sustainability in Community Q&A

This community studies how moderation, question quality, and user activity shape community-driven question-answering (CQA) platforms, especially Stack Overflow and Stack Exchange. Key problems include characterizing and predicting closed or deleted questions, distinguishing clear from unclear questions requiring clarification, and explaining why some Q&A instances become sustainable while others remain niche or inactive.

Typical methods combine large-scale analysis of publicly available platform data with supervised classification and predictive modeling. Studies examine closure categories and deletion patterns, construct datasets of clear/unclear questions, and use similarity-based features to identify questions needing clarification. Machine-learning comparisons include shallow and deep neural networks, with explicit analysis of the trade-off between network depth, predictive accuracy, and computational cost. At the community level, quantitative analysis across 50 Stack Exchange instances is used to derive activity archetypes and factors relevant to community management.

Recent work trends toward automated quality-control and moderation support rather than purely descriptive analysis. Prediction of undesirable content is extended from closed questions to deleted and unclear questions, while the scope broadens from individual posts and Stack Overflow to cross-instance explanations of long-term Q&A sustainability.

77ac22c0b415ee6031b2a881984e86b6f2fd0a9c.text:
### Big Data Benchmarking, Generation, and Stream Analytics

This community focuses on building realistic, scalable benchmarks and improving the performance evaluation of big-data systems. A major theme is synthetic data generation: **BDGS** targets the four Vs—volume, variety, velocity, and veracity—while a feature-tweaking framework addresses the difficulty of scaling empirical datasets without losing their characteristics. **BigDataBench** develops application-driven benchmark suites from Internet services and web search engines, using incremental construction to handle workload diversity, confidentiality, and rapidly changing systems.

Another central theme is distributed stream processing. Two benchmarking frameworks compare Apache Storm, Spark, and Flink, particularly through throughput and latency measurements for windowed and other stream workloads. These studies emphasize detailed performance characterization rather than simple system comparisons.

Typical methods include configurable data generators, feature extraction and manipulation, workload suites derived from real applications, controlled experimental evaluation, and cross-system performance measurement. At the hardware level, StreamBox investigates stream analytics on hybrid DDR4–HBM memory, addressing HBM’s limited capacity and preference for sequential, highly parallel access despite the random-access demands of grouping operations.

Recent trends include broader and more application-specific benchmark coverage, support for diverse data and workloads, reproducible synthetic-data control, fine-grained stream-engine analysis, and hardware/software co-design for high-bandwidth memory systems.

0f5bbfa7472cada4212421198d218b97bc11150b.text:
### Research Software as Citable, Reproducible Scholarship

This community examines how research software can become a recognized, durable, and measurable component of scientific scholarship. Key themes include integrating software into citation graphs, improving reproducibility in computational science, establishing consistent terminology, and creating incentives and evidence of software impact.

Typical approaches are conceptual and infrastructure-oriented: proposing directed graph models that represent relationships among papers and software; designing publication venues such as the Journal of Open Source Software (JOSS) to provide quality review and academic credit; and advocating for complete software environments, code, and data rather than isolated source archives. Other work uses literature surveys and decision trees to classify competing meanings of “reproducible research,” while empirical analysis investigates whether citation data can measure software impact, using the lme4 R package as a case study.

Recent trends point toward treating software as a first-class research object. Efforts increasingly connect publication, credit, citation, and reproducibility, including applications such as transitive credit. At the same time, the community highlights unresolved challenges: inconsistent citation practices, fragmented terminology, and difficulty establishing reliable impact measures. Together, these works promote more sustainable computational research through formal recognition, improved sharing, and better measurement of software contributions.

d3dca25f9b61d639127a30501e23e8d79a391dca.text:
### Mapping Bias, Attention, and Events in Global News

This community studies how global news is selected, distributed, and interpreted across media systems, audiences, languages, and data platforms. A central theme is **selection bias**: editorial constraints, ideology, resources, fragmented information, and media ownership can shape which world events become visible. Several works also examine whether media coverage reflects public interests and how attention varies across countries.

Typical methods include large-scale computational analysis of news streams, comparisons of news databases, and network-based modeling. One study compares GDELT and Event Registry in terms of scale, sources, and geography. Another combines longitudinal online news with Google Trends to construct multiplex networks of media and public attention across 193 countries. Dynamic embedding is used to represent the media landscape and investigate ownership-related influence, while multilingual event tracking relies on cross-lingual document similarity and linking article clusters across languages.

Recent directions emphasize dynamic and structural analysis rather than isolated content analysis: measuring changing media landscapes, comparing media and public attention, tracking events across languages, and developing empirical tools to quantify otherwise difficult-to-observe biases.

c35a2349fe60d40b3c60c27f4fcaeeb0bbcb84f7.text:
### Resource-Efficient Systems for Large-Scale Video Analytics

This community develops systems that make visual analytics practical under growing data volumes and constrained resources. A central theme is shifting computation and data management closer to cameras: **AutCam** supports counting queries on battery-powered autonomous cameras, while **zero-streaming cameras** retain video locally and communicate with the cloud only when analytics is requested.

Another theme is accelerating exploratory and machine-learning workloads over large video collections. **BlazeIt** targets fast exploratory queries using neural networks, addressing both inference cost and the complexity of imperative analytics pipelines. **VDMS** provides machine-oriented access to images, videos, and feature vectors through graph-based metadata search and specialized storage formats.

The systems typically combine approximate or selective processing, learned or neural models, metadata-driven retrieval, and hardware- or storage-aware optimization. **VStore** explicitly manages the full video path—from ingestion and storage to retrieval and consumption—and uses backward derivation to choose among video-format configurations while balancing quality, quantity, and multiple resource types.

Recent trends emphasize privacy-preserving edge analytics, avoiding unnecessary network transfer, exploiting cold or sparsely queried video, and jointly optimizing accuracy, latency, energy, storage, and compute rather than treating video storage and analytics as separate problems.

68c341478b4be1100459a1cda96cb577cfe57f3f.text:
### Decentralized Transactions and Asset Management Across Blockchains

This community focuses on making blockchain systems support reliable, interoperable transactions and broader asset management without centralized intermediaries. A central theme is atomic cross-chain exchange: protocols seek all-or-nothing execution across two or many permissionless blockchains while preserving transaction consistency and ACID properties. Existing approaches based on hashlocks and timelocks are examined, including their vulnerability to expired timelocks and resulting atomicity violations.

Typical methods include peer-to-peer smart contracts, cryptographic hashlocks, timelocks, and distributed commit protocols. Proposed approaches extend two-phase commit to transactions spanning an arbitrary number of blockchains, eliminating centralized coordinators and targeting improved scalability. The work also explores transaction primitives for smart contracts, such as TXSC, which hides concurrency anomalies from developers.

A broader research direction is using permissionless blockchain infrastructure to manage assets beyond native currencies, including real-world assets such as cars and houses. Overall, recent trends move from two-party swaps toward scalable many-party interoperability, from centralized coordination toward distributed commitment, and from cryptocurrency transfers toward general-purpose global asset and transactional management.

f604d0ee56412c8b8d9648d067b67c551bb07405.text:
### Topic, Event, and Social-Stream Intelligence

This community centers on extracting structure, knowledge, and actionable signals from large, dynamic text and social-media collections. Major themes include probabilistic topic modeling for hypertext, scientific literature, reviews, and evolving text streams; user-interest inference and recommendation; entity summarization and timeline construction; and automated hypothesis generation and validation.

A particularly strong focus is real-time event detection from Twitter and other geo-tagged streams, including sports, protests, disasters, disease outbreaks, social action, and environmental incidents. Related work addresses spatial clustering, bursty-region discovery, event summarization, misinformation analysis, and visualization. Location-based search, tourism analytics, and facility placement extend these ideas to spatial decision support.

Typical methods include LDA, PLSA, dynamic and hierarchical Dirichlet processes, clustered topic models, and topic-based networks. Systems also use CNNs, character-based neural embeddings, statistical machine learning, keyword-volume analysis, power-law verification, density-based clustering, ontology similarity, fuzzy logic, information extraction, active learning, and candidate ranking.

Recent trends emphasize scalability and continuous processing of massive streams, multilingual and multimodal analysis, richer temporal and spatial modeling, and practical early-warning or decision-support systems. Applications increasingly target public health, emergency response, scientific discovery, and summarization, with greater attention to systematic evaluation and validation.

a1d4baba0a2f0756f2a4665b4f4aacba4d5784e7.text:
## Scalable Data Analytics, Retrieval, and Mathematical Information Access

This community combines intelligent text processing with high-performance data management. Major themes include probabilistic and user-guided document clustering, automated text classification, authorship analysis, topic diversity, active learning, and high-recall technology-assisted review. Mathematical information retrieval is prominent, encompassing formula-aware indexing, presentation- versus content-based search, query-result merging, identifier-definition extraction, and digital mathematical libraries.

Typical methods include multinomial and hierarchical topic models, metric learning with minimal feedback, association-rule pruning and hyperonymization, k-nearest-neighbor and k-medoids classification, genetic feature selection, graph-based score propagation, deep regression, and relevance-feedback simulations. Retrieval systems combine textual and formula queries using canonicalization, semantic enrichment, and faceted interfaces.

A parallel systems strand addresses scalable analytics: Accumulo, D4M associative arrays, Graphulo/GraphBLAS kernels, external graph processing, provenance ingestion, polystore architectures, and memory-aware query optimization. Research also develops relational-lattice algebra, cloud cost/performance models, dynamic scaling, and learning-based workload management.

Recent trends emphasize autonomous and continuous learning, uncertain or progressive data enrichment, performance guarantees and cost-aware cloud execution, SSD-oriented graph analytics, and associative arrays as a unifying foundation for AI data wrangling across spreadsheets, databases, matrices, and graphs.

5dc4f80d186bfa248b9d4d705a1c56a908451a7c.text:
### Bibliometric Evaluation and Collaboration in Italian Academia

This community centers on measuring scientific performance and understanding academic inequality, primarily in the Italian university system. Major themes include individual, university, and national research evaluation; gender differences in productivity, collaboration, recruitment, and rankings; nepotism and regional disparities; academic careers and the persistence of “top scientists”; and the effects of collaboration, internationalization, interdisciplinarity, geography, and author order on research impact.

Typical methods are large-scale bibliometric analyses of Web of Science and national census data, using publication and citation indicators, field normalization, FSS and MNCS comparisons, productivity distributions, regression and quantile regression, gravity models, Granger causality tests, network analysis, stochastic models, funnel plots, and simulation of assessment rankings. Considerable attention is devoted to methodological validity: uncertainty, counting methods, publication-window length, journal impact factor versus citations, and cross-field comparability.

Another strong strand addresses data quality, especially author-name disambiguation. Studies evaluate initials-based, topological, semi-supervised, ethnicity-sensitive, and digital-library approaches using labeled datasets and collaboration networks.

Recent directions include more probabilistic and uncertainty-aware evaluation, explicit accounting for gender and contribution, network-based analyses of collaboration and knowledge diffusion, improved disambiguation using curated data and machine learning, and publication-recommendation methods designed to overcome limited ground-truth data.

42dd2676a4db35a4016387d3e9e11652e8813290.text:
### Bias, Evaluation, and Tools in Recommender Systems

This community examines the reliability, social effects, and research infrastructure of recommender systems. A central theme is the limitation of offline evaluation: historical interaction data may omit novel items, making it difficult to estimate whether recommendations would be relevant to users. Another major focus is bias, including preference-bias amplification, marketing-induced distortions in product interactions, and possible gender-related discrimination in book ratings and recommendations.

Typical methods include simulation studies of offline evaluation error and bias, comparisons across model-based and memory-based algorithms, and analysis of recommendation calibration and bias disparity across user groups and item categories. Studies also investigate how correlations in interaction data—such as product presentation or demographic patterns—shape collaborative-filtering outcomes.

The community additionally emphasizes reproducible experimentation and practical research tools. Experience developing and deploying the LensKit toolkit motivates next-generation tools through the LKPY package, informed by research, education, services, and community feedback.

Recent trends move beyond raw predictive performance toward assessing fairness, representation, and the causes of observed interaction patterns, while improving experimental software and questioning whether static datasets can support trustworthy evaluation of novel recommendations.

f5236526824cd05bfc87df6156a6f3e2ee974cd4.text:
## Principles and Systems for Scalable Data Management

This community combines foundational query theory with practical systems for large-scale analytics. Core themes include join ordering and optimization (MILP, worst-case-optimal joins, inequalities, XQuery, metaquerying), distributed query evaluation (communication complexity, parallel-correctness, coordination freedom, MapReduce), and database-backed graph processing through SQL, Datalog, relational joins, and specialized hardware.

Typical methods include formal complexity and correctness analyses; cost-based and learned optimization; sketches, sampling, maximum-entropy summaries, and speculative approximation; incremental and dynamic data structures; and columnar, sparse, model-based, or hardware-aware representations. Several systems emphasize declarative abstractions without sacrificing performance, including high-level query engines, relational graph systems, and integrated data-science platforms.

A strong trend is convergence between databases and machine learning: systems increasingly support feature extraction over normalized data, in-database inference, gradient optimization, model selection, and multi-tenant resource allocation. Analytics is also becoming more interactive and user-oriented through visual-insight recommendation, fast-stream exploration, revenue-aware recommendation, and collaborative dataset versioning. Other recent directions address operational realities—replication staleness, divergent index tuning, privacy in cloud processing, noisy metadata, and scalable time-series compression—while retaining the central goal of efficient, automated, and reliable data processing.

19715c2544a629076bd58c09755dcd1411df4774.text:
### Scholarly Networks, Editorial Influence, and Bibliometric Evaluation

This community studies the social and intellectual organization of scholarly communication, with particular attention to journal relationships and the behavioral effects of research assessment.

A central theme is **interlocking editorship**: scholars serving on multiple editorial boards are treated as links between journals and as a proxy for similarity in editorial policies. Network analyses of information and library science and economics journals identify clusters and relatively distinct subfields. Related work compares **editor, author, and co-citation networks** to examine whether intellectual proximity corresponds to shared social communities.

A second theme concerns **bibliometric evaluation and citation behavior**, especially in Italy. Studies investigate whether national evaluation systems encourage self-citation, scientific inwardness, or citation gaming. They use large bibliometric datasets, country-level comparisons, indicators of self-referentiality, and analyses of highly cited researchers.

Overall, the research combines exploratory network analysis with quantitative bibliometrics. Recent work increasingly moves from mapping scholarly structures toward evaluating how performance indicators shape researchers’ practices, while also challenging claims of widespread increases in self-citation and assessing the effects of national evaluation policies.

94814d5b1bdc426732ec4559482e0d1004612865.text:
## Scholarly Web Metrics, Search, and Online Communities

This community centers on computational approaches to mapping and evaluating science through scholarly web data. A dominant theme is bibliometrics: comparing Google Scholar, Web of Science, Scopus, and Microsoft Academic Search; estimating database coverage; ranking journals and institutions; measuring citation impact, h-index, cited half-life, and research quality; and testing whether metrics correspond to peer assessment. Google Scholar is repeatedly examined as a broad but imperfect, manually curated and potentially manipulable source.

A second theme concerns scholarly communication and openness, including evidence of open-access availability, green-OA mandates, self-archiving costs, and indicators combining multiple data sources. ResearchGate is studied as both an academic social network and a source of institutional visibility and influence scores.

Typical methods include large-scale citation and webometric collection, automated querying, longitudinal and cross-database comparisons, correlation and benchmarking analyses, network construction and modularity-based community detection, visualization, model selection, and computational-complexity analysis. Information-retrieval work applies learning-to-rank and query expansion to topic selection and library catalogs.

Recent work shifts toward online-community dynamics: Wikipedia reverts, disagreement, collective behavior, and evolving norm networks. It also highlights declining academic search services, stronger OA mandates, citation growth for older literature, and vulnerabilities in profile-based metrics.

737fbc51b6c6264882a9b0599b181eb7db6de967.text:
## Geographical, Contextual, and Personalized Location Recommendation

This community focuses on personalized recommendation of points of interest and venues in location-based social networks, with a broader interest in improving recommender expressiveness beyond conventional matrix factorization. Core themes include addressing sparse check-in data, modeling users’ preferences and mobility, and exploiting geographical, temporal, contextual, social, categorical, and textual information.

Typical methods include metric factorization using Euclidean distance, matrix-factorization and logistic matrix-factorization models, and collaborative ranking approaches. Several studies augment these models with geographical similarity, local spatial influence, popularity and activity dynamics, or jointly modeled geographical and temporal effects. Other work uses probabilistic mappings between user tags and location taste keywords, venue content and reviews, contextual scoring functions, and social-centric relevance scores.

Recent trends move toward richer representation learning: neural POI embeddings combine sequential behavior with categorical information, while time-sensitive and two-phase ranking models better capture changing popularity, activity, and geographic influence. Across the papers, auxiliary contextual and location-based signals are consistently used to mitigate sparsity and improve personalized ranking.

b778b8500099d01d2146d32663d6bd8eb12b4d89.text:
### Resource-Efficient Video Analytics from Cameras to Archives

This community focuses on making visual analytics practical under scale, energy, network, storage, and compute constraints. Two systems target autonomous, battery-powered cameras: iCam provides approximate query services with frugal resources, while AutCam supports counting queries by exploiting trade-offs between sample quality and resource use. Zero-streaming cameras extend this direction by storing video locally and contacting the cloud only when analytics are requested, using learned knowledge about video sparsity to reduce communication.

For larger-scale analytics, BlazeIt addresses the high cost and programming complexity of deep-learning video queries through fast exploratory processing and opportunities for cross-operator optimization. VDMS treats images, videos, and feature vectors as first-class data, combining graph-based metadata search with machine-friendly storage formats to accelerate machine-learning pipelines. VStore manages ingestion, storage, retrieval, and consumption of archival video, handling the large configuration space of video formats through backward derivation from application requirements and multi-resource goals.

Overall, the work trends toward approximate and adaptive analytics, local processing and storage, selective cloud interaction, learned or profiled resource trade-offs, and data systems co-designed with downstream visual workloads.

55f97b67d1a2eb5c227fdf63f7a336141966c0ab.text:
## Structured Search and Navigation over Web Data

This community studies how to make heterogeneous, web-scale data discoverable and directly usable. A central theme is answering natural-language and keyword queries with tables, including list, superlative, factoid, non-factoid, multi-entity, and multi-column requests. Related work focuses on discovering relevant knowledge-graph patterns, completing user-specified tables, and querying document tables without costly schema mapping.

Typical methods combine information-retrieval features, textual and column-level matching, semantic similarity, knowledge-graph structure, RDF/SPARQL, database dependencies, and table transformations. Neural semantic models are combined with engineered signals to improve precision and coverage. For large-scale domain search, Jaccard set containment and locality-sensitive hashing support efficient retrieval despite substantial differences in domain sizes.

A second major theme is organizing data lakes for navigation rather than search alone. Organizations are modeled as graphs of attribute sets linked by subset relationships, and probabilistic user models guide optimization for table discoverability.

Recent directions emphasize automation and scale: open-domain QA over noisy web tables, heterogeneous tabular-query completion using example rows, schemaless querying of irregular documents, and internet-scale domain search. Across the papers, the trend is from manually defined schemas and isolated retrieval toward semantic, navigational, and integrated systems that assemble structured answers from diverse sources.

aa7dfbd13b65b6780c760f2f7e4ea0f5f1c85991.text:
### Research Software, Reproducibility, and Scholarly Credit

This community examines research software as a central scholarly artifact and addresses how scientific communication, evaluation, and infrastructure should adapt. Major themes include integrating software into citation graphs, improving reproducibility and transparency, establishing terminology for reproducible research, and measuring software impact. The papers also emphasize the mismatch between software’s importance to computational scholarship and the limited credit it receives under conventional merit systems.

Typical methods include conceptual and directed-graph modeling of software and research relationships; reviews of publishing infrastructures and practices; classification of reproducibility terminology using decision trees; and empirical examination of software citation, including the R package **lme4**. Institutional and publishing interventions are represented by the design and early evaluation of the Journal of Open Source Software (JOSS), which links software quality improvement with formal scholarly credit. The ReScience initiative further frames complete software environments, code, and data as the substantive basis of computational results.

Recent trends point toward open science requirements from funders, journals, and reviewers, alongside growing expectations for accessible code and data. At the same time, the community identifies persistent challenges: providing reproducible computational environments is more demanding than sharing files, citation practices remain inconsistent, and competing definitions of reproducibility complicate coordination and assessment.

edcc5a55dc11b6d5623026e9fbdab09a8445a2ad.text:
## Mobile Networks, Credit, and Socioeconomic Analytics

This community studies how mobile-phone communication and transaction data reveal socioeconomic structure and improve financial and telecommunications decisions. A central theme is alternative-data credit scoring for smartphone-based microlending and financial inclusion, especially for unbanked populations. Related work evaluates the economic and predictive value of call networks and social-network information in credit models.

Typical methods include feature engineering from mobile usage, network construction and analysis, classification, profit-based evaluation, and relational learning. Researchers compare network representations—including directed, reciprocal, and statistically validated calling ties—and assess how construction choices affect results. For churn prediction, studies rank relational learners and combine network-derived features with relational-learner scores; collective inference does not consistently improve performance.

Another theme is socioeconomic stratification: coupled mobile communication and bank-transaction datasets are used to examine correlations between social ties and economic capacity at large scale. Recent trends therefore emphasize multimodal, large-scale behavioral data; network-aware and relational predictive models; and evaluation beyond statistical accuracy, including profitability and financial inclusion. At the same time, findings highlight that carefully engineered network features and network design may matter more than increasingly sophisticated inference alone.

254a14b0ce5b826a810b89103be5f429a5b7be85.text:
## Ontology- and Similarity-Driven Discovery in Text, Agriculture, and Cultural Data

This community focuses on extracting knowledge from heterogeneous or deceptive data, with recurring emphasis on semantic representation, integration, and similarity search. Two studies address online opinion spam in Vietnamese and broader e-commerce/social-media reviews, motivated by misleading product or service evaluations. Their approaches use ontology-based features to improve fake-review recognition, reporting accuracy above 75% in one study.

Semantic text search is enhanced by discovering latent concepts and exploiting ontological properties of named entities and WordNet words, including aliases, classes, identifiers, synonyms, hypernyms, hyponyms, and senses. Related concepts are introduced through constrained spreading activation.

A separate line develops structural similarity search for textile archives. Textile patterns are modeled as hypergraphs; multisets of *k*-neighborhoods are compared using Jaccard, Hamming, and cosine measures, supporting clustering and querying.

Agricultural studies emphasize big-data integration and warehousing. Data from IoT devices, sensors, satellites, weather stations, farm equipment, laboratories, farmers, and agencies are heterogeneous, inconsistent, and large-scale. Proposed directions include normalization, homogenization, unified representations, and data warehouses enabling downstream knowledge discovery.

Recent trends therefore include ontology-aware detection and retrieval, graph/hypergraph representations, scalable similarity computation, and systematic integration of increasingly diverse agricultural data.

fbed98d108f5cf1d1e5b221ed23133b319bf5c67.text:
### Counterfactual Ranking, Bias Estimation, and Efficient Evaluation

This community focuses on improving search and recommendation ranking under biased, incomplete, and costly feedback. A central theme is presentation or examination bias: papers develop contextual position-based models, intervention harvesting, and consistent propensity estimation without intrusive interventions or manual relevance judgments. These estimates support inverse-propensity weighting and counterfactual learning-to-rank.

Methods increasingly combine statistical causal reasoning with flexible ranking models. Counterfactual approaches are extended beyond average-rank objectives to additive metrics such as DCG and Precision@k, including nonlinear and deep ranking functions. Reinforcement learning is also applied to optimize sponsored-search ranking, balancing advertiser and user objectives and enabling personalized advertising.

A second theme is efficient, unbiased evaluation. Active sampling reduces the human effort needed to construct large-scale relevance collections, while probabilistic and Monte Carlo sampling provides unbiased comparative evaluation across common IR metrics, including settings with missing judgments.

Finally, the community explores better data acquisition for recommender systems through preference-elicitation interfaces that collect dense visual preferences and rich user information. Recent trends therefore include contextual rather than purely positional bias models, non-disruptive propensity estimation, deep counterfactual optimization, and statistically principled, labor-efficient evaluation.

5426a48cabc964cafb5f9b9da7c4117134eb5f8e.text:
### Learning to Rank and Semantic Search

This community centers on information retrieval, especially relevance ranking, query understanding, and search over increasingly diverse resources. Core themes include document and passage retrieval, web-quality and spam detection, expert and entity finding, dataset and mobile-app search, personal-memory QA, and temporal or cross-lingual retrieval.

Typical methods combine learning-to-rank with neural language modeling. DeepRank, monoBERT, duoBERT, and other BERT-based systems model local relevance, pairwise comparisons, passage length, and multi-stage ranking. SetRank and groupwise scoring explicitly capture interactions among candidate documents, while axiomatic regularization incorporates formal retrieval principles into neural models. Query expansion and clustering use word2vec/query2vec, concept hierarchies, pseudo-relevant web knowledge, and segment-specific context. Other approaches include matrix factorization for overlapping beliefs, kernel models for entity salience, semantic hashing and signatures for efficient search, graph models for web-assisted imputation, and adversarial profile generation for recommendation attacks.

Recent work emphasizes large-scale benchmarks and reusable datasets, including LETOR, TREC Deep Learning, and WikiPassageQA. It also highlights practical constraints—latency, long passages, private collections, and heterogeneous metadata—and advances semantic dataset and entity retrieval, multilingual zero-shot transfer, interpretability, dynamic search utility, and temporally aware recommendation.

d5affdbf39addf38736b9d38742f01efa8dfcf42.text:
**Temporal and Scalable Graph Network Analysis**

This community centers on modeling, querying, and understanding networks whose structure, interactions, or attributes evolve over time. A major theme is temporal-network formalization: stream and link-stream models extend graph notions such as paths, density, connectivity, cliques, clustering, and centrality, while time-varying graphs and temporal quantities provide algebraic and multiscale descriptions. Temporal shortest, fastest, foremost, latency, and reachability paths are recurring analytical targets.

A second theme is efficient graph querying at scale. Papers develop indexes and oracles for reachability, \(k\)-hop reachability, shortest distances, single-source paths, and temporal paths, including interval labeling, landmark labeling, hub acceleration, and distributed or vertex-centric parallel computation. Dynamic indexing addresses constantly changing graphs, while graph window analytics and query-plan optimization support large-scale analysis.

Methods also include diffusion and influence models, dynamic monopolies, opinion spreading, temporal centrality, graphlets, network alignment, and time-series analysis. Applications span hospitals, mailing lists, cryptocurrencies, scientific communities, movie narratives, recommendations, software repositories, and biological networks.

Recent work increasingly preserves fine-grained temporal information rather than aggregating snapshots, supports weighted, directed, bipartite, and multilayer networks, and combines scalable indexing with temporal-aware recommendation, dynamic graphlets, alignment, and graph-variate signal analysis.

c8634e3ae9cabd2c02f20cef5dfeae8c47bfb09f.text:
### Collaborative Web Knowledge and Personalized Search

This community studies how user-generated platforms—especially Wikipedia, Wiktionary, folksonomies, and professional networks—can organize, enrich, and retrieve knowledge. Major themes include collaborative tagging and vocabulary growth; Wikipedia categories as thesauri, ontologies, and navigation structures; multilingual lexical and ontology resources; entity linking; expertise discovery; and personalized search and recommendation.

Typical methods combine large-scale behavioral analysis with statistical modeling of power-law and allometric growth, co-occurrence and similarity measures, graph centrality, clustering, HITS, matrix factorization, and learning-to-rank. Systems transform semi-structured Wiktionary and Wikipedia content into relational or machine-readable representations, use category and link graphs for ranking and semantic navigation, and exploit clickthrough logs and social labels as implicit feedback. Taxonomies and visualization are also used to characterize collaboration, semantic coverage, and collective attention.

Recent directions emphasize scalable, multilingual processing of user-generated data, including densely annotated Wikipedia corpora and high-throughput entity disambiguation. Search is becoming increasingly personalized through inferred intent, homophily, collaborative filtering, and ideal-candidate interfaces. At the same time, researchers address presentation bias in clicks, societal and data biases in recommendation, and improved identification of influential users and locations in dynamic social networks.

fc4521b7c8f85a9316f06b68ba9e3baddb309421.text:
## Data-Centric Systems: Learning, Scale, and Resilience

This community spans database performance, distributed data management, and scientific data infrastructures. A major theme is **learning-augmented data systems**: deep models estimate cardinalities and correlations, generate approximate aggregate answers, optimize query plans, learn representations for relational integration, and replace traditional indexes. Methods include multi-set convolutional networks, autoregressive models with Monte Carlo integration, deep generative models, reinforcement learning, embeddings, and adaptive learned indexes.

A second theme is **high-performance transaction processing**. Work addresses multicore OLTP under contention, distributed transactions over fast networks, MVCC conflict repair, predictive execution, latency variance, synchronization tradeoffs, recovery, and consistency checking. Techniques include application-aware parallel recovery, contention-centric partitioning, adaptive concurrency control, flat combining, and formal complexity analysis.

The community also studies **distributed and blockchain data systems**, including blockchain/database comparisons, blockchain layers for existing systems, lightweight emulation, and geo-scale Byzantine fault tolerance.

Finally, papers address **data-intensive science and integration**: scalable indexing and batch processing for astronomy, relational backends for finite-element analysis, heterogeneous-data tunneling, public scientific access, and reproducible notebooks. Recent trends emphasize learned components, approximate and interactive analytics, cloud- or geo-scale resilience, heterogeneous integration, and energy and performance predictability.

c1f3d575472931318a968a15efd659296fa23934.text:
### Persistent Memory and Heterogeneous Storage for Databases

This community examines how emerging persistent-memory (PM) and heterogeneous storage technologies can reshape database architecture. A central theme is exploiting PM’s byte addressability, low latency, persistence, and rapid recovery while addressing practical concerns such as scalability, load factor, concurrency, and efficient I/O.

Typical methods include empirical evaluation on real or representative PM hardware, decomposition of existing data structures into reusable design primitives, and development of systems tailored to device characteristics. The papers propose PM-specific I/O primitives for log writing and block flushing, as well as Dash, a scalable dynamic hash table designed for high performance and instant recovery. hStorage-DB uses semantic information from the DBMS to manage data across heterogeneous storage devices, reducing reliance on monitoring access patterns in dynamic workloads.

Recent trends move away from isolated or emulated components toward holistic, hardware-aware designs and systematic evaluation of individual design choices. More broadly, the work anticipates a shift from a single traditional storage hierarchy toward multiple workload-specific hierarchies spanning diverse memory and storage technologies.

2977b6f59f9e8a28167ef09022d0edc472f29e09.text:
### Digital Preservation, Web Archives, and Semantic Knowledge

This community studies how to represent, preserve, discover, and reuse evolving digital information. Major themes include web archiving and temporal search; durable repositories for heterogeneous digital objects; linked open data and version management; provenance, annotation, and scholarly communication; and contextualized digital-library services.

Typical methods combine standards-based modeling and infrastructure—Fedora, aDORe, OAIS packages, MPEG-21, SharedCanvas, Open Annotation, PROV-O, PAV, nanopublications, SPARQL, and persistent identifiers—with empirical analysis of large collections and access logs. Researchers develop temporal retrieval interfaces, focused crawlers, social-bookmark and social-media signals, graph-based web analysis, caching, machine-learning prediction, and supervised ranking. They also evaluate models through longitudinal web studies, annotation loss measurements, archive performance experiments, and case studies in genomics, manuscripts, education, and mathematical software.

Recent work shifts from static preservation toward continuously evolving, socially mediated information. Trends include freshness-aware crawling for crises, event detection from Wikipedia and Twitter, learning-to-rank and archive optimization, preservation of linked-data histories, and attention to “scholarly orphans” and disappearing annotations. At the same time, studies expose persistent challenges: incomplete archives, orphaned content, unreliable timestamps, changing formats, heterogeneous schemas, and limited support for searching the temporal web graph.

de563ef109b476befd99963525008f3acc8b77b0.text:
### Utility-Oriented Pattern Mining in Complex Data

This community focuses on extending pattern mining beyond frequency toward **utility**, incorporating profit, importance, risk, cost, occupancy, and other item-specific values. Core applications include retail and cross-marketing, recommendation, click-stream and Web behavior analysis, route planning, medical and bioinformatics analytics, and IoT data.

A major theme is mining utility-aware structures in **ordered and temporal data**, including high-utility episodes, sequential patterns, multidimensional sequences, and multiple sequences. Typical methods develop specialized utility bounds and efficient search strategies, including projection-based mining, threshold-driven pruning, and algorithms designed to reduce memory and processing costs. Other work addresses high-utility occupancy, correlations among items, uncertain data, and individualized or varied minimum-utility thresholds.

Several papers are surveys, consolidating advances in utility-oriented mining, privacy-preserving utility mining, and parallel sequential pattern mining. Privacy is treated as a necessary complement to utility maximization when sensitive data are analyzed, while parallelism targets large-scale computation.

Recent trends move toward more realistic settings: recency and trend-aware utility mining, uncertainty, item-specific thresholds, correlations, occupancy, multidimensional and multi-sequence data, and privacy preservation. Overall, the field is evolving from static, uniform-threshold mining toward adaptive, scalable, temporal, and application-sensitive analytics.

31fef80ec123140cb71831d4b0053f47cd186719.text:
### Computational Analysis of Narrative Character Networks

This community studies fictional narratives through networks of characters and their interactions, with applications to plot summarization, classification, role detection, recommendation, and understanding television storytelling. A central theme is the extraction and comparison of narrative social networks: researchers evaluate manual annotation, co-occurrence-based automation, and machine-learning approaches, highlighting trade-offs in precision and scalability.

Methods include static and temporal network analysis, dynamic conversational networks for tracking subplots, and causal or interaction-based graphs. Case studies of *Friends* and *Game of Thrones* examine evolving friendship patterns, prominence, social balance, and violent relationships. Network properties and metadata are also used predictively, including attempts to forecast killer–victim pairs.

The community increasingly addresses long-running serial narratives rather than isolated episodes, motivating resources such as the *Serial Speakers* dataset of annotated episodes from *Breaking Bad*, *Game of Thrones*, and *House of Cards*. Recent work also extends beyond interaction structure: ecological diversity and Shannon-entropy measures estimate effective movie cast sizes, while Jensen–Shannon divergence compares casts across films. Overall, the field is moving toward automated extraction, temporal modeling, predictive analysis, and reusable multimedia datasets.

d7f63e3af79276d8da2b6893fd04112ff930b1bf.text:
### Graph-Based and Semantic Keyphrase Extraction

This community focuses on automatic keyword and keyphrase extraction, often motivated by improving document navigation, search, and news aggregation. A large-scale aggregation system first categorizes more than 500,000 news articles into 12 classes using a neural network, then applies statistical, graphical, and numerical extraction methods, with category labels guiding relevance.

A dominant theme is representing text as a graph and ranking candidate words or phrases. Supervised methods learn from node-level complex-network properties to distinguish keywords from non-keywords. Unsupervised approaches use PageRank-like scoring, multipartite graphs, and mutually reinforcing relationships between topics and keyphrase candidates. Graph construction and scoring are increasingly informed by semantics: semantic connectivity captures contextual relations without parameter tuning, while semantic roles and sentence position provide additional relevance features.

Reported evaluations generally show improvements over graph-based or state-of-the-art baselines, including experiments on scientific articles and multiple standard datasets. Overall, the work trends from purely lexical or statistical ranking toward hybrid systems that combine graph structure, topical information, document position, semantic roles, and supervised learning.

37cbcf1d08f34a76ac65f128bc27e8481cf72806.text:
### Mapping Funding, Acknowledgements, and Research Evaluation

This community examines acknowledgements as overlooked evidence for understanding research support, credit, and collaboration. A major theme is the characterization and responsible use of funding-acknowledgement (FA) data in Web of Science (WoS), including its historical development, distribution across citation indexes, languages, document types, disciplines, and time periods. Studies emphasize persistent coverage gaps and analytical biases, while noting improved collection in humanities and social sciences.

Typical methods include bibliometric analysis of WoS records, comparative examination of FA coverage, and combining co-authorship with acknowledged individuals to reveal broader collaboration and credit-attribution patterns. Humanities-focused work uses acknowledgement analysis to make otherwise invisible scholarly contributions and interactions visible.

A related methodological strand applies data-driven evidential reasoning to multi-criteria R&D project selection, acquiring evidence from historical expert assessments and weighting evidence by reliability to rank projects.

Recent trends include the rapid growth and refinement of FA-based studies, increasing attention to database limitations and interpretive caveats, expanding acknowledgement research beyond funding to social and collaborative contributions, and integrating multiple forms of scholarly credit rather than relying solely on authorship and citations.

11aef0ed5e8954d4267379738429a183aa36e1a2.text:
## Online Social Networks: Structure, Diffusion, and Prediction

This community studies online and complex social networks as systems of interaction, influence, risk, and information flow. Major themes include identifying important or anomalous users, detecting communities and polarization, measuring tie strength and vulnerability, and understanding network growth, decay, and temporal dynamics. Information cascades, rumor propagation, memes, reviews, product adoption, and malicious URLs are examined alongside popularity, virality, attention, and video engagement.

Typical methods combine graph-theoretic measures—betweenness, pair-dependency, centrality, modularity, edge overlap, assortativity, and fractal dimension—with community detection, clustering, principal component analysis, and visualization. Researchers use threshold and game-theoretic models, continuous-time diffusion models, cascade analysis, statistical comparisons, and large-scale machine learning. Embeddings and multi-task learning support demographic and user modeling, while topic models and scalable visual-meme detection connect content with network structure.

Recent work increasingly emphasizes dynamic and heterogeneous networks, including tie decay, profile changes, network assembly, and information entering from outside the observed graph. It also broadens analysis beyond raw popularity toward engagement and early trend prediction, integrates text, images, video, and transaction data, and applies network analytics to disasters, political polarization, financial contagion, scientific collaboration, and online harms.

33f55718a50609701c01c7702fa35db88062b7cb.text:
## Semantic Preservation and Temporal Web Intelligence

This community studies how to preserve, model, retrieve, and interpret evolving digital information. Major themes include durable digital repositories and objects; web archiving and temporal search; linked open data and semantic knowledge representation; provenance, annotation, and scholarly communication; and aggregation of heterogeneous scientific or cultural artifacts.

Typical methods combine standards-based architectures (OAIS, MPEG-21, RDF, SPARQL, PROV-O, Open Annotation, nanopublications) with persistent identifiers, modular repositories, versioning, and lifecycle modeling. Researchers build large corpora and infrastructure, including archived web collections, annotated tweets, linked biological datasets, and manuscript models. Evaluation commonly uses longitudinal studies, access logs, collection analyses, quality criteria, and case studies. Retrieval approaches include temporal and structured queries, entity linking and summarization, social-bookmark signals, lexical and title-based discovery, focused crawling, caching, and machine-learning prediction of archival holdings.

Recent work increasingly addresses information loss and change: detecting disappearing or off-topic resources, orphaned annotations and scholarly objects, evolving linked datasets, and historical entity relations. It also emphasizes integrating social media with crawling and archive search, exposing semantic layers over archival collections, improving scalability and response time, and making scientific claims, provenance, and digital objects more interoperable and machine-actionable.

d7cef17eb531ef607c95e027e2a2dfe748832427.text:
### Network Mining, Representation, and Dynamic Graphs

This community centers on computational analysis of complex, social, temporal, and knowledge networks. Major themes include link and relationship prediction, community and core–periphery detection, graph classification, anomaly and fraud detection, and network sampling and querying. Knowledge-graph applications address triple scoring, entity normalization, and fact checking, while social-network studies examine relationship semantics, privacy preferences, team formation, and criminal or insider-trading networks.

Typical methods combine local structural indices, clustering perspectives, random walks, Markov chains, and scalable MapReduce algorithms for massive graphs. Machine-learning approaches include random forests, discriminative path mining, neural and deep graph embeddings, ensemble scoring, latent-space models, probabilistic graph grammars, and maximum-likelihood inference for uncertain networks. Evaluation increasingly uses real-world datasets alongside synthetic graphs, with explicit attention to computational cost, quality guarantees, and business-relevant outcomes.

Recent trends emphasize dynamics: continuous-time prediction, temporal event representations, dynamic embeddings, temporally robust reconstruction, and generative models whose communities evolve over time. Heterogeneous and multimodal data are integrated through metapaths, text, attributes, and knowledge bases. There is also growing interest in trustworthy applications, including fraud de-anonymization, privacy assistance, fact checking, and uncertainty-aware structural inference, alongside systematic benchmarks for graph-embedding evaluation.

d462499c396432dfd5a2daaa7445a4378c9cd121.text:
**Cross-Modal Retrieval, Hashing, and Multimodal Semantics**

This community is dominated by efficient cross-modal and multimodal retrieval, especially image–text, audio–lyrics, and multi-view visual search. The central challenge is bridging heterogeneous modalities in a shared semantic or Hamming space while preserving correlations, discriminative similarity, and retrieval efficiency.

Typical methods learn compact binary representations through supervised matrix factorization, latent-factor models, triplet or unary losses, correlation alignment, and discrete or quantization-based optimization. Deep approaches jointly learn modality-specific features, unified hash codes, and hashing functions, using CNNs, recurrent and attention networks, graph convolution, canonical-correlation architectures, and paired multimodal inputs. Several studies address practical search through probability-based indexing and query-adaptive ranking rather than exhaustive Hamming search.

A clear trend is the transition from handcrafted features and relaxed continuous codes toward end-to-end deep hashing, discrete optimization, decorrelated bits, asymmetric/composite quantization, and stronger semantic supervision. Research increasingly targets scalable training by avoiding pairwise or triplet data expansion, while also exploring unsupervised adversarial learning through coupled CycleGANs. Beyond retrieval, the community studies interpretable music recommendation, hierarchical lyric genre classification, audio–lyric temporal alignment, and EEG-regularized music semantics, broadening multimodal representation learning toward temporal structure, listener perception, and explainability.

9719aed03f74adf873617bbdbd3f260688d84aca.text:
## Persistent and Heterogeneous Storage for Resilient Databases

This community investigates how persistent memory (PM/NVM) and increasingly diverse storage technologies reshape database architecture. A central theme is replacing the traditional DRAM–disk boundary with multi-tier systems spanning DRAM, NVM, SSDs, and other heterogeneous devices. Work addresses buffer management, semantic- and workload-aware data placement, persistent buffer pools, and efficient I/O primitives for logging and block flushing.

A second major theme is fast, fine-grained resilience. Proposed techniques include redo-only recovery with committed persistent state, transactional page-recovery indexes for single-page failures, and instant, demand-driven restoration that permits read/write access during media repair. Persistent data structures are also studied through scalable hashing, optimistic consistency, and systematic decomposition into reusable design primitives.

Typical methods combine system and algorithm design with performance evaluation on emerging hardware, especially Intel Optane persistent memory. Researchers measure latency, bandwidth, scalability, recovery, and load-factor behavior, while contrasting real hardware with emulation and identifying the effects of individual design choices.

Recent trends favor holistic designs rather than isolated structures: exploiting PM simultaneously as memory and storage, dynamically managing heterogeneous tiers, supporting concurrent operation during recovery, and tailoring restoration and data movement to application demand.

5e76449f0475be69f12c407ba887d6c06747cb48.text:
### Data Management for Scalable Analytics and Learning

This community centers on principled and practical data management for large-scale analytics. Core themes include query optimization and evaluation (MILP-based join ordering, conjunctive queries with inequalities, XQuery complexity, metaquerying, dynamic and distributed evaluation), communication-efficient parallel processing, and consistency in replicated or stale data stores.

A major strand translates graph processing and pattern matching into relational joins, using column stores, specialized hardware, and high-level engines such as EmptyHeaded and Triε. Database systems are also being extended to support machine learning directly, including sparse-tensor representations, in-database inference, declarative end-to-end workflows, gradient descent over joins, and multi-tenant resource allocation.

Typical methods combine formal complexity and communication analysis with system building and empirical benchmarking. Techniques include MILP optimization, worst-case-optimal multiway joins, sketches and sampling, probabilistic summaries, model-based compression, adaptive indexing, materialized-view cleaning, and hardware-conscious execution.

Recent directions emphasize integrated, declarative data-science platforms; automated optimization of data structures, queries, and models; approximate and interactive analytics; collaborative dataset versioning; and bringing graph, ML, and visual analytics into relational systems. Parallelism, cloud deployment, governance, privacy, freshness, and efficient use of high-level abstractions remain recurring practical concerns.

c0577418e8f415baf5f6858d35f30df6295a16fb.text:
## Scalable Data Quality and Approximate Indexing

This community focuses on making large, heterogeneous, and continuously arriving data usable through efficient quality assessment, deduplication, indexing, and metadata management. A major theme is approximate processing: reservoir sampling, Bloom filters, Stable Bloom Filters, clustering-coefficient estimation, and probabilistic metrics reduce the cost of analyzing streams and massive Linked Data collections. Related indexing work develops compact and multidimensional Bloom-filter structures, including COBS for approximate \(k\)-mer and q-gram matching.

Linked Data quality is addressed through the Luzzu framework, its domain-specific metric language (LQML), and the daQ ontology for publishing multidimensional statistical quality metadata. Other studies examine collaborative correction and provenance tracking for erroneous linked facts. Spatial data quality research applies sampling to trajectory nearest-neighbor search, while categorical-data assessment uses association rules optimized with genetic algorithms.

Text analytics forms a secondary theme, using learned context, relation extraction, and fuzzy similarity for document categorization. Metadata frameworks also support spatial data warehouses through integration, lineage, and quality descriptions.

Overall, the work trends toward resource-efficient, probabilistic techniques; compact indexes for large collections; reusable and declarative quality metrics; and explicit, shareable quality metadata and curation workflows.

535cfac6fa78ef8392ea73cab72ff9b9f4f5fd54.text:
### Utility-Aware and Structured Pattern Mining

This community focuses on extracting useful, nonredundant patterns from sequences, graphs, relational data, and transactional databases. A dominant theme is utility-oriented mining, extending frequency-based discovery with profit, weight, occupancy, correlation, recency, uncertainty, individualized thresholds, and multidimensional or multi-sequence context. Several works target high-utility episodes and sequential patterns, while others address privacy-preserving utility mining.

Episode mining is another major strand, including serial, parallel, general, simultaneous, closed, and high-utility episodes. Research emphasizes reducing noise and redundancy through closure, free-rider screening, compression, and minimum-description-length summaries. Related work develops concise representations of frequent itemsets and association rules using closed itemsets, minimal generators, non-derivable sets, and statistical significance testing.

Typical methods include database projections, pruning and upper bounds, constraint-based search, partition models, equivalence classes, MDL encoding, and utility-specific thresholds. Scalable implementations use MapReduce for social-content matching, n-gram statistics, and parallel sequential mining; graph and relational approaches use tree queries and conjunctive queries.

Recent trends move beyond binary frequency toward richer semantics: item-specific importance, temporal recency, correlations, uncertainty, privacy, and simultaneous events. At the same time, scalable distributed algorithms and pattern summarization address the persistent problem of overwhelming output size.

53688176ece4b5d032b325e760e8383e40c10ded.text:
## Multilayer Social Networks, Identity, and Information Diffusion

This community centers on analyzing complex online social systems in which users, relationships, platforms, and behaviors form multiple interacting layers. Major themes include multiplex network structure and centrality; online–offline ties, homophily, and identity; group discovery and evolution; link prediction, influence, and recommendation; and the diffusion of information, epidemics, and misinformation.

Typical methods combine graph and multiplex-network measures, including degree centrality, reciprocity, triplets, clustering, layer-entanglement metrics, and structural–homophily similarity. Researchers use community-evolution algorithms such as GED and SGCI, independent-cascade and branching-process models, epidemic-threshold analysis, and mathematical results for random key graphs. Empirical work relies on Twitter, Facebook, blogs, email, Web 2.0, browse logs, cellular mobility, and cross-platform profiles. Machine-learning approaches include topic modeling, sentiment classification with distant supervision, factoid embeddings for unsupervised identity linkage, feature engineering, and model selection. Synthetic-network generation and mixture sampling address privacy, scale, and incomplete data.

Recent trends emphasize unified multilayer models, cross-platform and cross-device identity resolution, multiplex diffusion and seed selection, privacy-aware synthetic data, and applications to misinformation, disease containment, HR, advertising, and personalized social recommendation.

cc486026c7c6a0a5f23a60f6fc1d2bf8c2218e33.text:
### Diffusion, Influence, and Dynamics in Complex Networks

This community studies how information, opinions, products, epidemics, and failures propagate through social, temporal, uncertain, and interdependent networks. Major themes include influence maximization and online recruitment; epidemic containment, cost, and acceleration; source localization; hidden-network and infection-probability inference; and opinion formation under bias, antagonism, multiple topics, and recommendations.

Typical methods combine threshold, independent-cascade, SIS/SI, DeGroot, Friedkin–Johnsen, and continuous-time diffusion models with optimization and algorithm design. Researchers use submodularity and adaptive greedy policies, mixed-integer programming, message passing and factor graphs, random-matrix analysis, Jordan-center/cover methods, soft-thresholding, particle-swarm heuristics, and Markov or stochastic network models. Theoretical work emphasizes NP-hardness, approximation guarantees, stability, convergence, sample complexity, and recovery conditions, alongside simulations on synthetic and real-world networks.

Recent directions move beyond static, fully observed settings toward adaptive and myopic decision-making, time-varying and spatial networks, partial cascade observations, multiple sources, competing products, non-submodular spread, and arbitrary switching-time distributions. Increasing attention is also given to feedback between opinions and personalized recommendations, cyber-physical self-healing, external epidemic agents, and resource-constrained data collection.

20ef766061c410f24e3430d798d3310998a88a3b.text:
## Scientometrics, Research Evaluation, and Scholarly Networks

This community centers on measuring and mapping scientific activity, impact, and institutional performance. Major themes include citation-based evaluation of researchers, journals, universities, countries, and fields; field delineation and cognitive similarity; technology and journal-network mapping; and the effects of national evaluation systems on academic behavior and inequality. Gender, ethnic diversity, nepotism, regional divides, editorial influence, and collaboration are examined as social dimensions of research performance.

Typical methods combine Web of Science, Scopus, Microsoft Academic, Dimensions, and patent data with citation, co-authorship, bibliographic-coupling, and journal–journal networks. Researchers use centrality measures, PageRank, h-index variants, weighted and fractional counting, stochastic and multivariate models, regression and Granger causality, percentile-based indicators, and network visualization. Comparisons of databases and normalization procedures are frequent, reflecting concerns about field, time, and disciplinary bias.

Recent work emphasizes robust field-normalized and percentile metrics, significance testing, multidimensional assessment, and improved treatment of multiple authorship. Digital dissemination is weakening the historical link between journal impact factors and article citations. New databases such as Dimensions are validated against established indexes, while large-scale studies increasingly investigate diversity and collaboration. At the same time, studies critically assess ranking distortions and unintended consequences of performance-based national research assessments.

f48934af78b5ae2eedb0081288072e8d52981711.text:
## Social Network Structure, Diffusion, and Online Behavior

This community studies online and complex social networks as dynamic systems for information diffusion, influence, risk, and user behavior. Major themes include identifying important intermediaries and global bridges; detecting anomalies and malicious activity; discovering communities and assessing strong and weak ties; modeling network growth, decay, vulnerability, and systemic risk; and predicting content popularity, engagement, and demographic attributes.

Typical methods combine graph-theoretic measures—betweenness, pair-dependency, edge overlap, modularity, centrality, fractal dimension, and structural asymmetry—with community detection, clustering, embeddings, and machine learning. Large-scale analyses use Twitter, Facebook, YouTube, Yelp, transaction records, scholarly graphs, and software repositories. Diffusion is modeled through rumor and cascade processes, contagion and immunity equations, Hawkes processes, viral-marketing models, and graph models incorporating mass media, absent nodes, indirect co-location, or active intervention. Visual analytics and scalable content-mining methods, including visual memes and latent topics, support monitoring and event recognition.

Recent work shifts from static topology toward temporal, heterogeneous, and multimodal behavior: adaptive networks and collective intelligence, cascade structure and semantics, early popularity-trend prediction, video engagement rather than views, content-agnostic popularity factors, and real-time sensing. Increasing attention also addresses malicious URLs, financial contagion, suicide-related signals, and user incentives.

dc7e16344272651ea0f38a9c3498ee2bc5ec30fd.text:
## Mapping Scholarly Impact, Visibility, and Evaluation

This community studies how scientific impact and communication can be measured beyond conventional citation counts. Major themes include the validity and interpretation of altmetrics, relationships among citations, readership, downloads, social-media activity, and peer-assessed quality, and the effects of open access, preprints, and online visibility. Other work evaluates books, monographs, publishers, journals, research units, and countries through bibliometric indicators, while examining scholarly communication infrastructures such as arXiv, ADS, Mendeley, academic profiles, and social platforms.

Typical methods combine large-scale data integration from Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar, Altmetric, F1000Prime, Book Citation Index, ADS, and usage logs with correlation and regression analysis, principal-component and factor analysis, rankings, longitudinal comparisons, and validation against peer review or research assessments. Webometric and social-network analysis are used to map science parks, editorial-board structures, and institutional links. Machine-learning, optimization, and information-retrieval methods support bibliographic matching, venue recommendation, conference classification, and reviewer assignment.

Recent trends emphasize heterogeneous and rapidly generated indicators, online review mining, readership and download statistics, dynamic user-interest modeling, automated bibliographic disambiguation, and algorithmic support for peer review. Across the community, methodological concerns about coverage, data quality, bias, dependencies, and indicator validity remain central.

ea34fcdea8a2bed65d9ef7e18da8140e50992876.text:
## Social Media as a Lens on Urban Geography and Human Behavior

This community studies how geotagged and user-generated content can reveal spatial behavior, place meanings, and social dynamics. Major themes include inferring locations and urban boundaries from Twitter, Reddit, Weibo, and mobility networks; characterizing travel, preferential-return locations, group colocation, and functional urban regions; and mapping experiential qualities such as sound, smell, beauty, happiness, and affect. Other applications include business-site selection, tourism networks, personalized routes, recommendations, event scheduling, and prediction of ratings, sports outcomes, and social influence.

Typical methods combine natural-language processing, sentiment and semantic analysis, convolutional and other deep-learning models, graph representations, low-rank approximation, density-based clustering, trajectory and spatial-network analysis, and probabilistic geospatial reasoning. Researchers also exploit multimodal imagery, profiles, check-ins, and text, often at very large scale. Streaming detection and interactive learning support real-time situational awareness, especially for disasters and emergency aid, while supervised classifiers track sensitive events such as sexual violence.

Recent directions emphasize multimodal and scalable analytics, continuous detection of spatial bursts, user-in-the-loop relevance modeling, bias correction and external validation, and models that connect online signals with physical mobility, collective action, urban wellbeing, and practical planning decisions.

3471986f64284f4a9dcb468339522ffc41965da3.text:
## Topic-Centered Mining of Dynamic Web and Scholarly Data

This community studies methods for discovering, organizing, and exploiting information in large, evolving collections of text, social-media posts, scholarly publications, images, and knowledge-base entities. A central theme is topic modeling: LDA/PLSA extensions model hypertext links, temporal topic evolution, multi-grain review aspects, scientific-article bundles, and cross-domain “bisociative” connections. Dynamic and scalable variants address changing topic numbers, popularity, and distributions, including clustered and infinite dynamic models.

Another major focus is social-media analytics: event detection and retrieval from Twitter, geo-temporal burst analysis, real-time event summarization, sentiment and misinformation monitoring, tourism and organizational analysis, and popularity or longevity modeling. Typical methods combine TF-IDF, clustering, statistical and power-law analysis, named-entity and relation extraction, topic models, and visualization. Multimodal event detection fuses tweet text and images, while character-based neural embeddings and CNN recommenders address noisy multilingual content and sequential preferences.

Scholarly-information applications include citation and author-contribution extraction, semantic publishing, hypothesis-generation validation, paper recommendation, and explanation-based model tuning. Entity summarization, timeline generation, semantic question answering, and ontology/fuzzy matching target concise, user-oriented access to structured and unstructured data.

Recent trends emphasize real-time and large-scale processing, multimodal and neural representations, explainable recommendations, knowledge graphs, and actionable decision support.

f595a9e2f0fbe31eea2271a9bcf2d048aa252423.text:
### Recommender Systems: Sequential, Neural, and Responsible Personalization

This community studies personalized recommendation across collaborative filtering, sequential/session-based prediction, playlists, news, travel, advertising, and education. Core themes include combining long-term preferences with short-term behavior; addressing sparsity, cold start, anonymous sessions, shared accounts, cross-domain activity, and users’ diverse interests; and improving discovery of long-tail items and artists.

Typical methods range from matrix factorization, slope-one predictors, neighborhood models, metric learning, Markov chains, context trees, and ontology-based approaches to neural collaborative filtering, variational autoencoders, recurrent models, factorization machines, and nonlinear ranking networks. Graph-based methods model item transitions, signed user–item relations, content, temporal signals, and trust. Multimodal representations use text, images, audio, and video, while hybrid systems combine collaborative and content information.

Recent work emphasizes deep sequence and session modeling, including graph neural networks and inter-session information; robust learning with missing modalities; mixture-of-tastes representations; cross-domain and shared-account recommendation; and reinforcement learning for advertising and revenue optimization. A parallel focus addresses popularity and long-tail bias, diversity through personalized reranking and determinantal point processes, fraud and reputation, and the limitations and bias of offline evaluation.

7bc981691d75b962733a642463f6b423c51e8781.text:
### Semantic Preservation and Temporal Knowledge Infrastructure

This community studies how to represent, preserve, search, and reuse evolving digital resources across scientific, cultural, and Web environments. Major themes include web archiving and temporal retrieval; durable repositories for heterogeneous digital objects; semantic modeling of artifacts, mechanisms, claims, and annotations; linked open data and dataset evolution; and provenance, versioning, and data quality.
