Several studies examine how publication characteristics—author count, country references, editorial-board membership, author order, and citation distributions—affect visibility and rankings.

Typical methods are large-scale bibliometric analyses of Web of Science or Google Scholar data, using indicators such as citations, journal impact factor, h-index, FSS, MNCS, and field-standardized impact. Researchers apply regression and quantile regression, Granger causality tests, stochastic and multivariate models, network analysis, distributional and Gini/Pareto analyses, funnel plots, and simulation-based comparisons of ranking procedures. Author disambiguation uses probabilistic clustering and semi-supervised learning.

Recent work increasingly emphasizes methodological validity and fairness: uncertainty in institutional scores, appropriate assessment windows, field normalization, author-credit and counting methods, gender-sensitive rankings, and critiques of Italy’s VQR exercises. The community also extends bibliometrics toward knowledge-flow analysis, territorial specialization, publication recommendation, and more robust computational handling of author identities and incomplete ground-truth data.

8cd4906dcb0f981c257274f0c767f3913b2723f5.text:
## Community Detection in Complex, Dynamic Networks

This community focuses on defining, detecting, evaluating, and interpreting communities across complex network types. Major themes include overlapping, fuzzy, multiplex, multilayer, attributed, signed, weighted, two-mode, and time-varying networks. Researchers address ambiguous community definitions, resolution limits, polarization, low-degree-node bias, and the distinction between local centers and global bridges.

Typical methods include modularity and multislice modularity optimization; label propagation; stochastic block and geometric block models; spectral and local spectral techniques; density-based clustering with manifold learning; clique percolation; core–periphery and k-core/k-truss analysis; and multi-criteria or Pareto optimization. Probabilistic inference, variational Bayes, random-matrix analysis, metastable dynamics, and axiomatic modeling provide theoretical foundations. Evaluation increasingly compares multiple quality criteria and supports algorithm selection based on network characteristics.

Applications span social influence, churn and smartphone adoption, online dating, Twitter curation, Web services, bibliometric networks, recommendations, image segmentation, and public-private graphs. Recent directions emphasize scalable local algorithms for massive networks, stable and interpretable detection, joint modeling of shared and layer-specific structure, dynamic visualization and evolving importance, active learning, and more inclusive assignments for weakly connected nodes.

b2ddc715094d9d7e4f4baa340520930e9d7a4104.text:
## Mining Dynamic Text, Social Signals, and Events

This community centers on extracting structure and actionable knowledge from large, noisy, and evolving information streams. Major themes include latent topic discovery and evolution in document collections; social-media analysis for events, sentiment, rumors, crises, collective action, and user behavior; personalized recommendation; spatial-temporal mining; and summarization, visualization, and knowledge-base support. Several works apply these capabilities to biomedical hypothesis generation, disease surveillance, tourism, environmental warnings, and scientific literature.

Typical methods combine probabilistic topic models—including link-aware, hierarchical, infinite, dynamic, and clustered LDA—with graph analysis, centrality, clustering, burst and power-law detection, and spatial-textual retrieval. Streaming systems identify sub-events and representative messages, while supervised and neural approaches support hashtag extraction, tweet clustering, next-song recommendation, and multimodal representation learning. Ontology similarity, fuzzy logic, active learning, entity ranking, and provenance enhance retrieval, review, and interpretability.

Recent directions emphasize real-time and scalable processing of massive geo-tagged and social streams, including parallel dynamic topic modeling and large-scale event detection. Neural and character-based models increasingly address multilingual and heterogeneous evidence. Research also moves toward human-centered systems: explainable tuning, trustworthy rumor and hypothesis validation, interactive visualization, and concise timelines or entity summaries. Attention to revisits, longevity, and user motivations further broadens modeling beyond raw popularity.

172bf50c901c8b95034c91f13f8807c12ae2f562.text:
## Online Social Networks: Diffusion, Influence, and Risk

This community studies how online social networks form, evolve, and shape information, behavior, and risk. Major themes include information cascades, rumor and misinformation diffusion, meme and video popularity, recommendation effects, and the roles of strong/weak ties, homophily, attention, and community structure. Other work addresses anomaly detection, malicious URLs, privacy attacks, organizational vulnerability, financial guarantee networks, and suicide-related social isolation.

Typical methods combine graph analysis—centrality, edge overlap, modularity-based community detection, structural vulnerability, and segregation—with threshold, diffusion, game-theoretic, and dynamical models. Large-scale datasets from Twitter, Facebook, YouTube, Yelp, scholarly graphs, transactions, and software repositories support statistical analysis, embeddings, topic models, visual-meme detection, and supervised or crowd-assisted prediction. Studies also use randomized baselines, simulations, and visual analytics.

Recent directions emphasize richer signals beyond network topology or raw popularity: mass media and absent nodes in propagation models, cascade structure and semantics, video engagement rather than views, early per-object popularity forecasting, visual remix tracking, multifaceted transaction-based user modeling, and crowd signals for prioritizing fact checks. Research increasingly examines heterogeneity, demographic and ethnic diversity, network decay, and interventions intended to limit harmful diffusion.

d9d3a06aed3e5d534cb463c33d31050b0c74b1a2.text:
### Scientometrics, Citation Indicators, and Science Mapping

This community centers on measuring, mapping, and evaluating scientific research through bibliometric data. Major themes include field and institutional delineation, journal and technology relatedness, research-front emergence, scholarly reputation, and assessment of authors, institutions, countries, and journals. Particular attention is given to the limitations of citation counts, impact factors, h-indexes, and percentile-based indicators, especially their sensitivity to disciplinary, temporal, journal, and collaboration differences.

Typical methods include citation, co-citation, bibliographic-coupling, and collaboration networks; centrality, PageRank, modularity-based community detection, and network overlays; fractional counting and linked-network decompositions; and similarity-adapted publication vectors for cognitive distance. Researchers also use field-normalized percentiles, I3, Gini and diversity measures, statistical comparisons, precision/recall tests, and expert validation. RPYS and related visualization tools reconstruct intellectual histories and research fronts.

Recent work emphasizes fairer and more meaningful evaluation, including contribution-sensitive measures for large collaborations, calibrated cross-field indicators, and critiques of research-assessment side effects. Digital scholarly infrastructures motivate comparisons among Web of Science, Scopus, Microsoft Academic, and Dimensions, while finer-grained co-citation and MeSH representations enable more detailed mapping. The weakening link between journal impact factors and paper-level citations further supports article-centered assessment.

5d7db06895c57c3ea61630b283d4851bfa2bf50e.text:
## Scholarly Communication, Impact, and Discovery

This community studies how scholarly work is disseminated, discovered, evaluated, and used. Major themes include validating altmetrics and relating Twitter, Mendeley, downloads, readership, hyperlinks, and web traffic to citations, peer judgments, and societal impact. Other work examines open-access and arXiv citation advantages, repository use, positional visibility, and changing communication practices in astronomy and high-energy physics.

A second theme concerns bibliometric evaluation beyond journal articles: book and monograph use, publisher rankings, library loans, online reviews, and indicators for books, chapters, and edited volumes. Peer-review infrastructure is also prominent, including referee bidding, paper–reviewer matching, conference categorization, and reviewer-assignment optimization.

Typical methods combine large bibliographic, usage, social-media, and peer-assessment datasets with correlation analysis, regression, factor analysis, and statistical modeling. Researchers use text and review mining, citation and co-reading analysis, visualization, machine-learning classification, bibliographic record matching, and integer programming.

Recent trends emphasize heterogeneous and potentially noisy impact signals, earlier web-based indicators, social-platform metrics, open repositories, personalized scholarly-venue and article recommendation, and enhanced search portals. Across these topics, studies repeatedly stress validation, disciplinary differences, data quality, confounding factors, and the limits of treating any single metric as research impact.

338f3931807e7738c7079283ed4eebe632e543ec.text:
### Network Diffusion, Influence, and Epidemic Control

This community studies how information, infections, failures, and tasks propagate through social, technological, spatial, and interdependent networks. Major themes include influence maximization and marketing, epidemic cost and containment, diffusion-source localization, hidden-network recovery, and resilient network design. Applications range from online advertising and worker recruitment to malware tracing, wildlife dispersal, cyber-physical failures, and disease intervention.

Typical methods combine probabilistic cascade models—including independent-cascade, SIS/SI, complex-contagion, and continuous-time processes—with graph algorithms, stochastic optimization, mixed-integer programming, random-matrix analysis, factor graphs, and message passing. Submodularity and adaptive-submodularity support approximation guarantees for seed selection, while Jordan-center/cover methods address source localization from partial observations. Optimization and heuristic methods—including particle swarm, greedy, sampling, and random-walk approaches—handle uncertain parameters, limited probing, and large networks. Diffusion and superposition distances provide signal-comparison tools.

Recent work increasingly models realistic dynamics: temporal and adaptive networks, myopic or full-adoption feedback, online and sequential decisions, collective observations, non-submodular cascades, external spreading agents, and interdependent-network self-healing. Objectives are also broadening from reach to revenue, adoption, epidemic cost, reliability, coverage, fragmentation, and social consequences.

493e4c8e4dd29e0cafb2b9ea785caceb5d10aacb.text:
## Scalable Intelligent Retrieval and Data Systems

This community combines machine learning for text and document organization with scalable data management and mathematical information retrieval. Core themes include probabilistic and topic-based clustering, supervised text categorization, authorship analysis, sentiment and spam detection, and user-directed clustering. Typical methods include multinomial mixture and topic models, k-nearest-neighbor and k-medoids classifiers, association-rule mining with linguistic features, genetic feature selection, relevance feedback, active learning, and graph-based score propagation.

A substantial systems thread addresses large-scale analytics: Accumulo/D4M ingestion, provenance storage, Graphulo and GraphBLAS-style graph processing, external-memory graph analytics, associative-array representations, and polystore architectures integrating PostgreSQL, Accumulo, and SciDB. Database research develops memory-aware and least-expected-cost query optimization, relational-lattice algebra, cloud resource markets, dynamic scaling, and learning-based workload management.

Mathematical search is another major focus. Systems index formulas alongside text, compare presentation- and content-based representations, merge textual and formula queries, canonicalize expressions, and extract identifier meanings. Supporting infrastructure includes the DRMF, MIaS/WebMIaS, Mathoid, and large-scale notation studies.

Recent directions emphasize high-throughput and external-scale processing, autonomous or sentence-level active review, performance guarantees in cloud analytics, deep quality estimation, semantic enrichment of mathematics, and unified representations across databases, matrices, graphs, and spreadsheets.

ee20a1da2eb4153180dd7d0561fc5dfb0e178d31.text:
## Multiplex Social Networks and Dynamic Information Diffusion

This community centers on modeling and analyzing social systems as multiplex or multilayer networks, where users may be connected through friendship, communication, professional, semantic, or cross-platform ties. Major themes include multilayer centrality and similarity, online–offline identity linkage, group and community evolution, influence and link prediction, and the effects of missing or sampled data.

A second strong theme is diffusion: information cascades, viral campaigns, epidemics, behaviors, and opinions are studied across interacting layers. Work addresses epidemic thresholds, outbreak size, seed selection, mobility-informed containment, and sparse mobile-phone observations. Applications include marketing, recommendations, human resources, misinformation detection, and health campaigns.

Typical methods combine graph-theoretic measures, spectral analysis, random-graph theory, branching and cascade models, topic modeling, sentiment classification, association-rule mining, and embedding-based unsupervised identity linkage. Community studies use GED, SGCI, Louvain, and Infomap, while experiments rely on Twitter, Facebook, blogs, email, Web 2.0, cellular, and synthetic datasets.

Recent trends emphasize unified models of interconnected identities, scalable dynamic community detection, heterogeneous sampling, realistic synthetic-network generation, cross-platform privacy and deanonymization analysis, and theories of interacting spreading processes in multiplex networks.

4ac55a6ee29ebf31ea6a4404383411385b1d1e84.text:
## Social Media as a Sensor of Place, Mobility, and Urban Life

This community studies how social-media and location-based data can reveal human behavior, places, and urban environments. Major themes include geolocation inference for tweets and Reddit posts; human mobility, home and preferential-return locations, commuting, group colocation, and mobility-based urban boundaries; and urban perception through smell, sound, beauty, happiness, parks, and sentiment. Other applications include disaster response, sexual-violence tracking, business-location selection, recommendations, advertising, event scheduling, sports prediction, and food and tourism analysis.

Typical methods combine natural-language processing, sentiment and semantic analysis, supervised learning, convolutional and other deep neural networks, probabilistic and Gaussian-mixture models, graph representations and influence modeling, low-rank approximation, trajectory clustering, and spatial-temporal network analysis. Researchers frequently integrate text, images, profiles, check-ins, mobility traces, and social ties, often with crowdsourced dictionaries or labels. Evaluation uses benchmark datasets, precision/recall, calibration and uncertainty measures, independent travel surveys, and cross-dataset validation.

Recent trends emphasize multimodal and scalable analytics, inference without explicit geotags, bias correction and annotation-error mitigation, quantified uncertainty, and validation beyond platform data. The work increasingly shifts from describing online activity to supporting real-time humanitarian response, personalized routing, urban planning, and commercially informed decisions.

f0ffd29e518f3c37f121b07ea741fee30f750d34.text:
### Uncertainty, Provenance, and Reliable Data Management

This community studies how databases can represent, query, explain, and repair unreliable or incomplete information. A central theme is probabilistic and uncertain data management: query evaluation, joins, aggregation, top-k ranking, similarity search, and frequent-itemset mining under uncertainty. Work addresses both exact and approximate inference, including lifted inference, knowledge compilation, decomposition trees, semiring/semimodule representations, U-relations, probabilistic pruning, and statistics-aware algorithm selection.

A second major theme is provenance, causality, and explanation. Research characterizes causes and responsibility for query answers and non-answers, computes provenance graphs for queries with negation, applies Shapley values to tuple contribution, and connects causality with abductive diagnosis, view updates, database repairs, and answer-set programs.

Integrity and inconsistency management form another strand, covering integrity verification, active repairs, inconsistency measures, approximate query answering, access-control policy repair, and query answering under conceptual dependencies or tuple-generating dependencies. Chase-based reasoning and finite-controllability results establish tractable or decidable classes.

Recent directions emphasize scalable and practical systems: billion-vector search, progressive and schema-agnostic entity resolution, probabilistic ranking, workflow reproducibility, MapReduce performance explanations, fact-checking-oriented data cleaning, and benchmarks for knowledge graphs. Data markets and belief annotations further explore collaborative, explainable data sharing and curation.

95a1dce052cf40117e8c451b725bee2580168337.text:
### Graph Querying, Optimization, and Interoperable Graph Data

This community focuses on efficient, expressive, and usable querying of RDF, knowledge graphs, and property graphs. A major theme is SPARQL optimization: algebraic rewriting, query reordering, cardinality estimation, runtime and incremental evaluation, summary- and partition-driven execution, and specialized handling of OPTIONAL, OWL entailment, provenance, preferences, and incomplete information. Federated querying receives substantial attention, including source selection, heuristics, replication, large-scale deployments, and integration with relational databases and arbitrary RDF-bearing Web sources.

A second theme is graph-system foundations and interoperability. Work develops mappings between relational, RDF, OWL, and property-graph models; translates SPARQL to Gremlin; defines property-graph type systems; and studies graph storage architectures and traversal machines. Formal analyses cover multiset semantics, containment and subsumption, regular and context-free path queries, and complexity boundaries.

Typical methods combine formal semantics, Datalog, relational algebra, automata and grammar theory, static complexity analysis, indexing, graph summaries, adaptive storage, and experimental benchmarking. Usability-oriented approaches include keyword/SPARQL hybrids, query-by-example, schemas and shape validation, and provenance visualization. Recent directions emphasize scalable and adaptive execution, heterogeneous graph interoperability, replicated federations, data-science provenance summarization, and controllable graph workload generation.

c959380d95e607496b98ecf8bae29f1cc3b9817d.text:
## Social Media Networks, Polarization, and Information Integrity

This community studies how social platforms shape political opinion, collective behavior, and information diffusion. Major themes include polarized communities and overlapping beliefs; elections, voter preference, and computational propaganda; misinformation, rumors, fake news, and disinformation campaigns; extremist and fringe communities; spam, bots, autogenerated content, and malicious actors; and demographic inequality in online visibility and connections. Several works also address public-health interventions, environmental monitoring, decentralized search, and crowdsourced-platform security.

Typical methods combine large-scale Twitter, Facebook, YouTube, Reddit, and browsing data with network analysis, retweet and followership graphs, assortativity, community detection, and polarization measures. Machine-learning approaches include nonnegative and structured matrix factorization, sparse learning, latent Dirichlet allocation with regression, PCA-based ideological scoring, supervised and semi-supervised classification, deep neural networks, and metadata, temporal, content, and propagation features. Surveys, user studies, and manually annotated validation complement computational analysis.

Recent work increasingly emphasizes early, message-level rumor detection; distinguishing data-driven from ranking-induced search bias; measuring continuous intra-community conflict; identifying coordinated propaganda and extremist-content adoption; comparing platform-specific echo chambers; and designing interventions, verification systems, and defenses against malicious or Sybil actors.

2f5af301e54d17c326ad025b0d9f1b544882e131.text:
### Information Retrieval: Neural Ranking, Semantic Search, and Scalable Discovery

This community centers on improving information retrieval and ranking across web, enterprise, mobile, email, biomedical, and dataset-search settings. Major themes include relevance estimation, query understanding and clustering, answer-passage retrieval, expert and entity search, web-quality and spam detection, and retrieval from heterogeneous or temporal data. Dataset discovery and knowledge-base enhancement extend retrieval toward structured information and reuse.

Typical methods combine learning-to-rank with neural representation learning. Deep architectures model local relevance, cross-document interactions, groupwise scoring, and permutation-invariant rankings. BERT and multilingual BERT support pointwise, pairwise, multi-stage, and cross-lingual ranking, while multitask learning, entailment, query expansion, embeddings, kernels, and semantic field features improve matching. Traditional probabilistic or axiomatic principles remain useful for regularizing neural models. Graphs, hashing, sketches, and approximate nearest-neighbor structures address large-scale and time-series search.

Recent work emphasizes pretrained language models, large labeled benchmark collections, and end-to-end systems balancing quality and latency. Retrieval is becoming more conversational, agent-based, dynamic, and personalized, including mobile assistants and personal-memory question answering. Other emerging directions include interpretable ranking, temporal entity-aspect recommendation, schema-aware dataset search, semantic hashing, and zero-shot multilingual transfer.

72e8dbd1f5e390f69f3b6dddb54a0a6ceec2909a.text:
## Recommender Systems: From Collaborative Filtering to Context-Aware Personalization

This community centers on personalized recommendation across ratings, implicit feedback, sequences, sessions, news, movies, music, advertising, and education. Core themes include combining long-term preferences with short-term behavior; addressing sparsity, cold start, missing modalities, and anonymous users; and improving diversity, long-tail exposure, robustness, and trust.

Typical methods range from matrix factorization, slope-one predictors, nearest-neighbor and signed-bipartite ranking to hybrid collaborative/content-based models using ontologies, textual, audio, visual, and social information. Neural approaches increasingly model nonlinear user–item interactions through variational autoencoders, neural collaborative filtering, factorization machines, language models, and multimodal architectures. Sequential recommendation uses Markov chains, latent-state models, RNNs, session modeling, and graph neural networks such as SR-GNN. Other methods include metric learning, context trees, determinantal point processes for diverse ranking, and reinforcement learning for advertising.

Recent directions emphasize richer behavioral context: inter-session history, mixture-of-tastes representations, cross-domain shared-account recommendation, missing-modality learning, and graph-based transition modeling. Research also increasingly examines deployment concerns, including popularity bias, fraudulent reviews, reputation, offline-evaluation bias, real-time inference, and balancing advertising revenue with user experience.

c32769fd443f0868f1db03e13de96e748b52344c.text:
### Graph Learning for Dynamic and Heterogeneous Networks

This community focuses on modeling, learning, and mining complex networks across social, temporal, biological, financial, urban, and knowledge-graph settings. Major themes include network representation learning, link and relationship prediction, community detection, graph similarity, anomaly and fraud detection, and structural analysis of uncertain, covert, or sampled networks.

Typical methods combine local structural signals—triangles, clustering coefficients, degree correlations, motifs, and paths—with probabilistic models, random walks, Markov chains, matrix or graph embeddings, and machine learning classifiers. Neural and deep embedding methods increasingly integrate node content, heterogeneous relations, temporal snapshots, and metapaths. Knowledge-oriented work applies text mining, entity normalization, triple scoring, and discriminative predicate paths for fact checking and knowledge-graph completion.

The papers also emphasize scalable computation, including MapReduce triangle counting, approximate GED search, sampling with quality guarantees, and local-information algorithms. Applications include search-rank fraud attribution, insider-trading and lending fraud, privacy prediction, criminal and covert-network analysis, team formation, and urban-dynamics modeling.

Recent directions move toward continuous-time and generative dynamic-network models, temporally robust embeddings, uncertainty-aware inference, adversarial community deception, cross-network fusion, and latent-variable graph grammars. Overall, the community trends toward integrating structure, semantics, time, and application-specific risk objectives.

a9b74cc72458f0f22f7ba5824c2250d92ce03e12.text:
### Scholarly and Knowledge-Graph Network Analysis

This community studies how graph structure can organize, evaluate, and enrich scholarly and information resources. Major themes include bibliometrics and science mapping; author, paper, dataset, university, and patent ranking; coauthorship and citation-network structure; Wikipedia as a multilingual knowledge and geopolitical network; and information retrieval through knowledge maps, query expansion, and linked data.

Typical methods include PageRank, CheiRank, weighted and recursive ranking, reduced Google matrices, centrality and spectral analysis, community detection, stochastic block models, graphons, and network-flow measures such as DataRank. Studies also employ statistical models, PCA, bibliographic mapping, visualization, and LSTM prediction. A substantial strand addresses data quality: author-name disambiguation, metadata cleaning and record linkage, relevance-assessment reliability, and semi-automatic “seed+expand” oeuvre construction.

Recent directions emphasize dynamic and longitudinal analysis, including evolving Wikipedia, citation, patent, and disciplinary networks; prediction of community growth and emerging technologies; and distinctions between popularity, prestige, influence, and historical significance. Other trends include multilingual and cross-cultural comparisons, interdisciplinary knowledge organization using SKOS and Linked Data, integrated digital libraries, open and reproducible science via Jupyter, and attention to privacy, stewardship, and credit for research datasets.

305a69fa1449f13c7879ce05a73e24ec66a9f459.text:
### Collaborative Knowledge, Tagging, and Personalized Search

This community studies how user-generated and collaboratively structured data can support information access, knowledge representation, and social analysis. Major themes include Wikipedia and Wiktionary as multilingual knowledge resources; collaborative tagging, folksonomies, vocabulary growth, and emergent semantics; and Semantic Web representations using ontologies, SKOS, relational schemas, and linked data. Several works examine search and recommendation, including entity ranking, synonym expansion, semantic navigation, news detection, group information seeking, and evaluation of search metrics.

Typical methods combine large-scale platform data analysis with network and graph techniques: power-law and scaling models, co-occurrence and similarity measures, clustering, centrality and influence estimation, HITS/PageRank-like ranking, and visualization. NLP pipelines extract dictionary relations, link mentions to knowledge-base identifiers, and match multilingual ontologies. Applied systems increasingly use machine learning, including matrix factorization, learning-to-rank, collaborative filtering, and minimally invasive click-log randomization.

Recent work shifts toward scalable, multilingual, and personalized applications. Examples include dense Wikipedia entity annotations, language-agnostic entity linking, professional-network expertise and talent-flow analytics, personalized search, and behavior-based location forecasting. Overall, the research moves from describing collective structures and vocabulary dynamics toward operational systems that exploit social, semantic, and behavioral signals.

6e7ff7f634dd6e9a768e50c3bf80ef556bd2145c.text:
### Network Dynamics, Influence, and Social Information

This community studies how information, opinions, and influence evolve over complex, often dynamic networks. A major theme is opinion dynamics: DeGroot, Friedkin–Johnsen, bounded-confidence, Bayesian, biased, multi-topic, and signed-network models address consensus, disagreement, polarization, social power, antagonism, and heterogeneous susceptibility. Related work examines feedback between opinions and personalized recommendations, political affinity from voting data, and topic-specific behavior in social media.

A second theme is network structure and influence optimization. Papers develop and analyze centrality, PageRank, distinctiveness, navigability, communicability, robustness, discoverability, and backbone measures, often studying edge rewiring, node addition or deletion, delay reduction, and optimal network design. Game-theoretic formulations and best-response dynamics model strategic link formation.

Methods combine graph Laplacians, spectral embeddings, harmonic analysis, stability and asymptotic proofs, random-walk and thermodynamic path models, optimization, and simulation. Empirical studies mine Twitter, online conversations, voting records, traffic, fiction, and television-character networks, using motifs, temporal-topic mining, classification, and link prediction.

Recent directions emphasize scalable algorithms for large graphs, dynamic and signed interactions, local structural signals for controversy and moderation, and richer models incorporating content, time, individual biases, and closed-loop recommendation effects.

62653499778f420ae4d442aa6ea91f0b3ae1a5fd.text:
## Durable, Semantic Archives for an Evolving Web

This community studies how to preserve, model, search, and reuse changing digital resources. Major themes include web archiving and temporal retrieval; modular repositories for heterogeneous digital objects; linked open data and semantic modeling; provenance, annotation, and scholarly communication; and long-term integrity, quality, and accessibility.

Typical methods combine standards-based architectures (RDF, SPARQL, OAIS, MPEG-21, PROV-O, Open Annotation, SharedCanvas, and persistent identifiers) with ontologies, semantic layers, nanopublications, and version-aware data models. Researchers also use focused crawling, social-media signals, lexical signatures, title analysis, longitudinal web datasets, and large-scale access-log studies. Retrieval and infrastructure work applies caching, federated search, machine-learning prediction, and graph-based analysis.

Recent work increasingly addresses resources that are dynamic, distributed, or poorly preserved: evolving linked datasets, web-native scholarly objects, orphaned annotations, and disappearing social-media-linked pages. Studies emphasize freshness and event monitoring through social and Wikipedia activity, while repository and archive systems improve scalability and interoperability. Emerging concerns include data-quality principles for the Semantic Web, repeatable timestamping and cryptographic integrity for archived pages, and richer semantic access to archived documents and web graphs.

15491f2795d63853c9f612760afd5609af097e87.text:
## Flexible Search, Fair Recommendations, and Scalable Data Systems

This community spans database search, information retrieval, and high-performance data management. Major themes include querying imprecise or incomplete data through fuzzy summaries, flexible SQL, skyline and aggregate skyline queries, and concise relational object summaries. Search and recommendation research addresses re-ranking, tag consistency, graph-pattern retrieval, scientific workflows, and scholarly semantic publishing. A prominent recent direction is responsible ranking: measuring and mitigating demographic bias, correcting biased implicit feedback, using demographic representations, and injecting “antidote” data to improve fairness and polarization.

Typical methods combine formal query models and ranking algorithms with re-ranking, counterfactual inference, association rules, graph-pattern search, and top-*k*/any-*k* retrieval. Systems work emphasizes approximate nearest-neighbor hashing, set and bitmap intersections, compressed indexes, SIMD compression, learned graph query planning, and specialized GPU/CPU execution. Hidden-database crawling and third-party query re-ranking extend search over restricted interfaces.

Recent trends favor scalable infrastructure: distributed frequent-subgraph mining with Spark/Flink, Hadoop-based publication mining, GPU OLTP and pathology-image processing, and compact or low-maintenance indexing. Across the community, research increasingly connects efficient retrieval with richer semantics, large-scale scholarly and graph data, and explicit fairness objectives.

aa4584bf79d6718696d51d87fd775636a433126e.text:
### Scalable Graph Analytics and Utility-Aware Pattern Mining

This community combines efficient graph computation with actionable pattern discovery. Graph research targets reachability, distances, shortest paths, temporal paths, and information diffusion, including dynamic monopolies and opinion spreading. Typical methods use landmark and hop-doubling labels, distance sketches, reachability oracles, hub acceleration, temporal indexing, and parallel vertex-centric computation. Applications include social-network analysis, knowledge mobilization, sequenced routes, and revenue-oriented recommendations or content matching.

A second major theme is utility-oriented mining. Work extends frequent-pattern techniques to high-utility itemsets, episodes, and sequential patterns, incorporating occupancy, item-specific thresholds, recency, trends, privacy, and multidimensional sequences. Projection-based mining, pruning, closure and concise representations, generic association-rule bases, and Minimum Description Length are recurring techniques. Surveys consolidate developments in utility mining and parallel sequential mining.

Additional topics address graph-structured tree-query associations, relational rules, spatio-textual clustering, SQL window-function optimization, and reducing order-enforcement costs in query plans.

Recent trends emphasize temporal and dynamic data, massive-scale and parallel processing, compact indexes and summaries, privacy preservation, and moving beyond frequency toward utility, revenue, relevance, and recency.

5a10abeb5186fa39160aa5f6b75b87f2359a2744.text:
## Principles and Systems for Scalable Data Management

This community spans foundational query processing and practical data-intensive systems. Core themes include join ordering and evaluation, cardinality estimation, query complexity, distributed communication, dynamic databases, and coordination-free computation. Graph analytics is frequently recast as relational joins, enabling SQL/Datalog processing over relational and specialized engines.

Typical methods combine formal complexity and worst-case analyses with engineered systems. Examples include MILP formulations for plan search, worst-case-optimal multiway joins, matrix multiplication, functional-dependency reasoning, and specialized indexing or data layouts. Distributed work studies single-round reshuffling, communication bounds, partial quorums, and blockchain/database trade-offs. Systems papers emphasize column stores, high-level languages, associative arrays, relational graph engines, lightweight emulators, and hardware acceleration.

A strong trend is learning- and model-driven data management: deep networks estimate correlated join cardinalities and generate query plans, while generative and maximum-entropy models support approximate query processing. Approximation also appears in video analytics, streaming diagnosis, and probabilistic summaries. Another direction integrates analytics and machine learning directly with relational data and declarative lifecycle systems, reducing boundary crossings between data engineering and modeling. Recent work further emphasizes collaborative dataset versioning, secure processing that exploits non-sensitive data, adaptive time-series compression, replicated index specialization, and automated data-structure design.

b67b33b73de9c75225020d23e3dd07f4ade43d1f.text:
### Data Integration, Entity Resolution, and Human-in-the-Loop Quality

This community focuses on making heterogeneous, noisy, and conflicting data usable. Core themes include data fusion and truth discovery, entity resolution and consolidation, similarity joins, record linkage, and integration of Web, open, linked, social, and urban spatio-temporal data. A recurring concern is source dependence: copying and correlated sources can undermine majority voting, motivating explicit modeling of source reliability, recurrence, and multiple possible truths.

Typical methods combine probabilistic or hybrid truth-finding models, graph matching, blocking and partitioning, similarity search, distributed message passing, and scalable indexing. DeepER applies learned representations to reduce feature engineering in entity resolution, while other work uses regular-expression and structural-pattern discovery for schema and Web extraction. Integrity-constraint research automatically discovers functional, order, and ontology dependencies for data cleaning and exchange.

Humans remain central for ambiguous or quality-critical cases. Crowdsourcing studies address worker reliability, confidence intervals, latency, task assignment, route selection, and fault-tolerant entity resolution. Human–machine frameworks explicitly optimize labeling cost subject to precision and recall guarantees.

Recent directions emphasize scaling to millions of records and sources, adaptive and parallel algorithms, prediction-aware spatial assignment, robust handling of copying and unknown data, and democratized systems requiring less expert intervention.

aeb611a2c521ff47f66854e0b51249d4ffd013a7.text:
## Cognitive, Temporal, and Context-Aware Recommendation

This community focuses on improving recommender systems beyond popularity and accuracy, especially for sparse, long-tail, social, and location-based data. A major theme is cognitively inspired tag and hashtag recommendation: models draw on ACT-R-style activation, frequency, recency, forgetting, semantic context, and individual versus social reuse. User studies and multi-dataset evaluations examine both recommendation quality and acceptance.

Other work addresses novelty, diversity, coverage, cold start, trust, and confirmation bias in collaborative filtering. Hybrid methods combine collaborative signals with tags, metadata, search terms, sentiment, topic models, neural embeddings, and attention or interpretation dynamics. Re-ranking is used to balance accuracy with long-tail exposure and user-specific novelty.

A second strong theme is spatial and temporal recommendation. Geo-temporal embeddings, sequential models, sparse additive models, sentiment, and mobility traces support point-of-interest, venue, and out-of-town recommendations. Location and social-media data also enable semantic place discovery.

The community further develops scalable similarity search and ranking for streams and dynamic graphs, using sliding windows, time-dependent similarity, locality-sensitive hashing, decomposition, and link analysis. Toolkits such as TagRec support reproducible evaluation.

Recent trends move toward theory-guided, cognitively plausible models; neural and embedding-based representations; context-sensitive personalization; and explicit optimization of novelty, diversity, coverage, freshness, and computational scalability.

9b1c316fc7d16bcfb080d1b3a5a9f33b9468da53.text:
## Scholarly Metrics, Search, and Open Science

This community studies how scholarly information is indexed, ranked, measured, and disseminated. A central theme is comparative bibliometrics: Google Scholar, Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar Metrics, and Microsoft Academic Search are evaluated for coverage, citation counts, highly cited documents, journal rankings, research-unit benchmarking, and relationships between citation indicators and peer assessment. Particular attention is given to Google Scholar’s broad coverage, size, reliability, version management, and susceptibility to h-index manipulation.

A second theme concerns information retrieval and library discovery. Work examines ranking factors for library materials, search-engine technology in catalogs, credibility signals, query expansion, and learning-based selection of topics for lower-cost evaluation test collections, including the deep-versus-shallow judging problem.

Open access research measures freely available versions, combines evidence from multiple sources, and evaluates repository mandates and deposit rates. Related discussions address publication costs and self-archiving.

Typical methods include large-scale citation and web-data collection, automated querying, longitudinal and cross-database comparisons, correlation and regression analysis, bibliometric indicators, learning-to-rank, complexity analysis, and social/temporal network analysis. Online communities—especially Wikipedia—are modeled through edits, reverts, norms, and interaction networks.

Recent trends emphasize open science indicators, increasingly comprehensive academic search engines, reproducible large-scale measurement, algorithmic evaluation, and the governance and reliability of scholarly metrics.

e3ccfc1c01e3bb510fba61bedbe8ae7307ddd837.text:
## Privacy-Preserving Data Publishing and Analysis

This community centers on releasing and analyzing sensitive relational, graph, mobility, search, and transactional data while balancing privacy, accuracy, and usability. Differential privacy is the dominant framework, applied to histograms, sparse data, range and predicate queries, marginals, frequent itemsets, clustering, decision trees, community detection, recommendations, and hierarchical statistics. Complementary themes include \(k\)-anonymity and its variants, slicing and set-valued anonymization, provenance views, surrogate graph structures, randomized perturbation, and adversarial disclosure analysis incorporating algorithm knowledge and background knowledge.

Typical methods add calibrated noise, use wavelet or hierarchical decompositions, and optimize query strategies through matrix mechanisms, convex optimization, adaptive selection, or data/workload-aware partitioning. Other work reconstructs aggregate distributions while limiting individual inference, or uses trusted hardware for private federated SQL processing.

Recent directions emphasize stronger and more practical deployment: local differential privacy for marginals and location recommendations; scalable, high-dimensional query answering; private data exploration and cleaning through noisy interfaces; and accuracy-aware systems that reduce analyst burden. Applications increasingly address fairness, demographic bias, dynamic social links, transportation data, provenance, and decision-making, extending privacy research beyond release mechanisms toward trustworthy downstream use.

336cee946ec215680a82c3e6352d5c5e567f159d.text:
### Complex Networks for Software, Science, and Social Systems

This community applies complex-network methods to understand large, evolving systems, especially software architectures, scientific databases, collaboration networks, and online communities. Core themes include community and group structure, node mixing, centrality, preferential attachment, interdisciplinarity, social status, and network evolution.

Typical methods involve constructing graphs from software dependencies, citations, coauthorships, web links, or online interactions, then analyzing degree distributions, small-world structure, assortativity, centrality, communities, and local/global topology. Researchers also develop propagation-based group-detection algorithms, citation-dynamics models, network sampling and simplification strategies, and statistical comparisons across bibliographic databases. Data quality is a recurring concern, addressed through database-consistency analysis, entity resolution, redundancy elimination, and comparisons of DBLP, CiteSeer, Web of Science, PubMed, and related sources.

Applications span software quality, vulnerability, reuse, and controllability; forecasting influence in social networks; healthcare collaboration; and evaluation of scientific activity across individual, institutional, and national levels. Recent directions emphasize web-search-derived researcher networks, context-aware data integration, multilevel and longitudinal collaboration analysis, interdisciplinary research trajectories, and methods that preserve community structure and graph properties when networks are sampled or reduced.

95068d25b31fae176e6f2e3d7c675031da921a5b.text:
## Scalable, Flexible, and Responsible Data Retrieval

This community centers on advanced data retrieval and analytics across relational, web, graph, scientific, and recommendation systems. A major theme is flexible querying over imperfect or complex data, including fuzzy databases and linguistic summaries, incomplete-data streams, skyline and aggregate skyline queries, hidden databases, workflows, and object summaries.

Efficiency is pursued through specialized indexing and representation: bitmap and Roaring indexes, set intersection, integer and multidimensional compression, variable-byte encoding, locality-sensitive hashing, and learned or lightweight database indexes. Systems increasingly exploit SIMD, GPUs, hybrid CPU–GPU execution, and distributed in-memory frameworks such as Spark, Flink, and Hadoop for transaction processing, spatial comparison, and frequent subgraph mining.

Ranking and recommendation research addresses personalization, reranking, tag consistency, sponsored search, and academic-paper recommendation services. A prominent recent direction is responsible retrieval: fairness-aware ranking, demographic representations, counterfactual learning from biased clicks, and “antidote” data for reducing polarization and unfairness. Related work studies semantic representation bias in high-stakes classification.

Graph-oriented work develops top-k and any-k pattern retrieval, workflow search, and learned query planning. Overall, the papers show a trend toward practical, scalable services that combine richer semantics, learned optimization, heterogeneous hardware, and explicit social objectives.

28d16445d9736dcf26f83b684bfd5cbb8f36c16a.text:
## Network Dynamics, Influence, and Social Information

This community studies how information, opinions, and influence move through complex, social, and web-based networks. A major theme is opinion dynamics: DeGroot, Friedkin–Johnsen, bounded-confidence, biased-assimilation, and multi-topic models examine consensus, polarization, disagreement, social power, stubborn agents, individual biases, and signed (friendly/adversarial) interactions. Recent work increasingly models dynamic topologies, heterogeneous thresholds, recommendation feedback loops, and topic-specific user behavior.

A second theme is network structure and control. Papers develop centrality axioms and generalized-degree measures, analyze navigability, communicability, robustness, discoverability, PageRank, and backbone structure, and optimize edges, tags, coverage, delay, or social influence. Typical methods include graph and spectral analysis, Markov chains, Laplacian and harmonic-function techniques, optimization, motif analysis, information-theoretic criteria, and scalable algorithms evaluated on large real or synthetic networks.

Applications span social media controversy, stance summarization, event discovery, traffic and communication networks, and web crawling. Recent trends emphasize scalable computation for large graphs, temporal and content-aware interaction data, active sensing of social trust, strategic network design, and integrated models connecting user behavior, recommendations, and evolving opinions.

8dec55d84b623e44f4adf6eb34b28853949ebb33.text:
## Social Media, Misinformation, and Networked Influence

This community examines how social platforms shape political discourse, public opinion, collective behavior, and online safety. Major themes include misinformation, rumors, conspiracy narratives, fake news, extremist and alt-right communities, polarization and echo chambers, gender/race inequality, harassment, spam, fake followers, crowdturfing, and attacks on crowdsourced services. Several studies measure algorithmic bias in search and news feeds, while others investigate how fringe communities and state-sponsored campaigns influence the wider web.

Typical methods combine large-scale data collection from Twitter, Facebook, YouTube, 4chan, Gab, and other platforms with network analysis, cascade and propagation modeling, surveys, temporal analysis, and cross-platform comparisons. Machine-learning approaches include nonnegative matrix factorization, supervised and semi-supervised classification, domain adaptation, feature-based detection, image-based demographic inference, and personalized text generation. Graph integration and adjusted random walks support community discovery and unbiased population estimates.

Recent work increasingly emphasizes reproducible measurement of platform and data bias, fine-grained stance and rumor judgments, verification and fact-checking workflows, and the dynamics of misinformation. It also explores interventions: bots for health and activist outreach, crowd-powered flagging, content filtering, and strategies to detect or disrupt malicious automation, Sybil devices, and coordinated influence campaigns.

fdae6a285ccc6f59859d583c551906e87f4f8ca3.text:
## Graph Representation and Analysis of Complex Networks

This community studies how to model, represent, sample, and analyze large, uncertain, and evolving networks. Major themes include node and document representation learning; link, relationship, and fact prediction; community, core–periphery, and dense-subgraph discovery; and structural measures such as centrality, clustering, triangles, and balance. Applications span social, citation, semantic, affiliation, criminal, financial, and political-violence networks.

Typical methods combine graph structure with node content, text, knowledge bases, and attributes. Learning approaches include network and structural-identity embeddings, dynamic embeddings, stochastic blockmodels, latent-feature Bayesian models, and citation-context distributed representations. Prediction methods use path-based features, clustering perspectives, ensembles, trigger-word detection, and cross-layer signals. Structural analysis employs random walks, absorbing Markov chains, axiomatic models, maximum likelihood, and machine learning. To address scale, studies develop wedge and traversal sampling, hybrid-network crawling, MapReduce triangle counting, approximation algorithms, and external-memory distributed generation.

Recent work increasingly emphasizes temporal, continuous-time, heterogeneous, signed, uncertain, and coevolving multilayer networks. It also seeks robustness and quality guarantees in representations and sampling, integrates semantic or textual evidence into graph inference, and targets practical applications such as privacy advice, fact checking, anomaly detection, and recommendation.

67cc72957b32b332d9b2df45bf7471fc949b3b66.text:
## Recommendation Under Sparse, Dynamic, and Heterogeneous Signals

This community centers on personalized recommender systems across products, movies, news, education, images, and tags. Core themes include collaborative filtering from explicit ratings or implicit feedback; sequential and session-based recommendation; content and multimodal modeling; graph-based recommendation and link prediction; and trust, reputation, robustness, and fraud.

Typical methods range from matrix factorization, slope-one predictors, k-nearest neighbors, Bayesian Personalized Ranking, and co-clustering to Markov chains, context trees, random walks, and signed or bipartite network models. Neural approaches increasingly use nonlinear latent transformations, autoencoders, autoregressive models, recurrent networks, list-wise session architectures, and deep visual embeddings. Hybrid and collective models combine user–item interactions with text, audio, visual features, social information, and heterogeneous item relationships.

Recent work emphasizes practical limitations: sparse or missing feedback, cold-start users and items, anonymous sessions, noisy or manipulated ratings, and long-tail exposure. Models increasingly represent diverse user tastes through mixtures, exploit inter-session behavior, and infer substitute/complement product relations. Multimodal recommendation is expanding toward missing-modality handling and visual preference modeling, while interpretable co-clusters and robustness-oriented reputation methods address transparency and reliability. Social tagging research also incorporates cognitive factors such as frequency, recency, and semantic context.

20c5d259bde5fd441790870e8383a5c6e70b80af.text:
**Principles and Systems for Scalable Data Management**

This community centers on efficient query processing and analytical data systems. A major theme is join optimization: papers develop MILP formulations for plan search, worst-case size bounds and optimal algorithms, incremental Leapfrog Triejoin maintenance, cardinality estimation with deep learning, sampling algebras, and techniques for inequalities. Distributed evaluation emphasizes communication complexity, single-round multiway joins, parallel-correctness, coordination-free computation, and MapReduce optimization.

A second theme is scalable graph and streaming analytics. Relational databases are used for vertex-centric graph processing, while EmptyHeaded and RDF studies apply high-level Datalog-like languages and worst-case-optimal joins. Other work addresses continuous subgraph search over streaming graphs and data-cube analysis over large datasets.

Systems research seeks high performance with better abstraction and automation: Scala-based query engines, column stores, adaptive indexing on multicore systems, SQL-on-Hadoop comparisons, speculative analytics, and attention prioritization for fast data. Data science management is also prominent, including dataset version control, model lifecycle platforms, resource sharing, visual-insight recommendation, and revenue-aware recommendation.

Recent directions combine database techniques with machine learning, support dynamic and stale data, exploit parallel and cloud infrastructure, and address replication consistency, privacy, and security.

544ed406e446fd4c1b885b4916a3b620c52dbe0d.text:
## Social Media Signals for Political, Urban, and Behavioral Intelligence

This community studies how user-generated and location-aware data can reveal preferences, behaviors, mobility, and urban experience. A major theme is political inference and election forecasting from Twitter and Facebook: researchers analyze follows, likes, language, and temporal activity to estimate voter preferences, ideology, demographic effects, and candidate support. Related work predicts sports outcomes, business ratings, daily-deal success, and promising commercial locations from social activity and reviews.

Urban and geographic research uses geotagged tweets, check-ins, photographs, mobile networks, and trajectories to characterize global mobility, preferential-return locations, group colocation, functional regions, neighborhood signatures, urban boundaries, and tourist-location networks. Other studies map qualitative city experiences, including smell, sound, beauty, quietness, happiness, and the affective effects of parks.

Typical methods include sparse learning, supervised classifiers, convolutional neural networks, LDA topic modeling, sentiment analysis, negative-binomial and multinomial regression, low-rank approximation, probabilistic geospatial models, Gaussian mixtures, network analysis, clustering, and route optimization. Researchers also quantify uncertainty in inferred locations and trajectories and evaluate sampling bias in Twitter’s Streaming API.

Recent directions emphasize fine-grained and hyperlocal geolocation, multimodal qualitative mapping, uncertainty-aware inference, social diffusion and group behavior, and practical decision-support systems for elections, urban planning, mobility, wellbeing, and local commerce.

5eb30fc0847e270e23c6f1453db851e4d079e95c.text:
## Information Retrieval: Neural Matching, Efficient Search, and Interactive Evaluation

This community centers on improving search quality, scalability, and understanding of user intent. Major themes include learning to rank, ad hoc retrieval, query expansion and clustering, document similarity, web-content quality and spam detection, and entity- and event-oriented search. Applications span text, images, news, social media, time series, and knowledge graphs.

Typical methods combine classical retrieval signals (BM25, term distributions, phrases, and relevance judgments) with machine learning. Deep models use word embeddings, convolutional or recurrent networks, interaction matrices, kernel pooling, and entity-salience modeling to capture local and semantic relevance. Hashing, signatures, dimensionality reduction, K-tree clustering, and sketching support large-scale indexing and similarity search. Other work develops bipartite ranking, twin support vector machines, behavior models, and bandit-based online evaluation.

Recent trends emphasize end-to-end neural ranking while retaining explicit soft-match and traditional relevance features; unsupervised or self-taught representations for unseen content; and dynamic, list-level, and user-interaction feedback. Entity linking, relationship retrieval, knowledge-base table answers, and news-to-Wikipedia analysis extend search beyond document matching. Explainable search, credibility-aware evaluation, scalable theoretically grounded comparisons, and real-time query decomposition further address transparency, trust, and freshness.

660d5d1c6aca44059b74dee2a55dc00fa90437b4.text:
### Scholarly Networks, Retrieval, and Bibliometric Intelligence

This community studies how network structure and bibliometric evidence can improve scholarly information systems. A major theme is author identity: researchers evaluate initials-based and DBLP disambiguation, combine collaboration patterns with topological features, and develop validated semi-automatic “seed+expand” publication oeuvres.

PageRank and related Google-matrix methods form another central theme. Weighted and unweighted variants rank authors, papers, patents, Wikipedia articles, and Twitter users, while distinguishing popularity from prestige through citation weighting, bipartite models, CheiRank, and 2DRanking. Work also examines centrality stability, spectral structure, network communities, striations, and the emergence of technologies and geopolitical relationships.

Information retrieval research emphasizes domain-specific query expansion, thesauri, Bradfordizing, knowledge maps, visual interfaces, and metadata enrichment through Linked Data. Studies use user experiments, relevance-agreement measures, bibliometric mapping, and network analysis to evaluate retrieval and scholarly communication.

Typical methods include graph and coauthorship/citation analysis, PageRank-style recursive ranking, statistical and spectral modeling, controlled evaluations, visualization, and large-scale mining of digital-library, Wikipedia, patent, and social-media data. Recent directions favor interdisciplinary and multilingual analyses, interactive term suggestion, open and reproducible workflows using Jupyter, semantic metadata linking, and richer visual or network-based exploration of information spaces.

f7960cdb9a0d9a191cdc9c4229b9f81d082b011b.text:
### Topic Discovery and Real-Time Social Intelligence

This community centers on extracting structure, events, opinions, and actionable knowledge from large, heterogeneous text and social-media streams. A major theme is topic modeling: latent Dirichlet and related models are extended to hypertext, temporal streams, multi-grain reviews, scientific articles, and creative cross-domain discovery. Dynamic models capture topic birth, death, popularity, and evolution, while clustering and summarization improve scalability.

A second theme is social sensing and event intelligence. Twitter and geo-tagged streams support real-time detection, bursty-region discovery, event summarization, disaster response, sports monitoring, disease surveillance, and collective-action analysis. Related work addresses sentiment, tourism opinions, user interests, popularity and revisits, video longevity, and rumor veracity.

Typical methods include probabilistic generative models, neural networks and embeddings, character-level representations, active learning, ontology similarity with fuzzy logic, spatial and network algorithms, information extraction, and interactive visualization with provenance. Applications also include recommendation, semantic search, hypothesis generation, and optimal location queries.

Recent directions emphasize scalable and distributed processing, multimodal and heterogeneous evidence, near-real-time operation, richer temporal and spatial modeling, automated validation and ranking, and trustworthy analysis of misinformation and rare events.

e6d2d80bb2ebb94d96405e49183c78c836171d8a.text:
## Community Structure in Complex and Evolving Networks

This community focuses on discovering, evaluating, and exploiting community structure in complex networks. Major themes include the definition and quality assessment of communities, including multi-criteria and Pareto-based evaluation, overlapping and fuzzy modularity measures, and taxonomies of detection methods. Researchers address diverse structures: multilayer and multiplex networks, attributed graphs, weighted and directed relations, two-mode networks, core–periphery organization, and global bridges.

Typical methods span modularity optimization, label propagation (including stabilized LabelRank), clique percolation, density-based clustering with manifold learning, spectral and local diffusion techniques, personalized PageRank, generalized cores, and probabilistic or Bayesian latent-variable models. Optimization approaches include adaptive edge weighting and multi-objective evolutionary algorithms. Theoretical work uses random matrix theory, metastability, axiomatic modeling, and conductance analysis.

A strong recent trend is toward scalable, localized analysis for very large graphs, emphasizing seed-based communities, neighborhoods, and localized PageRank rather than whole-network computation. Other developments incorporate node attributes, multiple edge types, shared and layer-specific memberships, and temporal evolution. Applications examine bibliometric, web-service, social, wireless, and online interaction networks, including peer influence, churn, adoption, risk prediction, and social activity organization.

0e544fe67edbf5a12a02f2c4a3ce6450b3d85d9d.text:
**Bibliometric Mapping, Metrics, and Research Evaluation**

This community centers on scientometrics: mapping scientific and technological fields, measuring scholarly influence, and improving research evaluation. Major themes include citation, co-citation, author, journal, institutional, and country networks; technology relatedness and cognitive distance; research-front and knowledge-history reconstruction; and assessment of individuals, groups, journals, and universities.

Typical methods combine Web of Science, Scopus, Microsoft Academic, Dimensions, PubMed, and patent data with network analysis, community detection, clustering, fuzzy matching, overlays, text analytics, and visualization. Indicators include the h-index, K-index, PageRank, integrated impact measures, percentiles, field-normalized citation scores, fractional counting, Gini and diversity indices, and journal-impact alternatives. Reference Publication Year Spectroscopy (RPYS) and interactive tools such as RPYS i/o and CRExplorer trace historical roots and seminal works.

Recent work emphasizes comparing and validating databases, addressing field and journal biases, testing statistical and normalization assumptions, and developing fairer measures for large collaborations and individual contributions. Digital dissemination is weakening the link between journal impact factors and article citations, while national assessment exercises and rankings are increasingly scrutinized for unintended effects.

5b8b6241e998f2d3858ed1213ca8aee4a20879b3.text:
## Online Social Networks: Structure, Diffusion, and Risk

This community studies how online social networks form, evolve, and shape information, behavior, and risk. Major themes include influence and brokerage (centrality, weak and strong ties, malicious URLs), information cascades and virality, popularity and engagement prediction, and diffusion of products, rumors, and misinformation. Other recurring applications include anomaly detection, organizational security, demographic inference, suicide ideation, disaster response, financial guarantee networks, and scientific collaboration.

Typical methods combine graph-theoretic analysis—betweenness, modularity, community detection, homophily, segregation, and network vulnerability—with mathematical diffusion and adoption models, including threshold games, competing products, viral marketing, Hawkes processes, and models incorporating mass media or absent nodes. Empirical studies use large-scale Twitter, Facebook, YouTube, Yelp, scholarly, and transaction datasets. Machine-learning approaches include embeddings, multimodal content analysis, topic modeling, crowd-signal aggregation, ranking, and early trend prediction; visual analytics supports risk management.

Recent directions emphasize moving beyond static follower graphs toward temporal, heterogeneous, and multimodal networks; measuring engagement rather than views; detecting and mitigating fake or malicious content through crowds and fact checking; understanding content-agnostic drivers of popularity; and integrating external forces, user heterogeneity, and diversity into models of network assembly and diffusion.

49b22d4c0c19a4080c6d2c513af563ab41817d96.text:
## Data-Centric Retrieval, Learning, and Scalable Analytics

This community spans three closely related themes. First, it develops text and document intelligence: probabilistic and hierarchical topic models, clustering, supervised categorization, association-rule features, genetic feature selection, authorship analysis, and active learning for high-recall review. Feedback-driven clustering and sentence-level relevance assessment emphasize user goals, efficiency, and reduced annotation effort.

Second, it advances mathematical information access. Systems such as MIaS and WebMIaS combine keyword and formula retrieval, query expansion, result merging, formula canonicalization, and semantic enrichment. Related work builds repositories, identifier-definition extraction, namespace datasets, and accessible MathML rendering.

Third, the community studies scalable data systems and formal foundations. Accumulo, D4M, Graphulo, BigSparse, associative arrays, and Lara support high-throughput ingestion, graph processing, provenance storage, and unified array/database/key-value computation. BigDAWG addresses heterogeneous “polystore” execution, while relational lattices and relational semantics provide algebraic bases for query transformation.

Typical methods include probabilistic modeling, k-nearest-neighbor and k-medoids learning, regression, graph propagation, feedback control, reinforcement learning, cost-based optimization, and algebraic reformulation. Recent directions emphasize cloud cost and performance guarantees, adaptive workload management, external-memory analytics, unified data abstractions, automated quality estimation, and interactive, semantically enriched search.

da28b015a008f6b561f616aac8e8740a6732d8e6.text:
## Scholarly Impact, Discovery, and Digital Communication

This community examines how scholarly work is discovered, evaluated, disseminated, and connected across journals, books, repositories, social platforms, and digital libraries. Major themes include altmetrics and societal impact; relationships among citations, readership, downloads, tweets, and Mendeley saves; open-access and preprint citation advantages; book and publisher evaluation; and the reliability, heterogeneity, and dependencies of impact data.

Typical methods are large-scale bibliometric analyses using Web of Science, Scopus, Book Citation Index, F1000Prime, Altmetric, ADS, arXiv, Mendeley, Twitter, and library or download logs. Studies apply correlation, regression, principal-component and factor analysis, citation and readership distributions, comparative case studies, expert interviews, and qualitative reviews. Computational work includes machine learning for hyperlink classification, bibliographic-reference disambiguation, article and venue recommendation, visualization, and reviewer–paper matching through learned suitability scores and integer programming.

Recent directions emphasize broader and faster measures of impact beyond citations, while testing their validity against peer assessment and societal relevance. Research increasingly focuses on repositories, early online attention, open-access effects, and temporal dynamics. At the same time, recommender systems and automated classification address information overload and venue-selection challenges, alongside continued efforts to improve evaluation of books, publishers, conferences, and peer review.

ee9a0f986a5dfdb3376b085deb5189630d572bd7.text:
### Multilayer Social Networks and Evolving Online Communities

This community centers on modeling and analyzing online social systems as **multiplex or multilayer networks**, where users may share different social, semantic, professional, or platform-specific ties. Research examines multilayer degree centrality, reciprocity, clustering, link prediction, multiplexity, missing data, and unified models of online identity.

A second major theme is **community structure and evolution**. GED and SGCI identify group changes, while prediction models use historical evolution chains and classifiers to forecast future splits, merges, growth, and decline. Dynamic Louvain and Infomap methods improve scalability by updating only regions affected by graph changes.

Typical methods combine graph-theoretic measures, community detection, spectral analysis, independent-cascade simulations, branching processes, language models, topic modeling, sentiment classification, and statistical sampling. Applications include recommendations, influential-blogger detection, human resources, misinformation and fact checking, disease containment, information campaigns, and epidemic spreading.

Recent directions emphasize cross-platform online/offline analysis, multilayer diffusion and epidemic thresholds, seed selection for cascades, efficient dynamic clustering, and realistic synthetic network generation. Dataset construction—including cross-platform profiles, endorsements, and large Web or social-media collections—supports studies of privacy, identity, sampling bias, and robust network inference.

c839e615e39a90509a3d4532491770adfdf62fa5.text:
**Data Integration, Entity Resolution, and Human-Assisted Data Quality**

This community centers on integrating noisy, heterogeneous data into reliable, structured knowledge. Major themes include entity resolution and consolidation, record linkage, conflict resolution and truth discovery, Web/open-data extraction, and integrity verification. Work addresses both conventional and emerging settings: social networks, linked data, government addresses, uncertain databases, and spatial crowdsourcing.

Typical methods combine probabilistic models, source-reliability and dependence analysis, graph and multipartite matching, blocking and locality-sensitive hashing, deep representations, and generative models. Scalable string and vector similarity joins use partitioning, hashing, compression, and re-ranking. Data quality is further supported by automatically discovered functional, order, and ontology dependencies, syntactic patterns, and constraint-aware exchange. Several systems explicitly combine algorithms with human input, optimizing worker selection, task assignment, confidence guarantees, latency, and precision/recall.

Recent trends emphasize reducing expert effort and improving scalability: deep-learning-based entity resolution, collective matching across neighborhoods, billion-scale vector search, parallel processing, and adaptive linkage for difficult data. There is also growing attention to uncertainty beyond observed errors, including unknown data and multiple truths, as well as predictive spatial task assignment and interactive human-assisted search.

3a67c49151082dd5e5214ed6c571d6404d502e10.text:
### Social Media Communities, Misinformation, and Political Influence

This community studies online social networks as spaces for political communication, belief formation, inequality, and manipulation. Major themes include political community detection and polarization, echo chambers around conspiracy and scientific narratives, misinformation and fake news, extremist and pro-ISIS content, gender and race disparities, and platform or search bias. Several papers examine election campaigns, including U.S. primaries, the 2016 election, India’s 2014 election, and the 2018 midterms.

Typical methods combine large-scale data collection from Twitter, Facebook, YouTube, Gab, and search systems with network analysis, crawling, and temporal or propagation modeling. Machine-learning approaches include nonnegative matrix factorization, sparse learning, LDA with regression, convolutional neural networks, semi-supervised and real-time spam detection, stance classification, and metadata/network-based prediction. Surveys, experiments, browser logs, and user studies complement automated analysis. Systems such as Hoaxy and Twitter-list curation tools support monitoring and verification.

Recent work increasingly focuses on coordinated manipulation: bots, autogenerated tweets, crowdturfing, spear phishing, state-sponsored campaigns, and Sybil attacks. It also emphasizes intervention and resilience, including targeted health bots, decentralized search, credibility assessment, bias measurement, and defenses against malicious activity.

4b8606dc6b854300c4e4b484f65294ebbbd0780d.text:
### Recommender Systems: From Collaborative Filtering to Robust, Multimodal Personalization

This community centers on personalized recommendation across products, media, news, education, tagging, and events. Core themes include collaborative filtering from explicit and implicit feedback, personalized ranking, sequential and session-based prediction, and integration of heterogeneous signals such as content, social links, geography, and item relationships. Long-tail discovery, cold-start users/items, diverse user tastes, explainability, and filter bubbles are recurring concerns.

Typical methods range from slope-one predictors, nearest-neighbor and graph/network algorithms, matrix and collective factorization, co-clustering, Markov chains, and Bayesian Personalized Ranking to neural models including autoencoders, variational models, autoregressive networks, recurrent networks, factorization machines, and DeepFM. Context trees, latent semantic analysis, topic modeling, word embeddings, and multimodal textual, auditory, and visual features support content-aware recommendations.

Recent directions emphasize nonlinear and deep representations, inter-session modeling, mixtures of user tastes, missing-modality learning, and combining multiple heterogeneous relationships. Work also increasingly addresses reliability and security through rating centrality, reputation estimation, shilling detection, and adversarial fake-user attacks, while preserving scalability, interpretability, and real-time cold-start performance.

bfd4b7589169179d29db2b1c58f7dde6522345a5.text:
**Network Intelligence for Dynamic, Heterogeneous, and Social Graphs**

This community studies methods for representing, inferring, sampling, and mining complex networks. Major themes include dynamic and temporal graphs, heterogeneous and multilayer social networks, knowledge-graph reasoning, community detection, link prediction, anomaly and fraud detection, and structural analysis of real-world networks. Several works address signed, uncertain, bipartite, and affiliation networks, as well as diffusion through indirect co-location links.

Typical methods combine statistical modeling, machine learning, and graph algorithms. Examples include dynamic stochastic blockmodels, temporal event graphs, random walks and absorbing Markov chains, maximum-likelihood community inference, min-cut methods, dense-subgraph peeling, and convexity analysis. Representation learning is prominent, including deep graph clustering, multi-relational embeddings, semantic entity normalization, and temporally robust graph representations. Applications use random forests, neural networks, ensemble scoring, path-based fact checking, and behavioral profiling for fraud, privacy, insider trading, and team recommendation.
